ranges.en: Offerings slaughtered for a different purpose remain fit but do not discharge the owner's obligation.
The exception: Paschal and sin offerings are treated differently when slaughtered not for their sake.
Paschal offering is unfit only at its appointed time; sin offering is unfit at any time.
Rabbi Eliezer adds the guilt offering to the sin offering's rule, applying it at all times.
Rabbi Eliezer's argument by analogy: the guilt offering is like the sin offering, so both are unfit if misdirected.
Yosei ben Honi extends unfitness to any offering slaughtered for the sake of a Paschal or sin offering.
Shimon sets the rule by sanctity: a higher-sanctity purpose makes an offering fit, a lower one makes it unfit.
Illustration: most-sacred offerings slaughtered for lesser ones are unfit.
Illustration: lesser offerings slaughtered for most-sacred ones are fit.
Firstborn and tithe animals slaughtered for a peace offering are fit.
Peace offerings slaughtered for a firstborn or tithe animal are unfit.
Why teach the rule with the word but, instead of the simpler and not, if the meaning is the same?
The word adds that these offerings keep their sanctity, so the rites must still be done with proper intent.
Rava's ruling: sprinkling blood of a burnt offering slaughtered not for its sake is still prohibited.
The Gemara offers two ways to support Rava: a logical argument or a verse.
Logical support: one deviation in slaughter does not justify deviating in all later rites.
Scriptural support: Deuteronomy 23:24 read to mean a voluntary gift must be fulfilled as vowed.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse calls the offering a vow, and says it counts as a vow offering only if fulfilled properly; otherwise it is a freewill gift.
Is it permitted to deviate from protocol in a freewill offering from the outset? Clearly not, even if one rite was misdirected.
Ravina tells Rav Pappa that Rava raised a contradiction between two superior mishnaic statements and resolved it.
What exactly are these superior statements that Rava resolved?
The mishna: offerings slaughtered not for their sake are fit but do not satisfy the owner's obligation.
Rava infers that slaughter without specified intent counts as slaughter for its sake, since the mishna states only not for its sake.
A contradiction from a mishna on divorce: a bill written not for the woman is invalid, and so is one written without specification.
Rava resolves it: offerings are designated for their sake, while a wife is not designated for divorce, so the cases differ.
From where do we derive that unspecified slaughter is fit and satisfies the owner's obligation?
Proposed source: the mishna saying all offerings slaughtered not for their sake are fit but do not satisfy the obligation.
The mishna's wording does not prove the point, since its divorce parallel uses the same phrasing for an invalid case.
Rather, derive the halakha from another mishna.
The mishna's example: offerings slaughtered for their sake and then not for their sake, such as Paschal and peace offerings.
Inference: one who specified Paschal then peace is unfit, so one who specified Paschal then nothing is fit, meaning unspecified equals specified.
Perhaps there it is different: one who initially stated proper intent is presumed to keep it, unlike here.
The latter clause of the mishna: offerings slaughtered not for their sake and then for their sake, such as peace then Paschal.
Inference: unspecified then Paschal is fit, so unspecified slaughter still satisfies the owner's obligation.
Perhaps there it is different: the ultimate intent proves the original intent, while here no ultimate intent is stated.
Alternatively, the mishna uses parallel wording for symmetry, so it proves nothing about unspecified slaughter.
Rather, derive the halakha from a different mishna listing purposes of slaughter.
The mishna lists six purposes for slaughter, and says sin and guilt offerings are slaughtered for atonement of the sin.
Rabbi Yosei says even one with no intent for any of these purposes is fit.
Explanation: the court stipulated that one should not specify intent at all, lest he slaughter it not for its sake.
If unspecified slaughter were unfit, the court would not have stipulated a matter that disqualifies the offering, so it must be fit.
From where do we derive that a bill of divorce written without specifying the woman is invalid?
Proposed source: the mishna about a man who hears scribes dictating a divorce bill and claims it for his own wife.
Perhaps the mishna concerns scribes practicing drafts, not written for divorce, so it proves nothing about unspecified bills.
Rather, derive it from the subsequent clause of that mishna.

ranges.en: A bill of divorce written for one husband and wife is unfit for another man with an identically named wife and town.
Perhaps there it is different: that bill was designated specifically for the first man's divorce, so unspecified bills may still be valid.
Derived from the next clause: with two identically named wives, a bill written for the elder cannot divorce the younger, so specificity is required.
Perhaps there it is different: that bill was specifically designated for the other wife's divorce.
Derived from the next clause: a bill written for one of two identically named wives is unfit for either, so it must name a specific woman.
Perhaps there it is different: a designation cannot be made retroactively, so an unspecified bill may still be valid.
Derived from a Gittin mishna on pre-written bills: the scribe leaves the name blanks and the permission phrase, showing a bill must be written for a specific couple.
Rava raises another contradiction: a sin offering slaughtered for a burnt offering is unfit, but one slaughtered for non-sacred meat is fit.
Rava raises a contradiction from the Gittin mishna: a bill written for a gentile woman, by inference, must also be invalid.
Rava resolves it: a bill for a gentile woman is unspecified once that intent is removed, while removing non-sacred intent leaves sacrificial animals fit.
Rava raises another contradiction on the same sin offering case, with the same inference about intent of a different type.
A baraita on impurity: a vessel of a different type inside an earthenware vessel still protects the food inside, contrary to the claimed view.
Rava resolves it: a rinsed vessel is of the same type as earthenware, while non-sacred intent is like a partition that does not count as a vessel.
Mishna on an oven divided by boards or curtains: a creeping animal carcass on one side renders all the food impure, showing partitions are ineffective here.
Mishna on a broken barrel plugged with straw: it is not a vessel, so it blocks no impurity, and Rabbi Eliezer deems the food in it pure.
Rabbi Eliezer's a fortiori argument: a barrel protects food from corpse impurity, so a barrel should also protect from creeping-animal impurity.
The Rabbis reply that Rabbi Eliezer's inference is not correct.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restating the a fortiori argument: a partition protects against tent impurity, so it should protect food inside an earthenware vessel too.
How can Rabbi Eliezer hold a partition effective in an oven when an item is not affected by something not of its type?
Rabbi Eliezer accepts the principle but holds that his a fortiori inference overrides it in this case.
If an a fortiori inference overrides the principle, the same reasoning should apply to a sin offering slaughtered for non-sacred meat.
The reasoning of Rav follows Rabbi Elazar, not the a fortiori argument, so non-sacred intent does not desecrate sacred items.
Rabbi Elazar cites Leviticus 22:15, which limits desecration to improper intent for sacred purposes, so an inference from a verse can override an a fortiori argument.
If a verse can override an a fortiori argument, the verse about earthen vessels should rule out Rabbi Eliezer's inference about ovens.
The verse is needed for food kneaded in clay inside an impure oven, which must still become impure.
How do the Rabbis, who read the verse as making partitions ineffective, derive the case of clay-covered food in an impure oven?
Rav Yosef bar Ami introduces a contradiction between two of Rav's rulings on deviation in slaughter.
Rav's ruling that a sin offering slaughtered for a burnt offering is unfit suggests improper intent not of its type does not ruin it.
Rav's ruling on a sin offering slaughtered for a non-owner who needs a burnt offering contradicts that, since improper intent not of its type does not ruin it.
The verses resolve it: the sin offering type is written for the sin offering, while the owner phrase applies only to the offering's own owner.
Rav Haviva raises a contradiction between Rav's owner-deviation ruling and the baraita on the interior of its interior.
Rav's ruling on a sin offering slaughtered for another sin offerer suggests improper intent of the same type ruins it, not one of a different type.
A baraita: a rinsed vessel inside an earthenware vessel protects food, so something not of its type can block impurity in the airspace.
Rav Haviva resolves it: the word tokho appears four times, one instance teaching the basic rule and another a verbal analogy.
The verse's two instances show an earthenware vessel renders food impure, while a vessel of another type can block that, derived from a context unrelated to slaughter.

ranges.en: From where do we derive that slaughter must be performed for the sake of the offering?
Perhaps 'sacrifice of peace offerings' is only the name of the offering type and says nothing about the slaughterer's intent.
Other verses use the blood-offering phrasing without the word sacrifice, so this verse's wording must teach that slaughter is for the sake of peace offerings.
Slaughter requires intent for its sake, but from where do the other rites require it?
Deriving the other rites from slaughter fails, since slaughter alone is disqualified for a Paschal offering by intent for non-eaters.
The verse 'who sacrifices the blood' refers to collecting the blood, which must be done for the sake of a peace offering.
The Merciful One should have written the rule about collecting the blood alone, and it would then extend to slaughter.
Collection is unique in requiring a priest and a woman be excluded, so its rules cannot be transferred to slaughter.
Slaughter and collection require intent; from where do we derive that sprinkling does too?
Slaughter and collection are unique in location and in inner sin offerings, so their rules cannot transfer to sprinkling.
The verse 'who sprinkles the blood of the peace offering' teaches that sprinkling must be done for the sake of a peace offering.
The Merciful One should have written the rule only for sprinkling, and it would then extend to slaughter and collection.
Sprinkling is unique in that a non-priest performing it is liable to death at Heaven's hand, so its rules do not transfer.
The rule covers the other rites but not conveying the blood to the altar; from where is that rite derived?
Conveying the blood is dispensable, unlike the other rites, so their requirements cannot transfer to it.
Verses 'vehikriv' refer to conveying the limbs and to collecting blood, so conveying is included in the same language and rules.
From where do we derive the rule that an offering must be slaughtered for its owner?
Rav Pinhas derives owner-intent from the thanksgiving verse's meat of the sacrifice, since its type-intent source is already elsewhere.
That verse is needed for a baraita about a thanks offering slaughtered for a peace offering, so it does not teach owner-intent.
The superfluous word sacrifice teaches owner-intent, while the phrase peace offering teaches the baraita's ruling.
The word sacrifice is still needed for another midrash on eating sin and guilt offerings within the thanksgiving time limit.
If the word sacrifice did only that, the verse would be worded differently, so it must carry two lessons.
Slaughter must be for the owner's sake; from where do we derive that the other rites must be too?
Slaughter is unique in that intent for non-eaters disqualifies a Paschal offering, while other rites are not similarly disqualified.
Both slaughter terms are stated for type-deviation and owner-deviation, so the same non-differentiation between slaughter and other rites applies.
Type-deviation differs from owner-deviation in four ways: it affects the offering's essence, all four rites, the heir's offering, and communal offerings.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Two of the earlier distinctions are not strictly precise, but the other two are exact enough to base a distinction on.
What is different about deviation regarding the owner, such that it does not disqualify the offering itself?
Both are merely changes of intent; so if type-deviation disqualifies by intent, owner-deviation should too, and the distinction fails.
Rav Pineḥas holds owner-deviation applies after the owner dies, erasing one distinction, though two others remain available.
Rav Ashi derives from the verse that sprinkling must be done for the owner specifically, atoning for him and not for another.
The verse may instead teach Rabbi Shimon's ruling about an animal set aside after a personal obligation, so it is not needed for this halakha.
Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi explains Rabbi Shimon's distinction: a personal obligation is like a load on one's shoulders until discharged.
Rav Ashi replies that the derivation rests on the phrase for him in and accepted for him, not on the word alav the baraita uses.
We have a source for slaughter and sprinkling requiring the owner's intent; from where do we derive it for collecting the blood?
Slaughter and sprinkling are unique in that they carry death at Heaven's hand for performing them outside the Temple, so they cannot transfer.
Rav Ashi derives collecting-blood owner-intent from the nazirite ram verse, which is needed only for type-deviation if it is read from elsewhere.
Rav Aha bar Abba objects to Rava: a generalization followed by a detail includes only what the detail specifies, so only slaughter is covered.
Rava answers that the verse's phrase is an incomplete generalization, and the principle does not apply to incomplete generalizations, so the derivation stands for rites beyond slaughter.
Ravina offers a different answer: the principle does apply to such verses, and the added term unto the Lord creates a full generalization.
Rav Aha of Difti objects that the two generalizations differ: the second includes any sacrificial duty, including pouring and burning the portions.
Ravina replies that the school of Rabbi Yishmael uses generalizations and details this way, and that the verse includes only items like slaughter.
Alternative derivation: include any essential rite whose outside performance is punished by death, so collection is excluded and sprinkling included.
Another alternative: include rites performed in the north and in inner sin offerings, so slaughter and collection are included but sprinkling is not.
Both alternatives are equally valid, so either collection or sprinkling may be included, and both are treated equally.
Alternatively, sprinkling is derived from the verse Rav Ashi cited, so the verse about the ram refers to collection.
We have a source for a nazirite ram requiring owner-intent; from where do we derive it for other peace offerings?
A nazirite ram is unique because a nazirite must bring other blood offerings with it, so it cannot be the basis for all peace offerings.
If so, the verse would say simply peace offerings; writing the plural peace offerings includes all types of peace offerings.
A peace offering must be sacrificed for its own sake and its owner's; from where do we derive this for all other offerings?
A peace offering is unique in having hand-laying, libations, and breast and leg waving, so no other offering shares all three.
The verse listing all offerings alongside peace offerings shows every offering requires both kinds of intent, as peace offerings do.
Why not say that a rite done not for its sake disqualifies the offering, given the mishna's ruling that such offerings remain fit?
The verse on what goes from your lips shows a vow offering not sacrificed properly remains a valid freewill offering, and both verses are needed to teach this.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks what purpose the verse this is the law serves.
Without the second verse, one would conclude that offerings slaughtered not for their sake are disqualified.
The verse that which went out of your lips teaches that such offerings are accepted.
Reish Lakish asks: if these offerings are fit, why do they not propitiate, and if they do not propitiate, why are they brought?
Rabbi Elazar responds that posthumous offerings are fit yet do not propitiate, as a precedent.
A mishna about a woman after childbirth shows a burnt offering is brought even when it does not satisfy its owner.
Reish Lakish concedes the burnt offering point but asks where a guilt offering is derived in the same way.
Rabbi Elazar replies that the mishna itself includes Rabbi Eliezer's view that a guilt offering is unfit when slaughtered not for its sake.
Reish Lakish rejects this, saying the mishna's first tanna is the accepted halakha and Rabbi Eliezer cannot resolve his difficulty.
Reish Lakish offers his own solution, deriving from the verse about vows and gift offerings.
Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Yitzhak bar Abba and Abaye are sitting and discussing the matter.
They object that Reish Lakish's verse can only cover vows and gifts, leaving guilt offerings unexplained.
Abaye explains that Reish Lakish actually derived his solution from a different source.
The verse about slaughtering a sin offering for its sake shows an offering slaughtered not for its sake is unfit.
From this, other offerings slaughtered not for their sake are fit, and one might think they propitiate.
The verse that which went out of your lips teaches that such offerings do not propitiate.
Zeira and Yitzhak ask why only vows and gifts should be excluded, and not guilt offerings too.
Abaye rejects the claim that a guilt offering propitiates when slaughtered not for its sake.
Abaye uses an a fortiori inference from the burnt offering to show a guilt offering does not propitiate.
The Gemara challenges the inference: a burnt offering is totally consumed on the altar, unlike a guilt offering.
A peace offering, not totally consumed, still fails to satisfy its owner when slaughtered not for its sake.
The Gemara objects that a peace offering is unique in requiring libations and the breast and thigh waving.
A burnt offering can prove the point since those stringencies do not apply to it, so the inference returns to its start.
The halakha is derived from the shared element of burnt and peace offerings, so a guilt offering is included as well.
The Gemara objects that the shared element is communal offerings, which guilt offerings are not.
A thanks offering proves the point: it is not communal, yet slaughtered not for its sake it does not satisfy its owner.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks what is unique about a thanks offering, which requires an accompanying bread offering.
Burnt and peace offerings can prove the point, since no bread accompanies them, so the inference returns to its start.
The halakha is derived from the shared element of these offerings, so a guilt offering is included as well.
The Gemara objects that the shared element is that these are vow or gift offerings, unlike a guilt offering.
Rava derives from the verse listing offering types that a guilt offering is juxtaposed with a peace offering.
Why compare a guilt offering to a peace offering rather than to a sin offering, which is disqualified?
The verse about slaughtering a sin offering excludes all other offerings from the sin offering halakha.
A mnemonic is given to identify the amoraim in the following discussions.
Rav Huna and Rav Naḥman discuss with Rav Sheshet the difficulty Reish Lakish raised about guilt offerings.
They suggest Rabbi Elazar could reply that a guilt offering also comes after its owner's death, through its sale proceeds.
Rav Sheshet refutes this: only the remainder of a guilt offering is sacrificed later, which is like a sin offering.
Rav Huna and Rav Naḥman explain from a verse that a sin offering slaughtered not for its sake is wholly disqualified.
Why is a guilt offering not disqualified, when a verse also says it is a guilt offering?
That verse concerns the stage after burning the sacrificial portions, which is fit even if they were burned not for its sake.
Why is the phrase it is a guilt offering needed at all, if the previous answer already resolves the matter?
Rav Huna cites Rav: an unassigned guilt offering consigned to grazing is fit as a burnt offering if slaughtered unspecified.
Only a consigned guilt offering is fit that way, because the verse says it remains a guilt offering unless the court assigns it otherwise.
Rav Naḥman, Rav Sheshet and Rav Adda bar Mattana discuss Rabbi Elazar's precedent of posthumous offerings.
Why did Reish Lakish not argue that these posthumous offerings should also propitiate for the heirs?
Rav Adda bar Mattana replies that a woman's offering cannot propitiate after her death, since her children did not give birth.
Rav Asi objects that a woman's post-childbirth offering atones for other violations, so heirs could atone through it too.
Does this mean the heirs acquire the offering, which is why it atones for them?
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that a meal offering left to two sons is not a partnership offering, so the heirs do not acquire it.
Is the offering then not acquired by the heirs at all?
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that an animal left to two sons cannot be substituted, which he attributes to their being partners.
If the heirs acquire the offering, why can they not substitute another animal, given the partnership reasoning?

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If partners cannot substitute for an offering, then heirs of a deceased owner should not be able to either, unless the offering was acquired by them.
The verse's superfluous word includes the heir, but its singular form means only one heir can substitute, not two.
Rav Ya'akov of Nehar Pekod objects that the same reasoning would apply to redeeming second tithe, where partners must add a fifth.
Tithe redemption differs because the father could redeem it in partnership while alive, whereas offering substitution cannot be done by partners.
Rav Asi argues from the halakha that two heirs cannot substitute that the heirs must acquire the offering, since one heir can substitute.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule about consecrating an animal for another's atonement and about teruma is cited to show the heir acquires the offering.
A dilemma: after offerings slaughtered not for their sake are sacrificed, did they atone for the sins they were brought for?
Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, holds they did not atone, since otherwise a second offering would be unnecessary.
The Gemara challenges Rav Sheshet: if they did not atone, why is the first offering sacrificed, and Rav Ashi explains the difficulty.
A dilemma: does a burnt offering atone for positive mitzva violations committed after the animal was designated?
Should the burnt offering be treated like a sin offering, which atones only for sins committed before designation?
Perhaps a burnt offering differs from a sin offering, since it atones even for several violations, so it may atone for later ones too.
A baraita on placing hands on the burnt offering is cited as proof about atonement for violations after designation.
Does the baraita's final clause mean the offering does not atone for a violation committed after designation?
Rava replies that placing hands is a mitzva whose violation occurs only after slaughter, so it is not a case of post-designation atonement.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda proposes that the baraita means the offering atoned for the person, challenging Rava's reading.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An offering that does not atone before Heaven is not accepted by God as a perfect offering.
A mishna on the leper's oil: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri holds it atoned even without placement, though the verse faults the leper as if it did not atone.
What is the meaning of the phrase as though it did not atone for him?
It atoned for the person but not before Heaven, so the offering may atone for a transgression even without proper placement of hands.
The Gemara rejects this: in the leper case the oil atoned for one matter but not another, so no such inference follows.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon asks what sin the communal peace offerings of Shavuot atone for.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: the two lambs are peace offerings, so the question should concern the goats sacrificed as sin offerings.
Rabbi Shimon answers that the goats atone for defilement of the Temple or its sacrificial foods by impure persons.
The second goat atones for impurity arising between the two sacrifices, showing the verse spared the people from constant sacrifice.
The Gemara infers that a violation after designation is atoned for, since both goats were designated in advance.
The inference fails if the goats were designated sequentially, since impurity may have arisen between their designations.
The Gemara challenges this: the verse mandating the two sin offerings does not specify sequential designation.
Rav Pappa replies that communal offerings differ, as the court makes a non-verbal stipulation designating the second goat at sacrifice.
Rav Yosef, son of Rav Shmuel, asks whether Rabbi Shimon accepts that the court can stipulate about communal offerings.
Rav Idi bar Avin cites Rabbi Yoḥanan on daily offerings that were not needed for the public as a source.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon forbids redeeming unblemished communal animals, while the Rabbis permit it since they are not yet consecrated.
Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira about the Shavuot goats, showing an offering atones for violations after its designation.
Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma concerned violations after slaughter, implying he took atonement for post-designation violations as obvious.
The Gemara rejects that inference: his dilemma may have covered post-designation violations too, so nothing follows.
Rabba holds a thanks offering slaughtered for another's thanks offering is fit, while Rav Ḥisda holds it is unfit.
A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer that a thanks offering slaughtered for a peace offering is fit, but not the reverse, since thanks offerings are called peace offerings.
Rabba's baraita seems to refer to another's thanks offering, so why is a thanks offering slaughtered for another's thanks offering fit?
The baraita refers to the owner's own separate thanks offering, given for a different deliverance.
If slaughtered for another's thanks offering is unfit, why does the baraita teach the peace offering case instead of the thanks offering case?
The peace offering case had to be stated, since one might think a peace offering counts as a thanks offering, so it is fit.
Rava rules a sin offering slaughtered for another sin offering is fit, but slaughtered for a burnt offering is unfit.
What is the reason for this distinction?
The verse says slaughter it for a sin offering, so the sin offering must be slaughtered for a sin offering to be fit.
Rava rules a sin offering slaughtered for a person obligated to a burnt offering is fit, but for a person obligated to a sin offering is unfit.
What is the reason for this second distinction?
The verse says he shall be forgiven, so the offering must atone for the owner, and only someone similarly obligated to a sin offering is excluded.
Rava rules a sin offering slaughtered for someone with no obligation is unfit, since every Jew has some obligation to bring an offering.
Rava argues by a fortiori that a sin offering atones for those liable for failing positive mitzvot, since it atones for severe transgressions.
Does this mean the violation of a positive mitzva is the same type as sins atoned for by a sin offering?
The Gemara cites Rava's own ruling that a sin offering slaughtered for a burnt-offering obligee is fit, suggesting different atonement types.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A sin offering atones for a positive mitzva violation only incidentally, since prohibitions and positive mitzvot are different types.
Rava holds that sprinkling the blood of a burnt offering slaughtered not for its sake is still prohibited.
Rava supports this with a verse about fulfilling vows, or alternatively with a logical argument from the chapter's opening.
Rava holds that a burnt offering brought by heirs is disqualified if slaughtered for another type, but fit if slaughtered for another person.
Rav Pineḥas, son of Rav Ami, holds that an offering has an owner after death, namely the heir, so the wrong owner disqualifies it.
Rav Ashi asks whether Rav Pineḥas means this literally or only that the heir's offering atones for his several violations.
Rav Pineḥas clarifies that he means literally that the heir is the owner, and must bring another offering if slaughtered for someone else.
Rava holds a burnt offering is a gift to God and not primarily for atonement.
Rava cites Proverbs on the wicked sacrifice and a baraita on forgiveness before moving to show the burnt offering is a gift.
A mnemonic is given for Rava's series of statements: a sin offering atones, a burnt offering is a gift.
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon, who says the same about the purpose of the sin offering being brought before the burnt offering.
Why is the sin offering brought at all, if its purpose is not atonement, since it is brought to atone for transgression?
Rabbi Shimon likens the sin offering to an advocate who enters before the king to win a pardon, with the gift brought after.
The mishna teaches that all offerings are fit if slaughtered not for their sake, except the Paschal and sin offerings.
From where do we derive that a Paschal offering must be slaughtered for its sake?
The verse about observing the spring month and offering the Paschal offering teaches that all its rites must be done for its sake.
We have a source for deviation of offering type, but where is deviation regarding the owner derived?
The verse saying it is the sacrifice of the Lord's Passover teaches slaughter must be for the Paschal offering, applying the same to the owner.
We have a source for the Paschal offering's sake and owner's sake, but where is the disqualifying force of these intentions derived?
The repeated command to sacrifice the Paschal offering shows both intentions are indispensable to the sacrificial process.
Rav Safra objects that the verse about sacrificing is needed for Rav Naḥman's ruling, so it cannot be the source here.
Rav Naḥman holds that a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering afterward.
Rav Naḥman derives this from the verse mentioning both flock and herd, since Paschal offerings are otherwise only lambs or goats.
Rav Safra gives a revised exposition: each verse teaches a distinct halakha, and both intentions are indispensable to the Paschal offering.
If slaughter requires proper intent for the Paschal offering, where is it derived that other rites also require it?
Rav Ashi rejects inferring other rites from slaughter, since the Torah stated the halakha only for slaughter.
Rav Ashi derives it from the verse on the law of all offerings, which requires each to be sacrificed for its own sake.
A baraita reads the verse about offerings to include the firstborn, the animal tithe and the Paschal offering.
The juxtaposition with the peace offering teaches that all these offerings require proper intent, with the mitzva ab initio derived from it.
Just as a peace offering does not separate slaughter from other rites for proper intent, the Paschal offering should not either.
Since the Paschal offering derives from the peace offering, why is it necessary to write the phrase it is in Exodus?
The phrase it is teaches that intent is indispensable only for the Paschal offering at slaughter, not for a guilt offering after burning.
From where do we derive that a sin offering slaughtered for the wrong offering or owner is disqualified?
The verse saying slaughter it for a sin offering teaches that slaughter must be performed for the sake of a sin offering.
We have a source for slaughter; from where is the same requirement derived for the collection of blood?

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse about the priest taking blood of the sin offering teaches that its collection must be done for the sake of a sin offering.
We have a source for slaughter and collection being for the sake of a sin offering; where is sprinkling derived?
The verse on atonement by the priest for the sin offering teaches that the atonement, done by sprinkling, must be for its sake.
We have a source for deviation of offering type; where is deviation regarding the owner derived?
The verse says he makes atonement for him, not for another, so intent must be for the owner.
We have a source for the mitzva of sprinkling for the owner ab initio; where is its indispensability derived?
Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, derives it from the nazirite's sin offering, which the verse calls his sin offering.
Where is it derived that all rites require intent for the offering's type, and all rites other than sprinkling require intent for the owner?
Rabbi Yona derives it from the nazirite's sin offering, where the verse says all its actions must be for the sake of a sin offering.
Where is it derived that intent for the owner is indispensable in rites other than sprinkling, once type intent is known to be indispensable?
Rav Huna repeats that the nazirite's verse says his sin offering, which implies the offering is sacrificed for the owner's sake.
Ravina objects: the same logic would apply to the burnt offering, which is also described as his burnt offering.
If Ravina's view holds, what is derived from the verses on the meal offering and libation of the nazirite?
Those phrases teach that meal offerings and libations may be brought at night or the next day, so the burnt offering question remains open.
Further objection: sin offerings for different transgressions cannot be derived from one another, given their different stringencies.
Rava derives these halakhot from the leper's sin offering, where the verse says all its actions must be for the sake of a sin offering.
We have a source for type intent in the sin offering; from where is owner intent derived as indispensable?
The verse about atoning for the one purified teaches the sin offering must be for this person, not another.
Can the halakhot of the three sin offerings be derived from one another, given their differing features?
One halakha can be derived from the other two together, and the third case is apparently extraneous, teaching indispensable intent.
Which of the three sin offerings should the Torah not have written this halakha for?
Each option is refuted, since each of the other two sin offerings has a distinct feature that the excluded one lacks.
The verse juxtaposing the sin offering with the peace offering shows intent for its sake is a mitzva ab initio, while the other verses make it indispensable.
We have sources for these halakhot with regard to the sin offering for eating forbidden fat and the others; does the verse for the fat sin offering also teach them?

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: From where are these halakhot derived for idolatry and the other sin offerings that lack the phrase for a sin offering?
Idolatry is derived from the sin offering for forbidden fat, since both are punishable by karet, and the others from the three common sources.
A baraita teaches that a Paschal offering is fit if slaughtered for its sake at its time, but a Paschal offering of other days is fit if not for its sake.
A mnemonic is given for the names of the amoraim mentioned in this discussion.
From where are these matters derived, that a Paschal offering sacrificed in other seasons is fit if not for its sake?
Shmuel's father derives it from the verse on a peace offering from the flock, which the Paschal offering meets.
Rabbi Ila cites Rabbi Yoḥanan that the redundant for a sacrifice includes any offering, which challenges the derivation as limited to peace offerings.
If so, should a Paschal offering be rendered whatever offering it is slaughtered for, such as a burnt offering?
Had the verse said peace offerings and a sacrifice, that would follow; since it says a sacrifice of peace offerings, it restricts the result to peace offerings.
The verse may be a generalization and a detail, limiting the generalization to the specified peace offering.
The phrase unto the Lord is a second generalization, so the verse has a generalization, detail, and generalization.
Rav Ya'akov of Nehar Pekod objects that the second generalization is broader, so bird and meal offerings should also suffice.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael applies generalizations and details even in cases like this, so the objection does not hold.
Since the verse is generalization, detail, generalization, it covers only items similar to the detail, namely a peace offering not slaughtered for its sake.
If only items similar to the detail count, why not limit the Paschal rule to vow and gift offerings like peace offerings?
Instead, the verse should be read as an amplification, so any offering for which the Paschal offering is slaughtered is fit.
If it is an amplification, the Paschal offering should be rendered any offering, so why does Shmuel's father specify a peace offering?
Rabbi Avin's statement begins here and is cut off at the end of the daf.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Offerings that are eaten may be diverted to become other eaten offerings, but not uneaten ones.
Does this imply sin and guilt offerings are not eaten, making the diversion rule puzzling?
Emended answer: the rule concerns offerings eaten by every person, not offerings eaten only by priests.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin gives a different answer based on offerings of lesser sanctity.
Objection: a Paschal offering slaughtered for animal tithe should become a tithe, with practical consequences for libations and sale.
A verse says the tenth animal is sacred, so only that animal is a tithe and no other.
Objection: the same logic applies to firstborn designation, with consequences for libations and priestly gifts.
Reply: firstborn status is excluded by verbal analogy with the passing language of the animal tithe.
Objection: the same logic applies to substitution, with prohibitions on sale and redemption at stake.
A verse on substitution shows only the animal substituted is a substitute, not others.
Objection: the same logic applies to thanks offerings, which would then require forty loaves of bread.
Rhetorical refutation: no parallel exists where a Paschal offering needs no bread but its leftover does.
Objection: the parallel with libations raises the same problem, since leftovers would then require libations.
Refutation: a thanks offering itself needs no bread, yet its leftover does, so no parallel case exists.
Objection by Rav Yeimar: the verse could refer to a leftover guilt offering, which is also brought only from the flock.
Rava's proof: min in the verse includes both sheep and goats, unlike the guilt offering which is only rams.
Objection: min usually excludes, so the verse should refer to the guilt offering, limited to certain species.
Rabbi Mani: min also excludes here, since a Paschal offering excludes a second-year animal and females.
Objection by Rav Hana: subsequent verses about lamb and goat show the passage is not about a leftover Paschal offering.
Reply: those verses are needed for a baraita teaching that the tail rite applies to the Paschal offering.
Baraita: lamb includes old Paschal offerings in all peace-offering laws, while goat excludes the tail rite.
Objection: asks whether the peace-offering status of an old Paschal offering is derived from the verse Shmuel's father cites.
Reply: even without that baraita, the status is derived from Rav Nachman's teaching of Rabba bar Avuh.
From where is it derived that a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering?
Deuteronomy says to sacrifice the Passover offering from the flock and herd, indicating a second source.
Objection: a Paschal offering is brought only from lambs and goats, so why does the verse mention the herd?
The herd mention teaches that a leftover Paschal offering is brought from both flock and herd, as a peace offering.
What is the status of the leftover Paschal offering?
None of the derivations is superfluous, since three verses teach the peace-offering status of leftover Paschal offerings.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Three verses each teach a different case of a Paschal offering whose time or first year has passed, or neither.
Each verse is needed, since one alone would leave the other cases unresolved.
Continuing the explanation: all three verses are required to cover every case of rejected Paschal offerings.
Rav, citing Mavog: a sin offering slaughtered for Nahshon's sin offering is fit, since one law governs all sin offerings.
Narration: Rava sat and taught Mavog's halakha before it was challenged.
Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Shimon says meal offerings slaughtered with wrong intent still count, unlike animal offerings.
Baraita's reasoning: meal offering preparation reveals its true type, while slaughter, blood collection and sprinkling are uniform for animal offerings.
Rav Mesharshiyya's inference: meal offerings are valid because their preparation proves their nature.
Objection: why not derive from the meal offering verse that all meal offerings share one law regardless of preparation?
Restated: Mavog's ruling is that a sin offering slaughtered on condition Nahshon be atoned is fit, since the dead cannot be atoned.
Objection: why mention Nahshon at all? Let the ruling refer to a dead person in general.
The reason is death: sin offerings for the living, such as nazirite or leper offerings, are unfit.
Counter: nazirite and leper sin offerings are equivalent to burnt offerings, so deviation does not disqualify.
Restated: fit when slaughtered for one obligated to bring a Nahshon-type offering, since that offering is a burnt offering.
Alternative version: some say the Nahshon-type sin offering is unfit, since it is equivalent to a burnt offering.
Objection: why cite Nahshon's offering, which cannot be brought at all? Let it cite nazirite or leper offerings.
The primary individual sin offering is cited, since it is the first such offering recorded in Scripture.
Rav's ruling: fat-sin offerings slaughtered for blood or idolatry sin offerings are fit, but nazirite and leper ones are unfit.
Dilemma: if slaughtered for a Temple-defilement offering, is it fit as karet-level like fat, or unfit as sliding-scale?
Rav Aha teaches Rav's ruling as unfit in all cases, derived from the verse requiring slaughter for that sin offering alone.
Objection by Rav Ashi: how can Rava's dilemma assume fitness for other sin offerings under this version of Rav's ruling?
Reply: Rava's dilemma concerns deviation regarding the owner rather than the type, and is taught that way.
Rava's ruling on owner deviation: a fat offering for another obligated owner is unfit, but for nazirite or leper owners it is fit.
Dilemma on owner deviation: is a fat offering for a Temple-defilement owner unfit, or fit as a non-set offering?
The dilemma remains unresolved.
Dispute: slaughter done for its sake but blood sprinkling intended otherwise; Rabbi Yohanan says unfit, Reish Lakish fit.
Rabbi Yohanan: intent in one rite can affect another, derived from piggul intent, so the offering is unfit.
Reish Lakish: intent cannot transfer between rites, and piggul is not a model for deviation from offering type; fit.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan: an animal slaughtered with idolatrous intent for blood or fat is forbidden, since intent in one rite affects another.
Reish Lakish: the animal is permitted, since intent in one rite does not affect another and outside rules are not derived from inside rules.
Explanation: the two disputes must both be taught, since each alone would leave a different case open.
Continuing the explanation: the reverse case shows why both statements are needed to settle the dispute fully.
Rav Dimi reports that Rav Yirmeya supports Rabbi Yohanan with evidence, while Rabbi Ila supports Reish Lakish.
Rav Yirmeya's a fortiori argument from improper intent regarding time: deviation in type should likewise disqualify the offering.
Rava bar Ahilai objects: deviation in type is not more severe than intent beyond the time, which carries karet.
Rava bar Ahilai reformulates the inference using the designated area, which carries no karet, and the same a fortiori conclusion.
Rav Ashi objects: the outside-area disqualification applies to all offerings, but deviation in intent applies only to Paschal and sin offerings.
Rav Ashi reformulates the inference using the owner, which supports Rabbi Yohanan's line of reasoning.
Rabbi Ila argues the Torah would not need the redundant rule unless it teaches that intent in one rite cannot affect another.
Rav Pappa objects: the redundant requirement may instead teach that intent in one rite can affect another.
Reply: if so, the verse would be silent, and Rav Ashi's a fortiori inference would teach the point, so the verse must counter it.
Rabbi Yohanan refutes Rabbi Ila: slaughter and blood collection have extra stringencies that sprinkling lacks, so it must be stated.
Reish Lakish's reply: the matter is discussed regarding peace offerings, which lack those stringencies, so the objection is irrelevant.
Dispute: an offering slaughtered for its sake but sprinkled not for its sake; Rav Nachman says unfit, Rabba says fit, then Rabba concedes.
Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer says a guilt offering is also unfit when slaughtered not for its sake.
Baraita: a guilt offering, like a sin offering, is brought for a transgression, so improper intent disqualifies it too.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: the sin offering's blood is sprinkled above the red line, so the inference need not extend to guilt offerings.
Rabbi Eliezer replies: a Paschal offering, sprinkled below the red line, is still unfit if slaughtered not for its sake.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: a Paschal offering is special because its time is fixed, so it cannot serve as the source.
Rabbi Eliezer replies: a sin offering, which has no fixed time, is still disqualified if slaughtered not for its sake.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers Rabbi Eliezer, and the reply is left unstated.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A speaker returns to an earlier claim, calling the discussion circular and unproductive.
Eliezer's inference: the word it in the sin, Paschal and guilt verses teaches fitness only if slaughtered for its sake.
Yehoshua objects: the guilt offering's it is stated only after the sacrificial portions are burned, so it differs.
Eliezer cites the verse that sin and guilt offerings are alike, so a guilt offering not slaughtered for its sake is unfit.
Yehoshua restates his claim that a sin offering is unique because its blood is sprinkled above the red line.
The Gemara asks why Eliezer does not derive the guilt offering's status from the common sin and Paschal elements.
Reply: that derivation fails, since sin and Paschal offerings share karet liability, which a guilt offering lacks.
Yehoshua objects: sin and guilt offerings differ in blood placement and in entering the innermost sanctum.
Reply: the comparison concerns only external sin offerings, whose blood does not enter the innermost sanctum.
Counter: the sanctum-entry difference disqualifies external sin offerings, but guilt blood entering is not disqualified.
Reply: Eliezer holds that a guilt offering whose blood enters the sanctum is also disqualified.
Counter: Yehoshua could cite the karet difference, since sin offerings atone for karet-liable transgressions.
Reply: Eliezer derives it from the sin offering for hearing the voice, a transgression not punishable by karet.
Counter: Yehoshua could cite the four-placement requirement of sin blood, which a guilt offering lacks.
Reply: perhaps Eliezer follows Rabbi Yishmael, who requires four placements for almost all offerings.
Counter: even by Rabbi Yishmael, guilt blood goes on two corners, whereas sin blood goes on all four.
Reply: Yehoshua cited only one of several valid distinctions, such as finger placement and corner requirements.
Gemara challenges: Eliezer should answer that guilt blood is also above the red line, since the two laws are parallel.
Abaye argues guilt blood is below the red line, by a fortiori reasoning from burnt offerings, which are wholly consumed.
Rejected: burnt offerings do not atone for sin, which may alone explain why their blood is placed below the line.
Reply: a bird sin offering atones for sin, yet its blood is placed below the red line.
Rejected: bird sin offerings are killed by nape pinching rather than slaughtered, which may explain their placement.
Reply: combine burnt and bird offerings, both most sacred and placed below the line, to include guilt offerings.
Rava of Parzakya: Eliezer can refute this, since burnt and bird offerings lack fixed value, unlike guilt offerings.
Eliezer's reason: the verse says the priest offers it, so only sin blood is placed above the red line.
If the word it is exclusive, why is a guilt offering unfit if slaughtered not for its sake, when other offerings are fit?
Reply: the word it is not exclusive, since the Paschal offering is excluded from that generalization and is unfit anyway.
Alternative reply: even bird burnt offering blood may be placed differently from that of a sin offering.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds that the two placement areas are discrete and separate.
Baraita: blood placed on the lower half goes from the red line down, and on the upper half from the line up.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: the placement rule concerns bird burnt offerings only; sin blood goes on the corner itself.
Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva says any blood entering the Sanctuary to atone is unfit; the Rabbis limit this to sin offerings.
Rabbi Eliezer says guilt offerings share the sin offering's status, as the verse says as is the sin, so is the guilt.
Eliezer's reason is clear, but what is the Rabbis' reason for limiting the rule to sin offerings?
Rava rejects the claim that guilt blood entering the Sanctuary is disqualified, via a fortiori reasoning from burnt offerings.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori: a burnt offering, wholly consumed, stays fit even if its blood enters the Sanctuary, so a guilt offering should too.
The Gemara refutes: a burnt offering does not atone for sin, which may alone explain why its blood is not disqualified.
A sinner's meal offering can prove the point, since entering the Sanctuary does not disqualify it despite atoning for sin.
Objection: a bird sin offering, which has blood and atones for sin, should prove the point more closely than the meal offering.
Reply: it is uncertain whether a bird sin offering is disqualified by entry; this is a dilemma raised by Rabbi Avin.
Refutation: a sinner's meal offering is not a slaughtered offering, so a burnt offering should prove the point instead.
Reply: the halakha follows from the shared most-sacred status of burnt and meal offerings, so a guilt offering is also fit.
Rava of Barnish objects: burnt and meal offerings lack fixed value, unlike guilt offerings, so the inference fails.
The Rabbis' reason: the verse says whose blood, limiting this disqualification on entry to the blood of sin offerings.
Eliezer and the Rabbis read the phrase whose blood differently regarding the flesh and other offerings.
For the Rabbis, who hold a guilt offering slaughtered not for its sake is fit, the juxtapositions of meal offerings make sense.
Baraita of Rabbi Shimon: a sinner's meal offering is like a sin offering and a voluntary one like a guilt offering, per the verse.
But according to Rabbi Eliezer, what halakha is taught by juxtaposing the meal offering to sin and guilt offerings?
Reply: the juxtaposition teaches Rabbi Shimon's halakha that a meal offering conveyed not in a service vessel is unfit.
Rav Yehuda bar Rabbi Hiyya: the verse teaches the handful is performed with the right hand like sin, or the left like guilt.
Does Rabbi Shimon expound this one verse for both purposes, both the disqualification and the hand used?
Reply: the verse mainly teaches the hand rule, while the disqualification follows from the word it written in both verses.
According to the Rabbis, what halakha is taught by juxtaposing the guilt offering with the sin offering?
Reply: it teaches that a guilt offering, like a sin offering, requires placing hands on the head of the offering.
Mishnah: Yosef ben Honi says other offerings slaughtered for the sake of a Paschal or sin offering are unfit.
Rabbi Yohanan: Yosef ben Honi and Rabbi Eliezer agree on this matter.
Rabba: they agree about Paschal offerings but dispute other offerings slaughtered for the sake of a sin offering.
Baraita: a Paschal offering slaughtered at its time for its own sake; Rabbi Eliezer deems the related case unfit, Rabbi Yehoshua fit.
Rabbi Yehoshua's a fortiori: if other offerings are fit for a Paschal offering's sake outside its time, they should be fit at its time.
Rabbi Eliezer counters with the reverse a fortiori: a Paschal offering would then be fit for others' sake at its time, which is wrong.
Rabbi Yehoshua replies: disqualifying others for the Paschal's sake weakens the Paschal requirement and strengthens the peace offering's.
Rabbi Eliezer's a fortiori: a leftover Paschal becomes a peace offering but a leftover peace offering is not a Paschal, so the sacrifice should be unfit.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Yehoshua objects: a leftover sin offering is brought as a burnt offering, but a leftover burnt offering is not brought as a sin offering.
Eliezer's a fortiori: a burnt offering slaughtered for a sin offering's sake should be unfit, by parallel reasoning, yet the halakha says it is fit.
Eliezer replies: sin offerings are fit for others' sake all year, but the Paschal is fit only at its time, so others should be disqualified.
Mishnah: Shimon brother of Azarya says offerings slaughtered for a holier offering are fit, and for a less holy one unfit.
Rav Ashi and Rav Aha derive Shimon's view from the verse on not profaning holy things that are set apart, teaching holier-sanctity rules.
Why does the verse on setting apart holy things teach this halakha, when it is needed for Shmuel's derivation about untithed produce?
The future tense of set apart teaches two halakhot: the holier-offering rule and death at Heaven's hand for eating untithed produce.
Dilemma: do less sacred offerings slaughtered for holier ones propitiate or not, and does Shimon dispute one matter or two?
Abaye's argument: firstborn and tithe slaughtered for peace offerings are fit but do not propitiate, so lesser offerings for holier sake likewise do not.
Reply: the cases are not comparable; Shimon may hold such offerings propitiate, while firstborn and tithe do not.
What does the latter clause on firstborn and tithe teach, since the former clause already gives the example of higher and lower sanctity?
It teaches that lesser offerings also differ among themselves, lest one think the rule applies only between the most sacred and lesser sanctity.
Objection: the mishna already teaches this elsewhere, where peace offerings precede the firstborn because of their extra rites.
Reply: the distinction is primarily stated in that mishna, and this mishna mentions it only incidentally.
Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua deems fit a Paschal slaughtered on the morning of the fourteenth not for its sake; ben Beteira deems it unfit.
Shimon ben Azzai claims a tradition: unsanctioned offerings are fit, but only the Paschal and sin offerings satisfy the owner; the Rabbis disagree.
Gemara: Rabbi Oshaya reports that ben Beteira deems a Paschal slaughtered on the morning of the fourteenth fit, since the whole day is its time.
Why does the mishna say ben Beteira treats a morning slaughter as if in the afternoon, implying it is not fully equivalent?
Since Rabbi Yehoshua says as though on the thirteenth, ben Beteira's as though is only phrasing, and he sees no real difference.
If so, why not dispute the case of a Paschal slaughtered for its own sake, where ben Beteira fits and Yehoshua unfits it?
Had the mishna disputed only the for-its-sake case, one would think Yehoshua concedes the not-for-its-sake case, so both are taught.
How can ben Beteira allow morning slaughter, given the verse that says the Paschal is slaughtered bein ha'arbayim?
Ulla says ben Beteira reads bein ha'arbayim literally as between two evenings, so the Paschal may be slaughtered all day.
If so, is the whole day also fit for the daily offering, which is also written with bein ha'arbayim?
There the verse says the one lamb is offered in the morning, so bein ha'arbayim by inference refers to the actual afternoon.
Counter: perhaps one lamb is offered in the morning and the other all day; why must the second be in the afternoon?
The same question about the lamps: is the whole day fit for lighting, since bein ha'arbayim is written for them too?
Lamps differ: the verse says from evening to morning, so the Candelabrum must burn through the night, and other rites are by day.
The same question for incense: is the whole day fit for burning it, since bein ha'arbayim is written for incense too?
The Gemara answers that incense is different; the reply is cut off at the end of the daf.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the lamps verse says evening for the Candelabrum, the Paschal's evening verse should limit it too, so how can ben Beteira allow all day?
That verse teaches ordering: the Paschal, with both evening terms, is sacrificed after the daily afternoon offering, which has only bein ha'arbayim.
Is there a parallel to ben Beteira's view, where morning slaughter counts as its time, yet the Paschal waits until after the afternoon offering?
Yes: Rabbi Yohanan rules that missed morning prayers are recited after the afternoon prayer, a precedent for this ordering.
If bein ha'arbayim covers the whole day, why are the incense and lamp verses needed, since those rites are not performed all day?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's argument makes Oshaya's reading of ben Beteira difficult, since a morning Paschal not slaughtered for its sake fails.
Rabbi Yohanan's reading: ben Beteira deems a morning Paschal unfit whether slaughtered for its sake or not, since part of the day is valid.
Rabbi Abbahu mocks this: a Paschal designated on the fourteenth morning would be disqualified from the outset, so no fit Paschal could exist.
Rabbi Abbahu's alternative: the Paschal is fit if designated after midday, when it can already be sacrificed.
Abaye: even if designated in the morning it is fit, since an offering is not unfit for a time-not-yet-arrived when its time comes that day.
Rav Pappa: even if designated the previous night it is fit, since a night designation for next-day sacrifice is not premature, per a baraita.
Rabbi Appetoriki's contradiction: one verse makes an animal fit only from the eighth day, while another suggests the night before is fit.
Reconciliation: at night the animal is consecrated and the next day it becomes fit for sacrifice, so early consecration is allowed.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether Rabbi Yohanan holds that animals not yet sacrificeable at any moment are permanently disqualified.
Rabbi Abbahu says yes: Rabbi Yohanan's case of an animal of two partners, consecrated piecemeal, is consecrated but not fit to be offered.
A consecrated animal can make its substitute consecrated; three conclusions follow, including that unsacrificeable animals are permanently disqualified.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Permanent disqualification applies even when the animal's sanctity is monetary rather than inherent.
Ulla, citing Rabbi Yohanan: one who ate forbidden fat, designated an offering, then apostatized has a permanently disqualified offering even after recanting.
Rabbi Yirmeya, citing Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan: the same case with an imbecile who later regains competence; still permanently disqualified.
Both are needed: apostasy alone might suggest only self-caused disqualification is permanent, so the imbecile case shows automatic disqualification also is.
If only the imbecile case were taught, one might say it is permanent since recovery is out of his hands, so the apostasy case is needed too.
Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma: if a court permitted the fat and then retracted, is the offering rendered unnecessary permanently disqualified?
An elder replies: Rabbi Yohanan chose this example because here the offering itself is disqualified, making permanence more evident.
Mishnah: Shimon ben Azzai says he received a tradition from seventy-two elders that unsanctioned eaten offerings are fit.
Why does the mishna say zaken in the singular for seventy-two elders, rather than the plural?
Because all seventy-two agreed on one opinion.
Ben Azzai adds only the burnt offering to the sin and Paschal offerings, which the first mishna declares disqualified when not sacrificed for their sake.
Rav Huna: the verse on the burnt offering's pleasing aroma and its word it teach fitness only when sacrificed for its sake.
The word it also appears for a guilt offering, which is fit even when not sacrificed for its sake.
That guilt verse is written after burning the sacrificial portions, which are not part of the main rites.
Is the burnt offering's word it verse also written after the burning of the portions?
The word it is written twice for burnt offerings, and one instance is interpreted to refer to the main rites before burning.
Is the word it also written in two places for guilt offerings, undermining the earlier reading?
Ben Azzai's a fortiori: a sin offering is disqualified if not sacrificed for its sake, so a burnt offering, more strict, should be too.
Rejected: a sin offering atones for sin, unlike a burnt offering, so only sin offerings are disqualified in this way.
Suggested: a Paschal offering proves it, since it is not for atonement yet is disqualified; rejected because its time is fixed.
Reverted: the halakha comes from the common element of sin and Paschal offerings, so burnt offerings are included as well.
Rejected: the shared feature is karet liability, which a burnt offering lacks.
Ben Azzai's reply begins here but is cut off at the end of the daf.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Notes that the common karet element does not refute the inference.
Asks why the guilt offering should not also be derived from this inference.
Ben Azzai refutes the inference: communal and individual offerings share features that guilt offerings lack.
Alternative answer: Ben Azzai refutes the whole inference because only sin and Paschal offerings share karet.
Ben Azzai's ruling on burnt offerings is a tradition he learned, not derived by inference.
Objects that Rav Huna explicitly cited an a fortiori argument, implying it is the real source.
Rav Huna offered the a fortiori argument only to sharpen his students' minds.
Mishna: Paschal and sin offerings are unfit if slaughtered, collected, conveyed or sprinkled with improper intent.
Asks how the mixed-intent rites are actually performed.
Mishna gives examples of slaughtering a Paschal offering with mixed intent for different offerings.
A slaughtered offering is disqualified by improper intent in four rites.
Rabbi Shimon deems the offering fit when improper intent occurs during conveying the blood, since it is optional.
Rabbi Eliezer: improper intent disqualifies only when conveying the blood is required.
Asks whether improper intent during collection of the blood disqualifies the offering.
A baraita cites the verse about the priests presenting the blood.
The baraita asks whether the verse refers to collecting the blood or only to sprinkling.
Sprinkling is already stated later, so the verse must refer to collecting the blood.
The words sons of Aaron teach that collection requires a fit priest in service vestments.
Rabbi Akiva asks from where the restriction on collection is derived.
Akiva locates the phrase sons of Aaron in the Leviticus verse.
Akiva compares the Numbers verse calling priests fit and vested to the case of collection.
By analogy, collection likewise requires a fit priest in service vestments.
Rabbi Tarfon swears he heard a distinction between collection and sprinkling but cannot explain it.
Rabbi Akiva explains: intent counts for sprinkling but not collection, with differing consequences for location and priest.
Rabbi Tarfon praises Akiva for teaching the halakha consistently with what he heard.
Akiva replies that whoever separates from him is like one who separates from life.
Rava resolves the contradiction: the baraita concerns piggul intent, the Mishna concerns intent not for its sake.
Rava's resolution is supported by the Mishna's wording, which says unfit and not piggul.
Asks whether piggul intent during collection of the blood disqualifies the offering.
A baraita hypothesizes that intent counts only during sprinkling.
The baraita derives from Leviticus 7:18 that slaughter and collection are also included in piggul.
Objects that pouring the remainder and burning the portions should then also be included.
The third-day verse excludes pouring and burning, which are not included in the case.
Sprinkling is singled out to teach that any rite preventing atonement if omitted is included in piggul.
Pouring and burning are excluded because omitting them does not prevent atonement.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's resolution: slaughtering for tomorrow's collection is not piggul, but collecting for tomorrow's pouring is.
A Sage asks whether intent regarding pouring and burning does not disqualify the offering.
