Proposes an alternative reading of the baraita's repeated bull phrase, assigning each occurrence to a different bull, communal and priestly.
Asks what it means for one offering not to be equated with another: which offerings differ in kind yet share sprinkling rules?

Refutes this too: the communal bull and idolatry goats atone for known sins, while the Yom Kippur bull atones for unknown ones.
Offers a third pair, the communal bull and the Yom Kippur goat, and restates Yishmael's argument as an a fortiori on that basis.
Restates Yishmael's a fortiori in full: offerings unequal in kind share sprinkling rules, so offerings equated as bulls must share them too.

ranges.en: Concludes the prior argument: the sprinkling acts of both offerings are equated, since both are performed the same way in the Sanctuary.

Asks how a rule derived by juxtaposition can itself teach by a fortiori, given that such derivations are not done for consecrated matters.
Rav Pappa holds that Rabbi Yishmael's school allows a juxtaposition-derived rule to teach again by a fortiori, even for consecrated matters.
Asks why the bull's verse needs a special derivation, since the verse itself already refers to the communal bull.
Rav Pappa answers that the inclusion teaches burning the fat and kidneys for idolatry goats, so the rule need not be derived by juxtaposition.
A baraita in line with Rav Pappa asks what the repeated bull phrase adds.
The baraita answers via Numbers 15:25: the sin offering refers to idolatry goats and the error to the communal bull, so both burn alike.
Asks where the communal bull's burning rule comes from, if not by juxtaposition, which would itself be a derivation by juxtaposition.

Asks why the tanna does not derive the idolatry goats from the earlier sin offering verse, as already stated.

ranges.en: Explains that the extra derivation makes the two offerings alike in the diaphragm and kidney rule, which the communal bull's verse omits.

Rav Pappa replies that tanna'im dispute this: the school of Rav amplifies the halakha, while Rabbi Yishmael's school does not.
Asks why the diaphragm and kidneys are stated for the anointed priest's bull but not for the communal bull.
A parable answers: a king angry at a beloved servant speaks little of the offense out of affection, as God does with Israel.
Asks why the Curtain is stated for the anointed priest's bull but not for the communal bull.

Cites the mishna that a single misplaced placement disqualifies without karet, and the Menachot dispute on piggul intent during the full permitting act.
Resh Lakish explains Rabbi Meir's view: the handful was placed with improper intent and the frankincense silently, and one acts on the first intent.
Asks how Resh Lakish knows this: the mishna's wording implies that one misplaced placement with improper intent makes the offering piggul.
Asks whose opinion the mishna follows, proposing the Rabbis.
Objects: the Rabbis reject piggul from half the permitting act, and the placement here was proper, so the view must be Rabbi Meir's.
Objects that if Rabbi Meir's reason were half-act piggul, the offering would be piggul even as taught; so his reason is the initial-intent principle.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak resolves that the mishna follows the Rabbis, reading in their proper manner as intent that makes the offering piggul.
Objects that the mishna's inference, that a misplaced placement disqualifies, shows proper manner means intent that makes the offering fit.
Rava defends the mishna: improper manner means placement outside its designated area, which disqualifies, so the offering is not piggul.
Rav Ashi defends: improper manner means placement not for the offering's sake, which disqualifies, so again not piggul.
Objects that by inference, a silent last placement would make the offering piggul, contrary to the Rabbis' rule.
Answers that the mishna's wording is imprecise: its latter clause parallels the former, so no inference about silent last placement follows.
Objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita limiting piggul-by-first-placement to blood placed on the external altar, where one placement permits.

ranges.en: States the case: improper intent during any set of blood placements on the inner altar for the Yom Kippur and bull offerings.

The baraita's wording that intent in any set renders piggul supports Rabbi Meir's reliance on half a permitting act, against Resh Lakish.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avin: the case is improper intent during slaughter, a single permitting factor, so Rabbi Meir's view covers a whole service.
Asks what then is the Rabbis' reason, if the case concerns slaughter.
Rava identifies the Rabbis with Rabbi Eliezer, citing the meal-offering mishna where a service must be completed for liability.
Objects: Rava himself says Rabbi Eliezer concedes for blood, as the Yom Kippur mishna shows, so the identification fails.
Rava offers another case: intent in the first and third sets with silence in the second, a novel point for Rabbi Meir's initial-intent principle.
Rav Ashi objects: the baraita never mentions silence in the second set, though Rava's reading makes it the key detail.
Rav Ashi's own reading: intent in the first three sets and silence in the fourth; the baraita teaches that all sprinklings count as initial intent.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that Rav Ashi's reading, with intent in all three sets, conflicts with the baraita's wording of intent in one set or another.
Asks how Rabbi Meir can render piggul when, by the principle of acceptance, karet requires all permitting factors to be sacrificed.
Objects that the earlier blood, disqualified by improper intent, is like water, so the later sprinklings cannot complete the permitting factors.
Rabba explains the case: four bulls and four goats, each sprinkling set with its own slaughter, so every permitting factor is performed properly.
Rava says it can be one bull and one goat: the sprinkling completes the service, so all permitting factors count for piggul.
Objects: another baraita gives forty-seven presentations, not forty-three.
Resolves by opinion: forty-three assumes the bloods are mixed before placement, forty-seven that they are mixed only later.
Objects with a third baraita giving forty-eight presentations.
Resolves by whether pouring the remaining blood on the external altar's base is indispensable, which adds it to the count.
Objects to Resh Lakish's reading of Rabbi Meir with a meal-offering baraita, where improper intent in one part renders the offering piggul.
Objects that the baraita, with the handful silent and frankincense intended, shows Rabbi Meir disputes the Rabbis by half an act.
Reinterprets the baraita: the handful was silent only after the frankincense was already given with improper intent, so the second act follows the first.
Objects that this merely repeats the first clause, and an explicit baraita says the frankincense came with intent, which conflicts with Resh Lakish.
Mishna lists items not liable for karet over piggul, such as the handful, incense and frankincense, which need no other item or permit others.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna lists non-liable items for piggul; Rabbi Meir limits the libations to separate offerings, while the Rabbis extend it to those with animals.
Mishna on the leper's log of oil: Rabbi Shimon says no piggul liability, Rabbi Meir says yes, since the guilt offering's blood permits it.
Mishna explains which blood permits which parts: burnt offerings' flesh, bird sin offerings' meat for priests, and burnt bulls' portions.
Rabbi Shimon holds that burnt bulls and goats, whose blood goes inside, are not liable for piggul, unlike offerings with external-altar blood.
Ulla teaches that a piggul handful sacrificed on the altar loses its piggul status, arguing a fortiori from its power to make others piggul.
Asks what Ulla is saying, since the reasoning does not explain why the status should leave the handful.
Explains that an unaccepted handful cannot make others piggul, because a meal offering becomes piggul only with a properly sacrificed handful.
Asks what Ulla teaches: if it is that the handful is not liable for piggul, the mishna already says so.
Objects that the mishna already lists the handful among non-liable items, so Ulla's point must be something else.
Suggests Ulla teaches that piggul items that ascended the altar cannot descend, but a mishna already states this.
Objects that the mishna's symmetry says items that descended cannot ascend again, so the halakha seems already covered.
Answers that the ruling is needed where the fire has already taken hold, so the handful returns to the altar.
Objects: Ulla already said this, that the mishna's rule covers only where fire has not taken hold, making the ruling redundant.
Ulla's ruling: items that descended without fire taking hold do not ascend, but where fire took hold, they ascend.
Explains the novelty of Ulla's point, lest one think the rule for descent applies only where the fire has not taken hold.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla's ruling: a handful, unlike a limb, might not return whole once partly burned, so Ulla teaches it ascends in its entirety.
Rav Aḥai: since the handful is one unit, a piggul handful half on the ground is brought up entirely to the altar ab initio.
Rabbi Yochanan: piggul, notar and impure flesh lose their prohibition once brought up on the altar.
Rav Ḥisda objects: the altar is no bath of purification, so it cannot render impure flesh pure.
Rabbi Zeira answers: the case is where fire took hold, so the item belongs to the altar and its prohibition lapses.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna objects from a baraita: impurity departing via the fire would make impure flesh purifiable, which the verse excludes.
Rava defends: the baraita's departure refers to purification by a ritual bath, not by other means.
Objects that the term ritual bath is not written in the baraita, which speaks only generally of impurity departing.
Rav Pappa defends: the verse concerns peace offering meat, not fit for sacrifice, so bringing it up does not remove its impurity.
Ravina defends differently: the phrase upon him refers to a whole person, excluding sacrificial flesh whose impurity departs only when deficient.
The baraita argues the verse speaks of a person's bodily impurity, not the flesh's impurity.
Asks whether the verse means bodily or flesh impurity, since the masculine suffix matches basar rather than nefesh.
Answers by analogy: the phrase upon him appears in the corpse-impurity verse of Numbers 19, where it concerns bodily impurity.
Gives further proofs for bodily impurity: plural offerings versus singular impurity, and the next verse's eating reference; others infer exclusion.
Asks how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives bodily impurity from the eating term, which appears in a different verse.
Rava: any verse not explained by Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi, or baraita not explained by Ze'eiri, remains unexplained.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains: the verse opens and closes in feminine form, with masculine in the middle, so it concerns bodily impurity.
Cites a baraita on lenient and stringent consecrated-food cases while impure, whose meaning Rav Ze'eiri's skill is meant to elucidate.
Asks what the lenient and stringent cases are, testing whether second tithe and teruma fit the baraita's logic.
Objects that the a fortiori reading fails: the tithe case yields only flogging, which caps any derived teruma penalty.
Answers that the lenient case is impurity from a creeping animal and the stringent is impurity from a corpse, both in Leviticus 22.
Asks: if these refer to teruma, both corpse and creeping-animal impurity incur death, so the baraita's contrast fails.
Objects that reading the baraita as referring to second tithe is also difficult.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raises the worry that stringent corpse impurity might carry death; an a fortiori from creeping-animal impurity limits it to flogging.
Ze'eiri explains the baraita: creeping-animal impurity is lenient and corpse impurity stringent, the latter stated for second tithe to limit it to flogging.
The mishna: anything with permitting factors, for people or the altar, is liable for piggul; a verse and baraita extend piggul beyond peace offerings.
Baraita: perhaps piggul applies only to offerings like peace offerings, eaten for two days and a night, as the reasoning would suggest.
The verse about the flesh of the peace offering extends piggul to one-day offerings, and the word sacrifice extends it to burnt offerings.
Asks where birds, meal offerings and even the leper's oil log are derived for piggul.
Cites Leviticus 22:2, which speaks of consecrated items they set apart for Me, as the source including these offerings.
Explains the derivation: notar's profanation and piggul's iniquity are linked by verbal analogy, extending both prohibitions to all offerings.
Asks why piggul is stated specifically for peace offerings, since the verse eventually includes all items.
Answers: like peace offerings, any offering with permitting factors for people or the altar carries piggul liability.
The baraita specifies which blood permits which parts for each offering, and excludes meal offerings, frankincense, incense and blood by analogy.
Rabbi Shimon: only offerings whose blood is sprinkled on the external altar, like peace offerings, carry piggul, excluding burnt bulls and goats.
The Gemara identifies the similar offering as the firstborn, eaten for two days and a night like peace offerings.
Asks by what hermeneutic the firstborn is derived, suggesting an inductive comparison based on shared eating time, which can be refuted.
Refutes the comparison: peace offerings also require hand-laying, libations and breast-and-thigh waving, which firstborn offerings lack.
Derives firstborn piggul from the verse on peace offerings' flesh, using generalization, detail, generalization.
Objects that the two generalizations are adjacent, so the verse is not in the generalization-detail-generalization order.
Rava: the principle still applies; with adjacent generalizations, place the detail between them and read a generalization-detail-generalization.
Baraita includes even the leper's oil log among piggul-liable offerings.
Asks whose opinion this ruling follows.
Rabbi Meir's view: the leper's oil log is liable for piggul if the guilt offering became piggul.
Objects: the latter clause excludes libations and blood as lacking permitting factors, which reflects the Rabbis' view against Rabbi Meir.
Another baraita: animal libations are liable for piggul because the offering's blood permits them, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbis object: a person brings offerings and libations up to ten days later, so blood cannot be what permits libations.
Rabbi Meir replies: his ruling covers only libations brought together with the offering.
Rav Yosef: the view is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who says the oil's placements render it permitted and therefore piggul.
A baraita on the leper's oil log: misuse liability lasts until the blood is sprinkled, after which benefit is forbidden only rabbinically.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: misuse liability lasts until the seven oil sprinklings; both sides agree consumption is forbidden until the placements are done.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: a great man like Rav Yosef would not say that the oil's sprinkling renders the rest piggul.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that when the log of oil is brought alone, its placements permit the oil and do not make it piggul, by general agreement.
Cites Rabbi Meir's baraita: the leper's oil log is piggul-liable because the offering's blood permits it for the thumb and big toe.
Rabbis object: a person may bring the guilt offering and its oil up to ten days later, so blood cannot be the permitting factor.
Rabbi Meir replies that he spoke only of oil brought with the guilt offering, so blood is what makes it piggul.
Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye reconcile the baraita with Rabbi Meir, explaining which libations and oil are piggul-liable and which are not.
The mishna: a bird sin offering's blood permits its meat for consumption by the priests.
Asks the source for priests eating these items, and cites Levi's baraita on the word every in Numbers 18:9.
The every-offering wording of Numbers 18:9 includes the leper's oil log, even though the from-the-fire phrase might seem to exclude it.
Every meal offering in the verse includes the omer and jealousy offerings, which could seem excluded from the atonement-based priestly-food rule.
Every sin offering includes the bird sin offering, whose meat is eaten despite the nape-pinching method that seems to render it carrion.
Every guilt offering includes the nazirite's and leper's guilt offerings, which might seem only to qualify the offerer, not atone.
Challenges the derivation: the leper's guilt offering is explicitly priest-eaten, so the verse must add the nazirite's by analogy to it.
The baraita adds stolen property of a convert with its one-fifth to priestly gifts, and makes such gifts usable even for betrothal.
A baraita gives a third opinion: Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, says piggul arises only when intent concerns an act performed outside.
Illustrates: intent outside about sprinkling inside does not render piggul, while intent outside about pouring or burning outside does.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi finds the source in Leviticus 4:10, which ties the sin bull's portions to the peace-offering bull.
Juxtaposes the anointed priest's bull with the peace-offering bull: both become piggul only when acts and intent relate to the external altar.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh citing Rav: the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar, who speaks in Rabbi Yosei's name.
Rava's statement opens here and continues beyond this excerpt.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a halakha is issued for the messianic period, when the Temple will be rebuilt.
Abaye objects: if such halakhot are not taught, the tanna should not teach Zevaḥim, so learning is for reward.
Rava replies that his point is that this is a binding halakha, not merely a matter to study.
Mishna: gentile-consecrated offerings carry no piggul, notar or impurity liability; slaughtering outside is exempt per Rabbi Shimon, liable per Rabbi Yosei.
Baraita: gentile-consecrated items may not be benefited from ab initio, cannot be substituted or bring separate libations, though their animal offerings need libations.
Rabbi Yosei: stringency applies to gentile altar offerings in all these cases, while Temple-maintenance items carry misuse liability.
The Gemara explains that benefit is forbidden rabbinically and misuse is excluded by analogy to teruma, where only Israelites' items count.
The baraita again excludes gentile offerings from piggul, notar and impurity liability.
Explains piggul via iniquity linked to notar, and notar via profanation linked to impurity, where only Israelite items are named.
The baraita also says gentiles cannot render an animal a substitute.
Asks the reason gentiles cannot substitute animals.
Substitution is juxtaposed with animal tithe, which is juxtaposed with grain tithe, and Numbers 18:24 excludes gentiles from both.
Asks whether a juxtaposition-derived rule can again teach by juxtaposition, a principle limited to consecrated matters.
Answers that the principle does not apply here, since grain tithe is non-sacred food.
Objects: this works only if the principle follows the teaching source; if it follows the case itself, which concerns offerings, the answer fails.
Rather, gentiles cannot bring animal tithe because it has no fixed time, and substitution is juxtaposed with it, so gentiles cannot substitute.
Baraita: gentiles cannot bring separate libations, though their animal offerings require them.
Cites Numbers 15:13 and 15:11: only Israelites bring separate libations, yet every offering, including a gentile's, requires libations.
Rabbi Yosei repeats his stringency view for altar items, with Temple-maintenance items carrying misuse liability.
Explains Yosei: misuse via teruma analogy applies to inherently sacred items, not to Temple-maintenance items, whose sanctity is monetary.
Baraita: blood that became impure and was sprinkled unwittingly by a priest is accepted.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a sprinkling by an individual that is intentional is not accepted; for the community, unwitting or intentional sprinkling is accepted; for gentiles, neither.
Sages ask Rav Pappa whose view this is, since Rabbi Yosei's stringency for gentile offerings seems to conflict with it.
Rav Pappa replies the baraita may follow Rabbi Yosei, since the frontplate verse's for them applies only to Jews.
Rav Huna objects: Rabbi Yosei treats gentile and Jewish offerings alike, so the they-consecrate verse cannot exclude gentiles here.
Rav Ashi: the exclusion comes not from for them but because the frontplate's atonement does not cover gentiles, who lack acceptance.
Mishna: items exempt from piggul still incur notar and impurity liability, except blood; Rabbi Shimon limits impurity liability to items normally eaten.
Baraita: one might think impurity liability applies only to items with permitting factors, for people or the altar.
A fortiori: piggul, which needs one change in awareness and admits no exceptions, applies only to items with permitting factors, so impurity should too.
Objects that impurity is more lenient than piggul: sliding-scale offerings, two awareness changes, communal exceptions, so the a fortiori fails.
The verse which they consecrate to Me shows impure people are liable for eating any consecrated item.
Rabbi Elazar reads approaches in Leviticus 22:3 to mean liability only for eating, not merely touching consecrated items.
Yikrav alludes to sacrificing: liability starts when permitting factors are sacrificed, or when the flesh is sanctified in a service vessel.
Asks where notar's application to items without permitting factors is derived, given impurity already applies to them.
Objects: derive notar from piggul's iniquity instead, which would limit notar to items with permitting factors.
Answers that notar derives from impurity more reasonably, by the Gimel-Zayin-Lamed mnemonic: both affect the offering's body, unlike piggul's intent.
Responds that notar more reasonably derives from piggul, sharing time-dependence, the lack of frontplate atonement, and applying to pure offerings.
Levi's teaching: the verse's profanation applies even to time-caused disqualification, not only impurity, as profanation appears elsewhere.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse concerns two profanations, notar and impurity, teaching that notar, like impurity, applies even to items without permitting factors.
Asks from where the mishna's notar and impurity liability for piggul-exempt items is derived.
Ulla and Rabbi Yishmael's school read the words to you and to atone as showing blood is given for atonement, not for misuse.
Rabbi Yoḥanan derives this from the phrase it is, so blood's status is the same before and after atonement, and misuse ends once performed.
Asks whether the it-is wording could mean the blood stays subject to misuse both before and after atonement.
Rejects this: no item whose mitzva is performed remains subject to misuse of consecrated property.
Asks whether no such case exists, since ashes removed from the altar retain misuse liability after their mitzva.
Answers that ashes and High Priest's garments are two exceptional cases sharing a rule, which cannot model others.
Objects: this works for the Rabbis who require garment interment, but Rabbi Dosa's view makes ashes a single-case rule, so the answer fails.
Responds that ashes and the heifer's broken neck are two verses that come as one, both with post-mitzva misuse, so they cannot model others.
Challenges this: it works only if two verses that come as one teach nothing, but not for those who hold they do teach.
Answers that two exclusions appear: the heifer's whose-neck-broken wording and the ashes' and-he-shall-put-it wording limit the rule to them.
Asks why three verses are needed to exclude blood from misuse, given the three expositions of Ulla, Yishmael's school and Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Each of the three phrases excludes blood from one prohibition: misuse, notar and impurity respectively.
Piggul needs no verse for blood: the mishna already excludes the permitting factor itself, since blood renders the offering permitted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks why three karet mentions are needed for eating peace offerings while impure.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains three karet mentions: one generalizes consecrated items, the detail includes altar items, and impure-eating covers inedible items like wood and frankincense.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon's remaining karet mention includes, since he exempts inedible items from impurity liability.
Answers that it includes inside sin offerings: otherwise, following Rabbi Shimon's piggul logic, impure eaters would also be exempt.
The mishna: Rabbi Shimon holds liability for edible items but not wood, frankincense or incense; the Rabbis disagree, and amoraim split on the reason.
One amora says the dispute concerns impure flesh; for impure bodies all agree the eater is not flogged.
The other amora holds the dispute parallels across both cases, reading the flesh-touching verse to cover inedible items too.
Rav Tavyumi and Rav Kahana transmit the two positions differently, with one reading the dispute as about bodily impurity.
Rava: the parallel-dispute view is correct, since inedible items are not read into the soul-cut-off verse, so neither is read into the flesh verse.
Objects: the flesh verse includes wood and frankincense, which suggests they can become impure and count.
The inclusion concerns only disqualification by rabbinic law, with the verse cited as mere support.
Mishna: a slaughtered offering must be intended for six matters: its type, its offerer, God, altar consumption, aroma, and pleasing God; sin and guilt add atonement.
Rabbi Yosei: an offering is valid without any stated intent, since the court stipulates none ab initio, and intent follows the performer.
Rav expounds Leviticus 1:9: burnt means for a burnt offering, made by fire for full altar burning, excluding partial roasting.
Rav continues: aroma excludes limbs roasted before being brought up; pleasing and to-the-Lord require intent for God's acceptance.
Pleasing means intent for God's spirit to accept it, and to-the-Lord means intent for the One who spoke the world.
Rav: a sin offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt offering is disqualified, but for a non-sacred animal it is valid.
Rabbi Elazar grounds Rav in Leviticus 22:15: only intent for another offering profanes consecrated items, not intent for a non-sacred animal.
Rabba objects from Rabbi Yosei's mishna: validity without intent implies that intent for a non-sacred animal disqualifies.
Abaye reinterprets Rabbi Yosei: without any intent it is valid and effective, while non-sacred intent makes it valid but ineffective.
Rabbi Elazar: a sin offering slaughtered as non-sacred, thinking it non-sacred, is disqualified, since no sacrificial intent exists, like Shmuel's dilemma.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where it is derived that slaughter by one unaware of the sacrificial purpose disqualifies consecrated offerings.
Rav Huna cites Leviticus 1:5, requiring the slaughter to be done for the sake of a bull.
Shmuel accepts that intent is required as established, and asks from where it is indispensable.
Rav Huna cites Leviticus 19:5, requiring slaughter with your will, meaning deliberate, aware slaughter.
The principle: intent follows only the one performing the rite.
The Gemara says the mishna is not like this tanna, whose baraita has owners rendering offerings piggul by their intent.
Rava grounds Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei in Numbers 15:4: he who sacrifices includes the owner, who can render piggul.
Abaye: three Sages agree that intent of one person counts for another's performance.
Rabbi Eliezer's view, from a mishna: a slaughter on behalf of a gentile is valid for eating, but Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita: if one stores an unstorable item and another carries it out on Shabbat, the storer's intent makes the carrier liable.
Both Sages accept Rabbi Elazar ben Yosei: if intent works outside the Temple, it certainly works inside, as Leviticus 19:5 states.
Objects: perhaps intent counts only inside the Temple, so Rabbi Elazar ben Yosei need not accept those Sages' rulings for outside matters.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar accepts Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: since intent works on Shabbat, it surely works for idolatry.
Objects: intent may work only for idolatry, which resembles Temple service; Shabbat labor requires the doer's own creative intent.
Chapter-closing formula, then the mishna: the most sacred offerings are slaughtered in the north of the Temple courtyard.
Mishna on the Yom Kippur bull and goat: slaughter and collection in the north; required sprinklings are indispensable, while western-base pouring is not.
Mishna on burned bulls and goats: slaughter and blood collection in the north, with Curtain and golden altar sprinklings.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continues: missing a required sprinkling disqualifies, unlike the western-base pouring; both kinds of offerings are burned at the ash place.
Asks why the mishna omits collecting blood in a service vessel as a principle, given the leper's guilt offering collects by hand.
Objects: the mishna later says the leper's guilt blood is collected in a vessel, so why was it omitted earlier?
Answers: the tanna omitted it because the leper's blood is collected by hand, but later taught it since some blood must be vessel-collected.
A Tosefta: Leviticus 14:14 says the priest shall take and put, so taking is done by his own body, not a service vessel.
Leviticus 14:13 makes the leper's guilt like a sin offering, so its altar blood is vessel-collected, and two priests split the collection.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the Yom Kippur bull and goat are slaughtered in the north, and their blood collected in a service vessel in the north.
Asks why the mishna lists these sin offerings first, when the north rule is written for the burnt offering.
Answers that the sin offering's location is derived by interpretation, so it is dear to the tanna and taught first.
Challenges the order: external sin offerings should come first; the reply is that Yom Kippur blood enters the sanctum, so they are dear.
Asks where the north rule for burnt offerings is written in the Torah.
Leviticus 1:11 says to slaughter the sheep on the altar's north side, establishing the north rule for burnt offerings.
Asks from where the bull burnt offering's north slaughter is derived, since the verse addresses sheep.
Leviticus 1:10: the conjunctive vav adds to the prior passage, so the bull's slaughter location is learned from the sheep passage.
Asks: this works only for those who accept learning upper passages from lower ones; what of those who reject it?
A baraita: Leviticus 5:17 yields Rabbi Akiva's liability for uncertain misuse, while the Rabbis exempt; the dispute concerns learning upper from lower.
Asks whether the dispute is precisely about learning upper passages from lower ones.
Rav Pappa: everyone learns upper from lower; the Rabbis exempt via a verbal analogy with the sin offering for forbidden fat.
Verbal analogy: as the sin offering covers acts that carry karet if intentional, so the provisional guilt offering does too.
Asks what Rabbi Akiva derives: the provisional guilt offering covers only fixed sin-offering cases, excluding sliding-scale impurity offerings.
The Rabbis hold that a verbal analogy cannot apply to half a matter, so the analogy must fully match.
Asks why Rabbi Akiva does not share that principle, since he too must accept it.
Resolves: they dispute whether vav continues the prior matter, so Rabbi Akiva learns upper from lower via the conjunction.
Asks whether they dispute the priority of juxtaposition versus verbal analogy, since the Rabbis' text also has the and-if-anyone-sin phrase.
Rejects this: all accept juxtaposition as stronger; the Rabbis read the lower passage as derived from the upper for the silver-shekel ram.
Juxtaposition teaches the provisional guilt ram must be worth two shekels, like the misuse offering, not a one-sixth dinar sin offering.
Asks from where Rabbi Akiva derives this minimum value.
From Leviticus 7:1, this is the law of the guilt offering: one law governs all guilt offerings, including the two-shekel minimum.
Asks: if the law-word derivation is rejected, how do all guilt offerings share a minimum value?
A verbal analogy on according to your valuation links misuse, provisional and robbery guilt offerings.
Asks how the espoused-maidservant guilt offering gets its two-shekel minimum, since its text lacks according to your valuation.
Derived by verbal analogy on with the ram shared with the misuse guilt offering.
Asks from where a sin offering's north slaughter is derived.
Leviticus 4:29: the sin offering is slaughtered in the place of the burnt offering, which is in the north.
Asks from where the blood's collection is also in the north.
Leviticus 4:34: the priest takes the sin offering's blood, which follows the slaughter verse, so collection is in the same place.
Asks from where the collector must himself stand in the north, rather than reaching in from near it.
Reads velakach as he will take himself, lo yikkach, so the collector must personally perform collection.
Asks from where disqualification follows for slaughter or collection performed anywhere other than the north.
Leviticus 4:24 on a king's goat sin offering says slaughter where burnt offerings are slaughtered, which a baraita places in the north.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the verse on the king's goat is needed at all, since the place rule was already stated.
Offers the alternative reading: is the north rule limited to this goat, or does it apply to all goats.
Replies that the verse makes the sin offering a paradigm, so all sin offerings require slaughter in the north.
Notes that the goat of a king and other sin offerings each both fulfill the mitzva and disqualify if misplaced.
Asks what the source is that other sin offerings are disqualified if not slaughtered in the north.
Cites the lamb and she-goat verses, both saying to slaughter in the place of the burnt offering.
Challenges the earlier explanation: why is the word it needed in the king's goat verse?
Explains via a baraita that the word it excludes Nahshon's goat from the north requirement.
Quotes a baraita on laying hands: Rabbi Yehuda includes Nahshon's goat, Rabbi Shimon includes idolatrous goats.
Clarifies the supposition that the north rule follows the hand-laying rule, and why the verse excludes it.
Ravina objects that the explanation works only for Rabbi Yehuda, leaving Rabbi Shimon's view unexplained.
Mar Zutra objects that exclusion should apply only where inclusion applied, so the north rule would not be excluded.
Defends Ravina: the north rule cannot be derived by paradigm, as the Nahshon offering was a one-time case.
Concludes that the word it teaches the animal must be in the north, though the slaughterer need not stand there.
Challenges this: the slaughterer rule already comes from Rabbi Akhiya, so what does the word it add?
Replies that the priest standing in the north shows the verse's word it is needed for the animal's placement.
Resolves the question: the word it excludes a male bird from the north requirement.
Gives a baraita arguing a bird offering should need the north by inference from sheep, then refuted by it.
Objects that the sheep comparison fails, since sheep are notable for being slaughtered with a knife.
Concludes that the word it excludes the Paschal offering from the north requirement.
Quotes a baraita from Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that excludes the Paschal offering by the word it.
Tests inferences from burnt, sin and guilt offerings to the Paschal offering and rejects each as distinguishable.
Returns to the earlier view: the slaughterer need not stand north, and the Rabbi Akhiya challenge is answered.
Questions the inference that the blood collector must stand north, since the two verse wordings teach nothing.
Asks the source for disqualifying slaughter and blood collection performed outside the north.
Gives Rav Adda bar Ahava's a fortiori derivation from the burnt offering to disqualify sin offerings.
Rejects the a fortiori: a sin offering atones for karet-liable sins, which a burnt offering does not.
Ravina objects: a secondary prohibition is not more stringent than a primary one, so the inference fails.
Mar Zutra, son of Rav Mari, objects that a secondary prohibition can be more stringent after all.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenges the view that a secondary status is never stricter: second tithe food is more stringent in Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Replies that the purchased food's sanctity is too weak to be redeemed, so the stringency is not a general rule.
Mar Zutra objects with the substitution case, where a substitute consecration is stronger than the original animal.
Explains that substitute sanctity derives from a consecrated animal, so it is stronger than the original's sanctity.
Mar Zutra objects again with the Paschal offering, whose remainder as a peace offering has stricter rules.
Replies that the leftover Paschal animal becomes a peace offering, so only peace offering rules apply.
Offers an alternative proof from the verse: the repeated place wording disqualifies a burnt offering slaughtered elsewhere.
Asks the source for the requirement that a guilt offering be slaughtered in the north.
Cites the verse on slaughtering the guilt offering in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered.
Asks the source that blood collection must also take place in the north.
Derives blood collection in the north from the verse about the blood being sprinkled around the altar.
Asks from where the one collecting the blood must himself stand in the north.
Derives it from the word and that precedes its blood, which includes the collector.
Asks the source that disqualifies a guilt offering slaughtered outside the north, beyond optimal performance.
Points to a verse about the leper guilt offering, which teaches that all guilt offerings are disqualified outside the north.
Asks whether that verse is really needed for this halakha, or whether it teaches something else.
Cites a baraita: a case removed from a general category cannot return to it unless the verse says so explicitly.
Quotes the leper verse and explains how the baraita's principle applies to it.
Asks why the verse repeats the sin offering comparison, since it was already stated.
Supposes the leper guilt offering, being unique, needs no blood placement or burning, and so refutes the reading.
Replies that the comparison to the sin offering establishes blood placement and burning, so the verse must cover north as well.
Argues that the north requirement could be written in the leper context alone, so the repeated wording must teach something else.
States that this works only if a matter removed from its category does not learn halakhot from that category.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the alternative: if the principle that a matter leaving its category does not learn from it holds, the verse is needed for the leper's own halakha.

Mar Zutra objects that the category return covers only blood and burning, which need a priest, not slaughter in the north.
Ravina replies that the verse would have simply said the leper's offering is like the sin offering, so the phrase must add something.
Asks why the leper offering is juxtaposed to both the sin offering and the burnt offering.
Explains that the double juxtaposition blocks the mistaken idea that a juxtaposition-derived halakha can teach another via juxtaposition.
Mar Zutra objects that the juxtaposition to the sin offering is superfluous and could be dropped.
Ravina replies that the juxtaposition to both offerings is needed to show a juxtaposed halakha cannot teach via juxtaposition.
Rava derives the principle from the High Priest's sin offering verse on the diaphragm and kidneys.
Explains why the verse places the High Priest's halakha in the communal bull context, so it is not a juxtaposition chain.
Rav Pappa asks why the Torah did not simply write the halakha explicitly in the communal bull passage.
Rava replies that the verse both wrote and juxtaposed the halakha, to show juxtaposition cannot then teach via juxtaposition.
Gives a mnemonic listing the hermeneutic principles for the compounded derivations that follow.
Asks whether a matter derived via juxtaposition can teach its halakha further through a verbal analogy.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Natan ben Avtolemos deriving garment leprosy purity by verbal analogy to human leprosy.
Draws the verbal analogy: if human leprosy covering the whole body is pure, so is garment leprosy spread through the garment.
Shows the head analogy itself is derived via juxtaposition, so a juxtaposed halakha can teach via verbal analogy.
Rabbi Yohanan says this proves nothing for sacred matters, where verbal analogy from a juxtaposed halakha is not allowed.
Argues that if such derivation applied to sacred matters, the verse would not need to state the north rule for guilt offerings.
Concludes that for consecrated matters a juxtaposition-derived halakha cannot teach onward via verbal analogy.
Proposes the verbal analogy could be refuted by the sin offering's karet-atoning feature, so explicit writing is needed.
Replies that extra phrases in the Numbers verse show the sacred-order descriptions, which cannot be refuted by a logical claim.
Introduces the next question: whether a matter derived via juxtaposition can then teach through a fortiori inference.

ranges.en: Points back to the school of Rabbi Yishmael's teaching on the same hermeneutic question, discussed earlier.

Rabbi Yirmeya replies no: otherwise the north rule for guilt offerings could be derived from the sin offering instead.

Tries each offering as the derived one and refutes each derivation by a distinguishing feature.
Asks whether a matter derived via verbal analogy can teach its halakha further via juxtaposition.
Rav Pappa cites the thanks offering verse: its money can come from second tithe money, as peace offerings can.
Asks the source that peace offering money may come from second tithe, citing the verbal analogy of there.
Cites the Deuteronomy verses containing the word there, to support the verbal analogy.
Mar Zutra objects that the grain tithe is only non-sacred, so it cannot prove the consecrated-matter principle.
Ravina replies that the principle applies even when the derived halakha is itself consecrated, as with peace offerings.
Asks whether a verbal-analogy-derived halakha can teach another matter by verbal analogy.
Rami bar Hama cites a baraita on the fine-flour breads of the thanks offering, derived by verbal analogy.
Ravina challenges that the unleavened word may instead come from the oven-baked meal offering, not the thanks offering.
Rava says the source is a different baraita about the High Priest's bull offering.
Quotes the baraita: the bull is burned whole and its head and legs are cited, reasoning by analogy with the burnt offering.
Explains through Rav Pappa's reading of innards and dung that the flaying is not required, deriving the cutting by verbal analogy.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the bull and goat of Yom Kippur share the skin, flesh and dung terms.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes from the bull baraita parallel that a verbally derived halakha can teach another halakha by verbal analogy.
Asks whether a matter derived via verbal analogy can teach its halakha further via an a fortiori inference.
Answers by a fortiori reasoning from the Rav Pappa and Rabbi Yishmael school examples, so it can teach that way.
Notes the answer works only for whoever accepts Rav Pappa's statement, and asks what follows for Mar Zutra.
Offers a second a fortiori derivation from the Rami bar Hama example, supporting the same conclusion.
Asks whether a verbally derived halakha can teach via paradigm, and leaves the question unresolved.
Asks whether an a fortiori derived halakha can teach its halakha via juxtaposition.
Derives the answer by a fortiori from the verbal analogy and the Rav Pappa examples.
Limits the answer to those who accept Rav Pappa; for Mar Zutra the question stays unresolved.
Asks whether a halakha derived via a fortiori can teach via verbal analogy.
Resolves by a fortiori reasoning, citing the Rabbi Yohanan and Rami bar Hama examples for verbal analogy.
Asks whether an a fortiori derived halakha can teach via a fortiori inference.
Answers that this too follows by a fortiori, using the same chain of examples.
Challenges the phrasing: the chain is a grandson of a fortiori, not a son, so the label needs fixing.
Rather, the same question is derived by another a fortiori, drawing on the Rava and Ravina examples.
Asks whether an a fortiori derived halakha can teach its halakha via paradigm.
Rabbi Yirmeya says to bring a proof from a mishna on the tereifa bird offering.
Presents the mishna: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether the tereifa bird's meat transmits impurity.
Rabbi Meir proves his view by a fortiori: slaughter purifies a tereifa, as it does with an animal carcass.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the a fortiori premise: just as slaughter purifies a bird tereifa, so pinching should purify it too.
Rabbi Yosei rejects the extension: only slaughter, not pinching, purifies a tereifa, since the animal case limits the inference.
Asks whether a matter derived via paradigm can teach its halakha via juxtaposition, verbal analogy, a fortiori or paradigm.
Resolves by a baraita chain: blood, portions and offerings left overnight, removed or impure, are fit by paradigm.
Challenges the baraita: how can a disqualified matter be derived from a fit one, or a private altar from the communal case?
Replies that the tanna relied on the verse permitting many disqualified offerings to stay on the altar overnight.
The mishna teaches that the remainder of blood of inner sin offerings is poured on the western base of the external altar.
Asks the reason the remainder of blood must be poured on the western base.
Cites the High Priest's bull verse: pour it on the base encountered first on leaving the Tent of Meeting.
A baraita cites three verses with the same phrase, teaching the base requirement for the external altar only.
The baraita asks whether the verse teaches that sprinkling on the altar corners requires a base.
Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori: the remainder requires a base, so the initial sprinkling does too.
Rabbi Akiva gives a parallel a fortiori from the remainder that does not atone to the atoning sprinkling.
Asks: if so, why does the verse state the base again, and is that not needed for the matter itself?
Replies that the external altar rule is derived from the phrase at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
Cites the king's sin offering verse, which states the remainder is poured at the base of the burnt offering altar.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes the baraita: the altar of the burnt offering must have a base, and the remainder is poured onto it.
Asks why these verses are needed for the king's sin offering if the rule is already taught for this offering alone.
Replies that the remainders are poured on the external altar, since the sprinklings themselves are made there.
Raises the possibility that the priest might reverse the sprinklings, which would need the verse to rule out.

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the baraita's first clause: pouring cannot go from outer to inner altar, since the inner altar has no base.
Asks how the verse could mean the blood is placed where there is a base, given the wording of the base phrase.
Replies that the altar of phrase means the blood goes on the upper surface of the base, not its side.
Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori from the sin offering remainder that the initial sprinkling needs the base's upper surface.
Rabbi Akiva gives a parallel a fortiori with the sin offering remainder that does not atone.
Asks why the verse would need to state the base rule again, and what distinguishes the two Sages' views.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says the dispute is whether failing to pour the remainder disqualifies the offering.
Rav Pappa says all agree pouring is not essential, and the real dispute is squeezing out bird blood.
A baraita in line with Rav Pappa: the bull of the High Priest, the bull of Yom Kippur, and the phrase of the bull.
Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori from the High Priest's bull to the Yom Kippur bull for the base requirement.
Rabbi Akiva argues a fortiori from the High Priest's bull to the Yom Kippur bull, based on the blood entering the innermost sanctum.
Rabbi Yishmael's baraita on the phrase concluding the atonements, showing the remainder does not disqualify.
Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori from the king's goat to the High Priest's bull for the base pouring requirement.
Shows through a verse-based inference that the High Priest's sin offering pouring requirement is needed to be stated.
The baraita explains the verse inverts the clause, making pouring a non-essential mitzva, so failure does not disqualify.
Asks whether Rabbi Yishmael holds that failing to squeeze out bird sin offering blood disqualifies it, given his school's teaching.

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Replies that two tanna'im disagree about how Rabbi Yishmael's view on the remainder of blood should be read.
Rami bar Hama says this tanna holds that failing to pour the remainder disqualifies offerings sprinkled inside.
Cites a baraita on the verse about the sin offering eaten by the priest, excluding blood placed below the red line.
Asks: from where would one think such an offering is valid, so that the verse must teach otherwise?
The baraita derives from the Deuteronomy verse that a single placement of blood on the corners still atones.
Offers a counter-inference: the bird blood below the red line and the animal blood above should be treated alike.
Rejects that inference: bird blood can be moved above the red line, but animal blood cannot be the same.
The baraita responds that blood placed inside the Sanctuary proves the disqualification point.
Rejects that proof: the inner altar's need for further placements does not apply to the blood above the red line.
The baraita concludes from the verse that an animal sin offering with blood placed below the red line is disqualified.
Rami bar Hama asks what the inner altar's incomplete atonement refers to, if not the remainder pouring rule.
Rava argues a fortiori: if remainder pouring disqualifies inner offerings, then blood placed below the red line does too.
Rava says the inner altar alone does not complete atonement, which requires blood also on the Curtain.
A baraita on the Yom Kippur verse: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether completing the atonement is decisive.
Asks what is the difference between the two Sages' positions in the dispute.
Explains that Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dispute how to read the verses, and whether remainder pouring disqualifies.
Concludes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds remainder pouring disqualifies, citing a case of a spilled bull's blood.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan disagrees with that reasoning, since he states a halakha following the disqualifying view.
Replies that neither is taking a side in the Akiva-Yehuda dispute; each follows the disqualifying view generally.
Mishna opens: these are the halakhot of communal and individual sin offerings, starting with the New Moon and festival goats.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna describes the sprinkling of a sin offering's blood at the four corners, then the remainder poured on the southern base.
Asks how the priest performs the sprinkling on the corners of the altar, given the dispute between two Sages.
Presents the two positions: one allows blood within a cubit of the corner, the other requires the outer edge of the corner.
Explains that all agree sprinkling on the corner is fine; the dispute is only over the cubit on either side.
Objects with a baraita that describes the sprinkling as performed on the actual edge of the corner.
Replies that the baraita describes the optimal manner; sprinkling a cubit to either side still fulfills the mitzva.
Asks what the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon are.
Cites a baraita: upper blood from the red line up, lower blood below; the bird burnt offering is the exception.
Explains Rabbi Abbahu's Ezekiel verse as giving the corners a domain of four cubits beneath them.
Cites a mishna: a red line circumscribed the altar to separate the upper blood area from the lower.
Asks from where this red line matter is derived.
Rav Aha bar Rav Ketina derives it from the verse on the net reaching halfway up the altar.
Notes the mishna's southern base for the remainder, and a baraita reading the verse as the southern base.
Asks whether the phrase refers to the southern base, or only to the western base.
Derives the southern base by analogy with the priest's exit from the Sanctuary, pouring on the side nearest him.
Rabbi Yishmael says the western base for both remainders; Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai says the southern base.
Explains Rabbi Yishmael's view: the unspecified phrase is read from the explicit western-base phrase.
Asks the reason for the view that the remainder is poured on the southern base.
Rabbi Asi says the external altar stands in the north, so the southern base faces the Sanctuary entrance.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael holds Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai agrees with them: both blood types go on the western base.
The mishna lists the burnt offering's rules: most sacred order, northern slaughter, two placements of four, flaying, and full burning.
Asks why the tanna explicitly calls the burnt offering of the most sacred order, while not saying so for the sin offering.
Explains the verse calls only the sin and guilt offerings most sacred, so the burnt offering needed explicit mention.
Restates the mishna: the burnt offering's blood requires two placements, which make four.
Asks how the priest performs the two placements of the burnt offering's blood.
Presents Rav's view (place and return) and Shmuel's view (one placement in a gamma shape), noting a tanna dispute.
Derives the gamma shape from verses excluding a single sprinkling and a full thread-like circuit.
Rabbi Yishmael's baraita compares the burnt offering to the inauguration sin offering, supporting Rav's four placements.
Assumes the southeast corner lacked a base and asks what the reason for that absence is.
Rabbi Elazar says that corner lay in Benjamin's portion, and the altar occupied one cubit of Judah's land.
Gives an alternative: a strip of land went from Judah's portion to Benjamin's, where the corner base sat.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the Deuteronomy verse: Benjamin is privileged because the Holy of Holies was built within his portion.
Objects with a baraita on the bird burnt offering's pinching at the southeast corner, which would need a base.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says the airspace above the corner was assigned to Benjamin, so the rite is within the altar domain.
Asks what is meant by the southeast corner having no base, if a base was physically there.
Rav and Levi give rival readings of the no-base phrase, and of the Genesis verse about Benjamin.
Cites a mishna and baraita to test Rav's and Levi's readings, with each side offering an answer.
Cites a baraita describing the stepwise construction of the altar base on all four sides.
Begins an objection, cut off mid-sentence, that opens a further challenge.

ranges.en: Cites the Deuteronomy verse requiring unhewn stones for the altar, so the base cannot be cut afterwards.

Rava's reading of the Samuel and Deuteronomy verses, and the Joshua borders, locates the Temple in Benjamin's portion.
Explains why the Temple was lowered slightly from Ein Eitam, as a matter of tradition about Judah and Benjamin.
Links Doeg's jealousy to David's oath in the psalms, showing David's search for the Temple site.
Rava explains the psalm words: Ephrath refers to Joshua, the field of the wood refers to Benjamin.
The mishna lists the guilt offerings, which share northern slaughter, two placements, and eating within the Courtyard.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we derive that communal peace offerings require slaughter in the north.
Cites Rabba bar Rav Hanan: the Shavuot verse juxtaposes peace offerings with the sin offering, so both need the north.
Rava objects: a juxtaposition-derived halakha cannot itself teach via juxtaposition, so that source fails.
Rava gives Rav Mari's source: the Numbers verse juxtaposes peace offerings with burnt offerings, so they need the north.
Asks what the first juxtaposition with the sin offering was meant to teach.
Replies that peace offerings, like the sin offering, are eaten only by male priests.
Abaye objects with the nazirite's ram, which a nazirite's sin offering juxtaposition would limit to male priests.
Rava replies the nazirite's ram differs, since the foreleg verse shows the owner may eat the rest.
Asks why the cooked foreleg is eaten by priests' wives and slaves, if the juxtaposition should limit it to male priests.
Offers a second reply: the ram is not of the most sacred order, so the juxtaposition teaches a shaving rule instead.
The mishna lists the thanks offering and nazirite's ram as lesser sanctity, eaten in Jerusalem for a day and night.
Cites a baraita on the breast and thigh eaten in a pure place, reading the pure place as relative impurity.
Asks why the pure place could not instead be the Levites' camp, pure of zav but impure of corpse.
Abaye and Rava give rival readings of the verse on eating in a pure place, placing the portions in the Israelites' camp.
Asks why not bring the portions into the Levites' camp, which is also called pure.
Replies that the portions are brought into one camp adjacent to the Israelites' camp, not into two.
Asks why the removal should not similarly be to one place only, while the initial derivation points to the Israelites' camp.
Cites Deuteronomy against eating within the gates, and concludes Abaye's reading is clear.
The mishna on peace offerings: lesser sanctity, north or anywhere slaughter, eaten in Jerusalem for two days and a night.
A baraita derives from the repeated verse that all directions of the courtyard are fit for lesser offerings, including north.
Rabbi Eliezer argues the repetition only teaches that the north is fit, since lesser offerings' place is not like the most sacred.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the two tanna'im disagree about in the verses on slaughter at the Tent of Meeting.

Records Shmuel's rule, transmitted through several Sages, that peace offerings slaughtered before the doors opened are disqualified.
Rabbi Zeira says a curtain is made to be used as an open entrance, so it does not count as closed.
Asks the halakha if a tall item blocks the entrance, rather than a curtain.
Cites a baraita on the two wickets of the Chamber of Knives, eight cubits high, opening the courtyard for both offering types.
Asks whether the eight cubits refers to an obstruction in front of the wickets, rather than the wickets themselves.
