Replies that the wickets were set in the corner of the Chamber, one opening northwest and one northeast.
Asks the halakha for the area behind the Hall of the Ark Cover, from which the entrance cannot be seen.
Rav's niche behind the Hall, eight cubits high, served the same purpose, as the Chronicles verse suggests.
Asks the meaning of the word laparbar in the Chronicles verse.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila explains it as meaning facing outward.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel holds that one is liable for entering the courtyard impure only in a specific case, as stated.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita gives the Temple courtyard's dimensions: 187 cubits long by 135 cubits wide.
Rav Nahman's father explains that priests eat and slaughter there, and are liable for impurity, within that courtyard.
Asks what the specified dimensions are meant to exclude.
Objects that the windows, doors and wall thickness are inside the courtyard by a mishna, so they cannot be the exclusion.
Asks whether the exclusion is meant to cover chambers built in non-sacred ground but open to the sacred area.
Replies from a mishna that such chambers have sanctity only by rabbinic law.
Argues from the meal offering verse that the Torah grants sanctity to these chambers for eating the most sacred offerings.
Rava says the Torah sanctifies them only for eating, not for impurity or slaughter.
Asks whether a baraita making priests liable for impurity there still stands, if slaughter there is not allowed.
Rava replies that the baraita's text should be emended to add that no karet liability arises there.
Challenges: slaughter needs the courtyard entrance, but the reason for no impurity liability is still unexplained.
Explains that the slaughter ban is taught even before the entrance, so the chambers are not sacred and carry no liability.
Asks whether eating also must take place before the courtyard entrance, as slaughter must.
Cites a baraita on the two wickets of the Chamber of Knives, eight cubits high, rendering the courtyard fit for eating.
Ravina says to remove the eating clause, since eating need not occur before the courtyard entrance.
Asks whether the Tabernacle verse, which requires eating at the Tent of Meeting entrance, contradicts that conclusion.
Replies that offerings sacrificed only once at the inauguration are a special case and cannot set a general rule.
Rav Yitzhak bar Avudimi derives from the verse that blood of offerings is disqualified at sunset.
Challenges: why does he need this verse, since the derivation is already available otherwise?

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenges the proof: if the verse only stated the day-of-slaughter rule, why add the wording about sacrificing the blood?
Proposes an alternative reading: blood sacrificed on a given day lets the meat be eaten that day and the next.
Rejects that reading, since the verse would then have stated the eating rule plainly, so the wording must teach the blood rule.
Ḥizkiya rules that an offering remains valid when its intent is to eat it in the light of the third day.
R. Yoḥanan rules that such an offering is disqualified.
Ḥizkiya's reason: the meat was never designated for burning, so the intent does not disqualify it.
R. Yoḥanan's reason: the meat was already pushed off from eating, so the intent makes the offering disqualified.
Ḥizkiya rules that one who eats such meat in the third day's light is exempt, since it was not designated for burning.
R. Yoḥanan rules that such a person is liable, since the meat was already pushed off from eating.
A baraita is cited as being in accordance with R. Yoḥanan.
Baraita: for one-day offerings, blood counts until sunset and flesh and fats until dawn; for two-day offerings, flesh counts until the second sunset.
Hypothetical objection: peace offerings might be eaten on the night after the second day, by analogy to one-day offerings.
Leviticus 19:6 limits eating to the second day, so the remainder is not eaten in the light of the third day.
Hypothetical objection: the remainder should be burned immediately after the second day, by analogy to one-day offerings.
Leviticus 7:17 requires that the remainder be burned by day on the third day, and not at night.
Mishna: firstborn, tithe and Paschal offerings have lesser sanctity; their blood is placed at the altar base, and their eating rules differ.
Asks who the anonymous tanna of the Mishna is.
Rav Ḥisda identifies him as R. Yosei HaGelili.
Baraita of R. Yosei HaGelili: the verse says their blood and their fat, teaching that these three offerings require placement on the altar.
Asks from where we derive that the blood must be placed on the base of the altar.
R. Eliezer derives it by a verbal analogy to the sprinkling stated for burnt offerings.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we know that a burnt offering requires its blood placed at the altar base.
Leviticus 4:7 says to pour the blood at the altar base, teaching that an obligatory burnt offering needs that placement.
Objects: if derived by analogy from burnt offerings, firstborn, tithe and Paschal offerings should need two four-part placements.
Abaye: two verses that teach the same matter do not teach beyond their own case, so these offerings need only one placement.
Asks how Abaye's reasoning holds for the view that paired verses do teach a common aspect beyond their case.
Replies that a third verse, about guilt offerings, makes three verses, which certainly teach beyond their case.
Mishna: firstborn offerings are eaten by the priests, in Jerusalem, for two days and one night.
Baraita derives the two-day, one-night period for firstborn offerings from Numbers 18:18, juxtaposed with peace offering portions.
Tarfon's ruling, given in Yavne: firstborn offerings are eaten for two days and one night.
Yosei HaGelili, a new student, asks Tarfon for the source of his ruling.
Tarfon argues by analogy: firstborn and peace offerings are both lesser-sanctity offerings, so both are eaten two days and a night.
Yosei objects by analogy to sin and guilt offerings, which are gifts to priests and are eaten one day and night.
Tarfon replies: like peace offerings, firstborn offerings do not atone for sin, so they keep the two-day period.
Yosei counters: like sin and guilt offerings, firstborn offerings are gifts and are not brought as vows, so one day and night.
Akiva joins in as Tarfon withdraws, and argues from the verse's juxtaposition of firstborn with peace offering portions.
Akiva's proof: Numbers 18:18 juxtaposes firstborn with peace offering breast and thigh, so the two-day period applies.
Yosei answers that the verse can equally be juxtaposed with the thanks offering's breast and thigh, which is eaten one day.
Akiva concedes the possibility but says the repeated 'it shall be yours' adds a second day, so the two-day period stands.
Yishmael tells Akiva he erred in conceding, since a detail derived by juxtaposition cannot teach another halakha by juxtaposition.
Asks what Yishmael derives from the extra phrase 'it shall be yours'; the answer is that a blemished firstborn is also a priestly gift.
Akiva derives from the plural 'their flesh' that both unblemished and blemished firstborn offerings are priestly gifts.
Explains that Yishmael reads the plural as referring to the flesh of all firstborn cattle, sheep and goats.
Asks what principle the Sages disagree about, given their shared premise about juxtaposition.
Yishmael counts a halakha derived both by juxtaposition and another principle as a juxtaposition; Akiva does not.
Explains that the Yom Kippur verse 'so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting' is written for Akiva's view, where such a derivation is not a juxtaposition.
Yom Kippur sprinkling: the bull and goat blood are sprinkled alike, once above and seven times below, so the details are derived from each other.
Asks how these halakhot can be derived according to the view that such a derivation still counts as a juxtaposition.
Only the sprinkling locations are derived from one another, through the second juxtaposition, so the two juxtapositions are unconnected.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternative resolution: the outside sprinkling is derived from the inside sprinkling, as one complex juxtaposition rather than two chained ones.
Granted on the view that a juxtaposition-derived detail cannot teach more: Leviticus 23:17 on the Shavuot wave loaves is the source.
Asks why 'you shall bring' is needed, since the verse already says present a new meal offering.
Anything brought from elsewhere that resembles this offering is made like it, so each thanks-offering loaf is a tenth of an ephah.
Objects: if compared, the ten thanks-offering loaves should total two-tenths of an ephah, like the two Shavuot loaves.
The word 'they shall be' restricts the two-tenths total to the Shavuot loaves alone.
Derives the ten-tenths measure for matza from the verse on leavened bread, so matza must match the leavened loaves.
Asks how the matza measure can be derived from the leavened bread measure if a juxtaposition cannot teach another juxtaposition.
The extra 'you shall bring' is a superfluous word, written as if it were explicit for the leavened bread, so no juxtaposition is used.
Mishna: the Paschal offering is eaten only at night, and only until midnight.
Asks who the anonymous tanna of this mishna is.
Rav Yosef says it is R. Elazar ben Azarya.
Baraita: R. Elazar ben Azarya derives the midnight limit by comparing 'on that night' in Exodus 12:8 with the firstborn plague's midnight timing.
Concludes that just as the firstborn deaths ended at midnight, so the Paschal eating ends at midnight.
R. Akiva objects: Exodus 12:11 already sets a time of haste, so the Paschal offering may be eaten until dawn.
Asks why 'on that night' is needed, since it might seem the Paschal offering is eaten by day like other offerings.
'On that night' teaches that the Paschal offering is eaten at night and not during the day.
Abaye objects: how do we know the midnight limit is Torah law per R. Elazar, not a rabbinic decree to distance one from sin?
Rav Yosef replies that the mishna's 'only until midnight' shows the midnight limit is by Torah law, like the other Paschal rules.
Chapter-closing formula that ends the chapter beginning 'Eizehu Mekomano'.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: offerings of highest sanctity slaughtered atop the altar are valid, as if slaughtered in the north, according to R. Yosei.
R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda: the half of the altar south of the midpoint counts as south, the half north of it as north.
Rav Asi reports R. Yoḥanan's view that R. Yosei held the whole altar stands in the northern section of the courtyard.
Asks what the phrase 'as if' slaughtered in the north is meant to indicate.
Lest one think slaughter must be on the ground beside the altar, R. Yosei teaches that slaughter atop the altar is still valid.
R. Zeira challenges: if the whole altar is north, then for R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda half is north and half south, yet he disqualifies slaughter opposite the north half on the ground.
Rav Asi replies that this is what R. Yoḥanan meant, and it does not show the altar lies wholly outside the north.
R. Yoḥanan says both Sages derive their opinions from a single verse.
Exodus 20:21 says to slaughter burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar, the source for both positions.
R. Yosei holds the whole altar fit for burnt and peace offerings; R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda holds half is for each.
If the whole altar were fit for burnt offerings, the peace offering clause would be superfluous, so the verse must split the altar between the two.
R. Yoḥanan says R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda concedes that slaughter opposite the north half on the ground is disqualified.
Rav Aḥa asks Ravina what is meant by slaughter on the ground opposite the north half of the altar.
If the base or ledge is meant, that is part of the altar; and if tunnels are dug beneath, the altar itself would still be unfit, which is objectionable.
A baraita on Exodus 20:21 requires the altar to be attached to the earth, not built over tunnels or arches.
The phrase about the north half is needed for the case where the altar's dimensions were reduced and slaughter took place where its north half stood.
R. Zeira asks whether R. Yoḥanan's statement is correct even though no mishna teaches it.
R. Zeira finds a mishna in Tamid that alludes to it: the second wood arrangement sits opposite the altar's southwest corner, a location set by the mishna.
Asks what the significance is of the mishna defining the precise location and the frankincense burning there.
The mishna follows R. Yosei's view that this arrangement must be in that precise location, as a baraita teaches.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yosei's principle: an item taken from the inner altar to be placed on the outer altar is placed only on the part nearest the Sanctuary.
Conversely, an item taken from the outer altar to the inner altar is taken only from the part nearest the Sanctuary.
Asks which items are meant by the first clause of the principle.
Suggests the remaining sin-offering blood, but rejects it: Leviticus 4:7 already states where that blood is poured out.
Asks which items are meant by the second clause of the principle.
Suggests the Yom Kippur coals, but rejects it: Leviticus 16:12 already specifies taking them from before the Lord.
The item is the two frankincense bowls of the shewbread, which are derived from the sin-offering blood placement.
The item is the daily coals taken from the outer altar, derived from the Yom Kippur coals.
If the whole altar were south, the wood arrangement would need to move 27 cubits, which strains R. Yosei's view.
Even if the Sanctuary and Entrance Hall share one sanctity, the arrangement must move 22 cubits, which is still difficult.
Even if half the altar were north, the arrangement would still move 11 cubits, or 6 cubits if the two halls were equal.
Only the view that the whole altar is north explains why the arrangement sits four cubits from the southwest corner.
The four cubits are base, ledge, corner area and priests' walkway, so the arrangement must sit exactly there, proving the whole altar is north.
Rav Adda bar Ahava offers an alternative: the mishna follows R. Yehuda, so the proof for R. Yoḥanan fails.
Baraita of R. Yehuda: the altar stood centered, 32 cubits wide, aligned with the Sanctuary's width.
Asks whether the mishna can follow R. Yehuda, since even by his view the arrangement must move 11 or 6 cubits.
The four cubits are in addition to the base and ledge, so the total is six cubits, and the mishna follows R. Yehuda.
Asks why Rav Adda did not read the mishna as R. Yosei's view, with the altar centered.
R. Yehuda's central-altar view was explicitly heard, whereas R. Yosei's was not, so the mishna is read as R. Yehuda's.
Rav Sherevya says the mishna follows R. Yosei HaGelili, who holds the whole altar is in the north.
Baraita of R. Yosei HaGelili: Exodus 40:7 and 40:6 place the basin between the Tent and the altar, showing the altar's position.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: From Exodus 40:29 R. Yosei HaGelili derives that the Basin was not at the Tent entrance but between the Entrance Hall and the altar, slightly south.
Tests R. Yosei HaGelili's view: if the whole altar is south, the Basin could stand elsewhere, so why does he place it so?
Even if Sanctuary and Entrance Hall share one sanctity, the Basin could stand south of the Entrance Hall wall; his failure to say so shows the altar is not south.
If half the altar is north and half south, the Basin could still stand between altar and Sanctuary without blocking the entrance.
Same objection with equal halls, then asks why the Basin must be south, concluding the whole altar must be north.
Asks why the Basin must be south of the altar if it could be north of the Sanctuary wall and still lie between the Entrance Hall and altar.
Even with equal sanctity of hall and Sanctuary, the Basin could stand north of the Entrance Hall wall between hall and altar.
That is not feasible: Leviticus 1:11 says the north must be kept clear of all vessels, including the Basin.
Asks who the tanna is who disagrees with R. Yosei HaGelili.
Baraita: R. Eliezer ben Yaakov reads 'northward before the Lord' as requiring the north to be clear even of the altar, so the whole altar is south.
Rav rules that sacrifices slaughtered on a damaged altar are disqualified, a halakha he traces to a verse he has forgotten.
Rav Kahana found Rabbi Shimon citing R. Yishmael son of R. Yosei on this rule.
Asks from where we derive that all offerings slaughtered on a damaged altar are disqualified.
Exodus 20:21 permits slaughter only on a complete altar, so a damaged one disqualifies, the verse Rav had forgotten.
R. Yoḥanan rules that both kinds of animals designated while the altar was damaged are disqualified, even if not yet slaughtered.
Asks what Rav and R. Yoḥanan actually disagree about.
They disagree whether living animals are permanently deferred: Rav says no, so only slaughtered ones are disqualified; R. Yoḥanan says yes.
Objects to Rav from a baraita on animals consecrated before the altar was built, which seems to disqualify them.
Proposes reading the baraita about altar destruction in the First Temple, but objects that the animals would be too old by then.
Reinterprets the baraita as a damaged-altar case, and rejects the proof by reading it as slaughter before damage, so the question stays open.
Objects to Rav from the rule that incense may be burned at a displaced golden altar, implying an altar is not essential.
Rava's principle: Rabbi Yehuda allows burning portions anywhere but requires blood on the altar; so Rav concedes blood needs an altar.
Asks what the context of Rabbi Yehuda's statement is.
Baraita on Solomon's inauguration: the bronze altar was too small, so the courtyard's middle was sanctified to hold the offerings, as Rabbi Yehuda says.
R. Yosei begins a reply to R. Yehuda, which continues on the next daf.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: the altar of Moses already received a thousand offerings, and the Temple altar received far more, so the Temple altar was not too small.
Notes that Solomon's offerings per square cubit were greater on Moses' altar, so the claim that the Temple altar was too small is hard to sustain.
R. Yosei: the verse is a euphemism for the Moses altar being disqualified, like calling a man a dwarf to mean he is unfit for service.
R. Yehuda holds consistently that Moses' altar was large, so R. Yosei's claim is persuasive to him on his own terms.
Baraita: Exodus 27:1 gives the Mosaic altar as five cubits by five, read as stated, per R. Yosei.
R. Yehuda derives from the word square in Exodus 27:1 and Ezekiel 43:16 that the Mosaic altar was measured from its center, so it was ten by ten.
Asks from where we know that the Ezekiel altar was measured from its center.
Ezekiel 43:16 says twelve cubits to its four sides, which teaches that the measurement was taken from the center.
Asks how R. Yosei responds to R. Yehuda's claim.
R. Yosei learns the verbal analogy with regard to the altar's height, not its length.
Baraita: Exodus 27:1 gives the Mosaic altar a height of three cubits, read as stated, per R. Yehuda.
R. Yosei: the altar's square form matches the incense altar's, whose height is twice its length, so the Mosaic altar was ten cubits high.
R. Yehuda objects: Exodus 27:18 gives the court height as five cubits, so a ten-cubit altar would expose the priest to the whole nation.
R. Yosei replies that Numbers 4:26 juxtaposes the Tabernacle with the altar, so the altar was ten cubits high like the Tabernacle.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yosei: Exodus 38:14 gives fifteen cubits for the courtyard curtains, and Exodus 27:18 means they stood five cubits above the altar.
R. Yosei continues: Exodus 27:1's three-cubit height is measured from the edge of the surrounding ledge and above.
Asks how R. Yehuda, who takes the Mosaic altar as three cubits high, reads the square-based analogy.
Asks whether, on R. Yehuda's view that the altar was three cubits high, the priest would be visible while serving atop it.
The priest is visible, but the service items in his hand are not.
If R. Yehuda holds the courtyard floor was consecrated to serve as an altar, I Kings 8:64 is explained.
Asks what 'sanctified' means for R. Yosei, who does not hold the courtyard served as an altar.
For R. Yosei, sanctifying the courtyard means setting an altar in it.
For R. Yosei, 'too small' describes the five-by-five Mosaic altar; for R. Yehuda it describes Solomon's stone altar, which was too small.
Asks what principle the two Sages disagree about in deriving dimensions by analogy.
R. Yehuda derives outer-altar dimensions from Ezekiel's outer altar, but not from the inner incense altar.
R. Yosei derives portable-vessel dimensions from another portable vessel, but not from the stone edifice.
Rava: R. Yehuda concedes blood must be presented on the altar, citing his Passover baraita about the cup of mixed blood.
Rava explains: if the whole courtyard had altar status, the Paschal mitzva would be fulfilled even when the blood was never presented on the altar.
Objects: R. Yehuda may require the cup be poured on the altar because a human must pour the blood, not because the floor lacks altar status.
Rejects Rava's proof: R. Yehuda may merely prefer the optimal performance, on the altar itself.
R. Elazar: the remainder of a meal offering may not be eaten when the altar is damaged, based on Leviticus 10:12.
Asks from where this halakha applies to all offerings of the most sacred order.
The phrase 'it is most holy' is also used of the other most sacred offerings, so the same rule extends to them by verbal analogy.
Asks from where the same rule applies to offerings of lesser sanctity.
Abaye cites a baraita in the name of R. Yosei, who states three matters on this point.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Introduces the opinion as that of one of three elders, R. Yishmael.
R. Yishmael: one might think second-tithe produce may be eaten in Jerusalem now, but a logical inference from firstborn offerings shows it may be eaten only in the Temple's presence.
Objects that the firstborn comparison fails: firstborn needs blood placed on the altar, while second tithe needs no such placement, and first fruits show that placement is not the factor.
Deuteronomy 12:6 juxtaposes second tithe with firstborn, so second tithe is restricted to the Temple's presence like firstborn offerings.
Asks why a verse is needed, since the shared element of firstborn and first fruits could derive the rule for second tithe.
That derivation fails: firstborn and first fruits share an altar-offering aspect that second tithe lacks.
Asks what R. Yishmael holds about whether the Temple's initial consecration was permanent, since it would then bear on firstborn too.
Ravina: R. Yishmael holds the consecration was not permanent, and the case is a firstborn slaughtered and sprinkled before the Temple's destruction.
Its meat is forbidden because Numbers 18:17-18 juxtaposes its blood and meat, so eating the meat requires an altar, and second tithe is derived from it.
Asks whether a halakha derived by juxtaposition can be extended to a third case by another juxtaposition, which the principle forbids for sacred matters.
Second-tithe grain is non-sacred, so the usual restriction on derivation does not apply.
Asks how the derivation works under the rival principle, which follows the matter that teaches rather than the matter derived.
Blood and meat are one matter, so there is one derivation, and Abaye's ruling on lesser sanctity is supported by R. Yishmael as cited by R. Yosei.
Ravin states in Eretz Yisrael that even lesser-sanctity items are disqualified if the altar is damaged, and R. Yirmeya rebukes the Babylonians for it.
Yirmeya cites a baraita: during the wilderness journeys, sacrificial food was disqualified while the altar was not in place.
Another baraita allows consuming sacrificial food in two locations, which seems to contradict Abaye unless it refers to lesser-sanctity items.
Ravina reconciles: both baraitot concern offerings of lesser sanctity, so there is no difficulty.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reconciles the two baraitot: the first follows R. Yishmael and the second follows the Sages, who disagree with him.
Alternative reconciliation: both baraitot concern the most sacred offerings, and the two locations are before the Levites set up the Tabernacle at a new camp.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: after the Levites dismantle the Tabernacle but before the altar is moved, the sacrificial food may still be eaten.
The ruling is stated to rule out that the food is disqualified once the courtyard partitions are removed.
Objects that the food should be disqualified once outside the partitions, and answers that Numbers 2:17 keeps the traveling tent counted as the Tent of Meeting.
Rav Huna reports Rav's view that the Shiloh altar was made of stones, unlike Moses' copper altar.
Baraita of R. Eliezer ben Yaakov: the triple mention of stone in the altar verses alludes to three stone altars, at Shiloh, Nov and Gibeon, and the Temple.
Rav Aḥa bar Ami objects: the fire departed the copper altar only in Solomon's day, which would be inconsistent with a Shiloh stone altar earlier.
Rav Huna follows R. Natan, who holds the Shiloh altar was copper, hollow and filled with stones.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the fire was not wholly removed, lingering on the copper altar beside the stone one, as sparks or as an occasional guest.
Mishna: the First Temple altar was twenty-eight cubits square and was enlarged to thirty-two on the south and west sides in the Second Temple.
Asks the reason for the enlargement.
Rav Yosef: the First Temple altar was not sufficient for the offerings.
Abaye objects: if the First Temple altar sufficed for its vast population, why would the smaller Second Temple congregation need a larger altar?
Rav Yosef replies: a heavenly fire aided the First Temple offerings, but no such fire aided the Second Temple, so more room was needed.
Ravin reports R. Shimon ben Pazi in Bar Kappara's name: the altar was extended over underground cavities into which libations flowed, since originally it had to be filled with earth.
Asks the meaning of 'altar of earth' once the altar was built over cavities.
Later the altar's drinking was held to be like its eating, so libations were poured on top; 'altar of earth' still means it must be attached to the earth, not built over arches.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes the verse about the altar, which may not be built on top of tunnels.
Rav Yosef: a baraita on Ezra 3:3 says the Second Temple altar reached its full measure, while the First Temple's did not.
Objects: I Chronicles 28:19 says the whole Temple design was written by God's hand, so the First Temple altar was not deficient.
Rav Yosef: the First Temple altar was ideal, but the Second Temple needed expansion, and I Chronicles 22:1 links the altar to the House's sixty cubits.
Asks how the builders knew the altar's proper location, since the House's shape could be seen from its foundations.
Rabbi Elazar: they saw a vision of the altar, with Michael offering on it; R. Yitzḥak Nappaḥa: they saw Isaac's ashes; R. Shmuel bar Naḥmani: the scents located it.
R. Yoḥanan: three prophets came up from exile, one for the altar's size and shape, one for its location, and one teaching that sacrifice is valid without a Temple.
Baraita of R. Eliezer ben Yaakov gives the same three prophets, with the third one instructing the Torah be written in Ashurit script.
Baraita: the corners, ramp, base and squareness are indispensable, and length, width and height are not; Rav Huna derives this from the term 'the altar'.
Asks why the engraving or surrounding ledge is not also indispensable, given Exodus 27:5 about the karkov.
Baraita: R. Yehuda HaNasi says the karkov is the engraving, while R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda says it is the surrounding ledge.
Yes, the karkov is indispensable: a damaged corner was sealed with salt so the altar would not appear damaged, and R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda holds the ledge too is indispensable.
Baraita defines the karkov as the cubit-wide area between corners, where the priests walked.
Rephrases it: the karkov is the cubit between corners, with an additional cubit for the priests' walking place.
Asks how the karkov can be on the altar's side if Exodus 38:4 places it under the grating reaching halfway up.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: there were two karkovs, one a slight protrusion for beauty and one an indentation on top for the priests' safety.
R. Mani: the dimensions are not indispensable, provided the altar is not reduced below Moses' altar.
Rav Yosef says Moses' altar was one cubit, which the study hall mocked, so the fuller answer is given by the verse.
Exodus 27:1 states the altar was five cubits long and five cubits wide, square, refuting the one-cubit claim.
Abaye suggests Rav Yosef meant the area of the wood arrangement, which would leave only one cubit for it.
Rav Yosef answers that Abaye, a great man, knows what he meant, and he applies the verse to those who mocked him.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Genesis 25:4 on the children of Keturah, as the opening for a remark on Rav Yosef's other students.
Narrative: Tarfon's sister's sons sit silent; Tarfon reads 'Yoḥani' and they correct it to Keturah, so he calls them the children of Keturah.
Abaye bar Huna reports R. Ḥama bar Gurya: Moses' logs were one cubit long and wide, and as thick as a leveler.
R. Yirmeya says the measures use a shortened cubit.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita on Leviticus 1:8: the superfluous 'upon the altar' limits the wood to the one-cubit square, so logs are one cubit.
Mishna: the altar's ramp lay on the south side, 32 cubits long and 16 wide.
Asks from where we derive that the ramp lies on the south side.
Rav Huna: Leviticus 1:11 places the altar's thigh in the north and its face in the south, like a person lying down.
Asks why not say the thigh and face are both north, like a person sitting.
Rava: place the man face down, so the analogy is to someone lying down.
Abaye objects: rather seat the man upright so that face and feet point the same way.
Rava cites Exodus 27:1, which says the altar is square, and suggests the word ravua alludes to crouching.
Abaye objects: the word is needed to teach squareness, and asks whether the verse says ravutz.
Rava answers that the verse says ravua, which alludes to lying down and so teaches the altar's position.
Another tanna derives the ramp's position from a different source.
Baraita of R. Yehuda: Ezekiel 43:17 says the altar's steps face east, so turns must go right, placing the ramp on the south.
Objects that the verse only shows the priest faces east after turning, so the ramp could be north with a left turn.
Rami bar Yeḥizkiya: II Chronicles 4:4 describes the Basin's oxen in the order north, west, south, east, showing only right turns and an east-facing ramp.
Asks why the verse repeats 'turns' if it is only to teach the Basin's description.
Asks whether R. Shimon ben Yoḥai held that there is an air gap between the ramp and the altar.
R. Yosei cites Deuteronomy 12:27, which juxtaposes flesh with blood, so flesh is tossed as blood is, across a gap from the ramp.
R. Shimon: the priest stands beside the wood arrangement and tosses the flesh onto it, with no gap needed.
R. Yosei objects: the flesh must be tossed onto burning wood, which cannot be placed directly, so the verse must require a gap.
Resolves that direct placement into the fire is impossible, so the verse must mean tossing across the gap.
Rav Pappa: the flesh is juxtaposed with blood, so as blood is tossed across space from the priest, so is the flesh.
Rav Yehuda: two small ramps branched from the main ramp, separated from the altar by a hair's breadth.
Asks whether the separation source is the word 'roundabout' in Leviticus 1:5.
R. Abbahu: the altar must be square, as the altar's lack of attached ramps shows; 'roundabout' and 'square' are both needed.
Both terms are necessary: 'roundabout' alone would allow a circle, and 'square' alone would allow a long, narrow altar.
Mishna: the ramp and altar together were 62 cubits, though 32 plus 32 gives 64.
The ramp overhung the altar's base and the surrounding ledge by one cubit each, so its effective length was 32 cubits.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rami bar Ḥama: minor ramps rise one cubit in three, and the main ramp slightly less steeply so priests can climb holding portions.
Mishna: handfuls of meal offerings are taken anywhere in the courtyard and eaten by priestly males, until midnight.
R. Elazar: a meal offering whose handful was taken in the Sanctuary is valid, as the frankincense bowls were removed there.
R. Yirmeya objects to R. Elazar from a baraita: 'from there' in Leviticus 2:2 means the handful is taken from the courtyard, not the Sanctuary.
Ben Beteira: the verse 'from there' also means a priest who took a handful with his left hand returns it and takes another with his right.
Some say Yirmeya raises and resolves the objection himself; others say R. Akiva explained it to him.
R. Akiva: the verse only validates the whole courtyard for taking the handful, not excluding the Sanctuary.
Hypothetical objection: as a meal offering is most sacred, like a burnt offering it might need taking in the north.
A burnt offering is wholly burned on the altar, and a sin offering atones for karet liability, so neither source fits the handful.
A guilt offering is a blood-rite offering, unlike meal offerings, so the analogy from it and the common element both fail.
The verse about bringing the meal offering to the altar's corner is what prompted the concern, and the baraita teaches that the handful may be taken anywhere in the courtyard.
R. Yoḥanan: peace offerings slaughtered in the Sanctuary are valid, since the courtyard, a lesser place, cannot be weightier than the Sanctuary.
Objects with a baraita of Ben Beteira: priests may eat most-sacred offerings in the Sanctuary when the courtyard is overrun, from Numbers 18:10.
Asks why a separate source is needed, since Leviticus 6:9 could give the same rule and show R. Yoḥanan's method is invalid.
Slaughter is a rite done in the master's presence, unlike eating, so the lesser-place argument applies only to slaughter.
Mishna: the bird sin offering was done at the southwest corner, with three rites below the red line and three above it.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: priests ascending for the bird sin offering rites go straight to the southwest corner and descend by retracing their path, not circling the altar.
Asks from where the mishna's southwest-corner rule derives.
R. Yehoshua: Leviticus 5:11 calls the sin offering a meal offering and the meal offering a sin offering, so their rules can be compared.
So the sin offering's north-side slaughter and southwest-corner sprinkling carry over to the meal offering's handful and bringing near the altar.
Asks where the meal offering itself must be brought near the altar.
Baraita on Leviticus 6:7: 'before the Lord' suggests the west side, 'in front of the altar' suggests the south, where the ramp is.
Continuing the baraita: 'in front of the altar' alone would suggest the south side; reconciled, the priest brings it at the southwest corner.
R. Eliezer's principle: when two verses conflict, follow the one that fulfils both, so the meal offering is brought at the southwest corner.
Bringing it on the south side fulfils both 'in front of the altar' and 'before the Lord', so the south side is required.
Asks how the south-side rite fulfils 'before the Lord'.
Rav Ashi: this tanna holds the whole altar is north, so its south side faces the Sanctuary entrance and counts as before the Lord.
Rav Ashi explains the bird sin offering mishna: any place was valid for pinching the nape, but the southwest corner was the place for sprinkling its blood.
Baraita: the bird's blood may be sprinkled and pinched in any place, but the rest of the blood must be squeezed at the altar base, valid as long as some blood is placed below the red line.
Asks what the baraita means, since it says the offering is valid anywhere yet requires blood below the red line.
Pinching or sprinkling anywhere is valid, but the squeezing of the blood must be specifically below the red line.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's conclusion: a sprinkled offering whose blood was not squeezed out is still valid if some blood is placed at or below the red line.
Mishna's first list: three matters performed below the red line at the southwest corner.
Sources for the three below-the-line rites: the bird sin offering's rite, the meal offering's bringing near the altar, and the blood poured at the base.
Mishna's second list: three matters performed above the red line, including the libations and the bird burnt offering in the east.
Asks the reason the bird burnt offering is ideally done at the southeast corner.
R. Yoḥanan: the southeast corner is closest to the ash place, where the crop and feathers are placed.
R. Yoḥanan remarks on the priests' strength, since they tossed bird parts over thirty cubits from the southwest corner.
Mishna in Tamid describes the ash-clearing procedure: coals are carried down the ramp and heaped about ten cubits away.
Objects that the distance from the southwest corner exceeds thirty-one cubits; answers that the priest's own space was not counted.
Mishna: everyone ascends the ramp's right side and descends its left, except those doing libations or bird burnt offerings at the southwest corner.
Asks the reason for these exceptions to the standard route.
R. Yoḥanan: libations would absorb the altar smoke, and a bird would die by inhaling the smoke, if the priest walked around.
Objects with a Tamid mishna: the High Priest circles the altar from the southeast and holds wine for libation, so the smoke concern is not real.
R. Yoḥanan begins his reply to the contradiction; the reply continues on the next daf.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The circling of the altar is done on foot, empty-handed, so the wine is given only later.
Rava proves this from the mishna's wording that wine is given to him, not that he is told to pour.
Baraita: everyone ascends the ramp on its right and descends on its left, with listed exceptions for west-side rites.
Asks whether the west-side ascent counts as the right side, or is in fact the left.
Ravina proposes emending the baraita to say left; Rava explains right and left as seen from the altar or from the person.
Objects that the baraita should be consistent, using either the altar's or the person's standpoint throughout; the Gemara concedes it is difficult.
Mishna: how the bird sin offering was performed, with blood sprinkled below the red line and the bird given to priests.
Proof from the verse that the sprinkling is taken directly from the sin offering's body, not by finger or vessel.
How it is done: the priest holds head and body and sprinkles on the altar wall, not the ramp, Sanctuary or hall walls.
Asks which wall is meant; answers that it is the lower wall.
Suggests the upper wall instead, by an a fortiori argument from where burnt and sin offering blood is applied.
The verse about the remaining blood being drained is cited to refute the upper-wall suggestion.
The verse teaches that blood is sprinkled on the wall from which it drips to the base; that is the lower wall.
Objects that one could sprinkle above and then drain below, following the order of the verses.
Rava replies that the text says it shall be drained, passive, so the blood must trickle down on its own.
Rav describes how to pinch a bird sin offering's nape: holding wings and legs with fingers and stretching the neck.
A baraita gives a variant grip, with the bird held outside the palm, calling this the hardest Temple service.

ranges.en: Resolving the two approaches, the verse says tereifa fat is pure only for animals whose species can become tereifa, i.e., kosher ones.

Rabbi Yohanan: Rabbi Meir deemed pure only unblemished bird offerings whose napes were pinched, not blemished ones.

Closing formula marking the end of the chapter beginning with the bird sin offering.

ranges.en: Asks how a disqualified bird sin offering pinched at the top of the altar can be sprinkled from its blood.
Rejects the proof: the blood is pressed against the wall, which is squeezing or pouring rather than sprinkling.
Objects that the sprinkling manner of the other offerings also cannot be done this way, so airspace must count as the altar.
Rav Ashi: the dilemma concerns holding items over the altar with a pole, and it remains unresolved.
Mishna: service vessels sanctify only the items of their type, only when whole and full, and only in the sacred area.
Shmuel: the rule that liquid vessels do not sanctify dry items applies to measures, but not to cups for blood.
Cites the verse about two silver cups full of fine flour, showing cups sanctify dry items.
Rav Aḥa of Difti objects that the meal offering is mixed with oil, so the verse proves nothing about dry items.
Ravina: the verse covers dry flour that was not mixed with oil, or the meal offering is dry compared to blood.
Shmuel's rule: vessels sanctify only when whole, full, and only from within; the baraita versions differ on this.
Asks what the difference is between the two versions of Shmuel's ruling.
The difference is heaping measures; a baraita is taught in accordance with both versions.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: full means the priest did not intend to add; if he intended to add, each initial amount is sacred.
A baraita teaches the same distinction, with Rabbi Yosei adding that intent to add makes initial amounts sacred.
Liquid vessels do not sanctify dry items.
Rav, or Rav Asi, holds that such vessels sanctify dry items only to be disqualified, not for sacrifice.
Some teach this about meal offerings and first fruits mixed with teruma, orla, or diverse kinds, which may not be brought.
If such items were brought, they are not sanctified for sacrifice, but are sanctified to be disqualified.
Baraita: perforated sacred vessels, damaged knives, and vestments are not to be repaired, plus Abba Shaul's story of a hidden knife.
Baraita: priestly vestments are woven, not sewn, and soiled ones are laundered only with water, not natron or soap.
Asks whether this implies that the vestments may be laundered with water.
Abaye: the baraita means that garments soiled only enough to need water may be laundered with natron and soap.

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye's conclusion: with water only, vestments may be laundered; some say they may never be laundered, since poverty has no place in wealth.
Baraita: the High Priest's robe was entirely sky-blue wool, as the verse on the robe of the ephod states.
Baraita describes how the robe's skirts were made, with pomegranates and bells in exact numbers.
Rabbi Dosa in the name of Rabbi Yehuda gives a different count of the bells on the robe.
Rabbi Inini bar Sason compares the bell dispute to the dispute over the number of shades of leprous marks.
Rabbi Inini: just as offerings atone, the priestly vestments atone, since the sections are juxtaposed.
The tunic atones for bloodshed and the trousers for forbidden relations, each supported by a verse.
The mitre atones for arrogance, reasoned from the fact that it sits at the height of the head.
The belt atones for thoughts of the heart, the breastplate for improper judgments, and the ephod for idolatry, each supported by verses.
The robe atones for malicious speech.
Rabbi Ḥanina explains by logic: an item that makes sound, the bells, atones for an evil sound.
The frontplate atones for brazenness, based on the verses about the frontplate and the harlot's forehead.
Asks whether the vestments atone for these sins, given Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view that bloodshed and slander are atoned elsewhere.
Bloodshed is atoned by the heifer whose neck is broken, and malicious speech by incense.
Baraita of Rav Ḥananya: the verse on Aaron putting on incense and atoning for the people proves incense atones.
School of Rabbi Yishmael: incense atones for slander because the priest offers it alone in private, like a private act.
Notes the apparent conflict: the robe atones for slander and bloodshed, while the baraita assigns them to other means.
Bloodshed: the tunic atones when the killer is known, and the heifer when he is not; a known killer not punished by a court is only forewarned.
Slander: incense atones for private slander, and the robe for slander spoken in public.
End-of-chapter marker: the chapter Hamizbeaḥ Mekadesh is concluded.

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: more frequent offerings precede less frequent ones, e.g. daily before additional, Shabbat before New Moon additional.
Cites the verse on the additional offerings, 'besides the burnt offering of the morning', as the source.
Asks from where the principle of frequency is derived, since the verse might only cover daily offerings.
Asks from where we derive that the more frequent precedes the less frequent among additional offerings.
Rabbi Ile'a derives it from the verse 'like these you shall offer daily for seven days'.
Objects that this verse is needed to teach its own halakha, that the additional offerings recur each day.
Suggests the verse would then say 'these you shall offer daily' so the principle comes from 'like these'.
Rejects the suggestion: 'these' alone would imply all offerings are sacrificed together over the seven days.
Objects that 'these' could cover only the first day, leaving the other days' offerings unknown.
The verse says 'you shall offer', so all rites on every day of Passover are equal.
Abaye derives the principle from the verse itself, since 'which is for a daily burnt offering' would otherwise be superfluous.
Mishna: more sacred offerings precede less sacred ones; sin offering blood precedes burnt offering blood, as it atones.
Burnt offering limbs precede sin offering portions, since the burnt offering is wholly consumed on the altar.
Sin offering precedes guilt offering, since its blood goes on four corners of the altar.
Guilt offering precedes thanks and nazirite offerings, which precede peace offerings for their one-day eating and loaves.
Peace offering precedes firstborn, since it needs placements, hand-laying, libations, and waves; firstborn precedes tithe.
Firstborn is sanctified from the womb and eaten by priests, while everyone may eat the tithe.
Animal tithe precedes birds, since it is a sacrifice with blood and fats offered on the altar.
Bird offerings precede meal offerings, since blood atones; a sinner's meal offering precedes a voluntary one, since it atones a sin.
Bird sin offering precedes bird burnt offering, and likewise in consecration.

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where the mishna's rules on sin and burnt offering precedence are derived.
A baraita cites the verse about the Levites' consecration, with a second bull as a sin offering.
Asks why the verse says two bulls, when another verse already states one sin and one burnt offering.
The verse teaches that the sin offering is second in order, not first for all rites of the burnt offering.
If the verse named only the second bull, one might think the burnt offering precedes in all rites, so both verses are reconciled.
Summarizes the baraita: sin offering blood precedes burnt offering blood because it atones, and burnt offering limbs precede sin offering portions.
Asks why all four placements of the sin offering blood precede the burnt offering blood, when only the first atones.
Ravina: the verse concerns the Levites' sin offering, and the Torah makes all placements precede; Eretz Yisrael adds that starting completes the rite.
Raises a dilemma: which precedes, sin offering blood or burnt offering limbs?
Suggests resolving it from the mishna: sin offering blood precedes burnt offering blood, but not its limbs.
Rejects that inference: the latter clause shows limbs precede only sin offering portions, so the mishna settles nothing.
Raises a dilemma: burnt offering blood or sin offering portions, which precedes?
Suggests resolving it from the mishna's sin offering blood before burnt offering blood, with portions not included.
Rejects this as well: the latter clause gives the burnt offering limbs precedence over sin offering portions only.
Raises a dilemma: burnt offering blood or guilt offering blood, which precedes?
Suggests resolving it from the mishna: sin offering blood precedes burnt offering blood, so guilt blood does not.
Explains that the mishna mentions a sin offering in the former clause because of the latter clause's subject, and not for the guilt offering.
Suggests from the mishna that sin offering precedes guilt offering, but burnt offering does not.
Rejects this: the mishna concerns sacrificial portions, as shown by its phrasing about four corners.
Mishna: a sin offering precedes a guilt offering, since its blood is placed on four corners and poured at the base.
Challenges that the guilt offering should precede, since it has a minimum value; the four placements still outweigh that.
Mishna: a guilt offering precedes a thanks offering and nazirite ram, since it is most sacred.
Challenges that thanks and ram should precede, since they need loaves; the guilt offering's higher sanctity still outweighs.
Mishna: thanks and nazirite ram precede peace offering, since they are eaten for one day.
Challenges that peace offerings precede, since they are communal too; one-day eating still outweighs.
Raises a dilemma: thanks offering or nazirite ram, which precedes?
A baraita answers: the thanks offering precedes, since it requires four types of loaves, and the ram only two.
Mishna: the peace offering precedes the firstborn offering, due to its additional rites.
Challenges that firstborn should precede, since it is sanctified from the womb and eaten only by priests; more rites still outweigh.
Mishna: the firstborn offering precedes the animal tithe offering.
Challenges that the tithe should precede, since it is consecrated in its surrounding space; womb sanctity still outweighs.
Mishna: the animal tithe precedes bird offerings.
Challenges that birds should precede, since they are most sacred; animal kind still outweighs.
Ravina bar Shila: the fats of lesser-sanctity offerings that went out before sprinkling are disqualified, and are called most sacred.
Asks what the teaching adds, since fats of birds are not offered; it must teach that fats precede sprinkling like blood.
Argues from blood and flesh: since blood is disqualified when it goes out, fats are too, supporting the view on flesh.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the flesh that went out is fit, while Reish Lakish holds it is disqualified, since its time to go out has not come.
The dispute is only about flesh, not fats, though the Gemara notes they may dispute fats too.
The dispute over flesh is cited to show Reish Lakish's view: even flesh whose end is to go out is not yet at its time.
Asks whether this is a tanna dispute, where Rabbi Eliezer holds that fats which went out before sprinkling cannot be misused.

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a person is not liable for piggul, notar, or impurity for these portions; Rabbi Akiva holds he is liable for misuse.
Explains the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds portions taken out of the courtyard are disqualified, while Rabbi Akiva disagrees.
Rav Pappa rejects that: returned portions are fit for all, and the dispute concerns portions outside when blood is sprinkled.
Challenges Rav Pappa from the two loaves of Shavuot, which should show the same dispute.
Reply: the loaves are not part of the offering itself, so the dispute on portions is only when they are outside the courtyard.
Mishna: bird offerings precede meal offerings, since their blood is sprinkled and it atones.
Challenges that meal offerings precede, since they come communally too; the blood-type status of birds still outweighs.
Mishna: a sinner's meal offering precedes a voluntary meal offering.
Challenges that voluntary meal offerings precede, since they require oil and frankincense; atonement still outweighs.
Raises a dilemma: a sota's meal offering or a voluntary meal offering, which precedes?
Suggests resolving it from the mishna: a sinner's meal offering precedes a voluntary one, but not a sota's.
Rejects the proof: the mishna gives the reason of atonement, and a sota's offering also comes because of sin.
A baraita: one meal offering precedes another since it is made of wheat rather than barley; suggests a sota comparison.
Asks whether the baraita concerns a voluntary offering versus a sota's, rather than a sinner's offering.
Explains that the baraita gives one of two reasons, so no inference can be drawn from the omission of the other.
Mishna: a bird sin offering precedes a bird burnt offering.
Asks from where this rule is derived.
A baraita cites Leviticus on the poor sinner's offering: the verse teaches the sin offering precedes the burnt offering.
The verse establishes a general rule that all sin offerings precede the burnt offerings brought with them, including bird and animal combinations.
Rabbi Eliezer's baraita: in every exchange of a bird for an animal sin offering the sin offering precedes, but a birth offering reverses this.
Rava reconciles this with the rule: the verse mentions the burnt offering first only for reading, but the sin offering is offered first.
Another baraita: bulls precede rams, rams precede sheep, and sheep precede male goats, apparently contradicting the rule.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the baraita's list refers to the additional offerings of Sukkot.
No: all these animals in the baraita are free-will gift offerings.
Explains the order by libations and portion size: bulls before rams, rams before sheep, and sheep before goats.
Comes to contradict the rule that sin offerings precede burnt offerings, citing a baraita on communal idolatry bulls and goats.
Reply: the opposite is derived from the first clause, where the communal sin bull precedes the idolatry burnt offering.
Dismisses the reply: the rule only holds for two species, and here a burnt offering precedes a sin offering.
Reconciles the baraitot: the idolatry sin offering is written without an alef, and 'according to the ordinance' fixes its order.
Raises a dilemma on whether a bird sin offering, an animal burnt offering, or an animal tithe comes first.
Babylonia and Eretz Yisrael give different answers on which factor governs this order.
Mishna: all sin offerings precede guilt offerings, except a leper's guilt offering, which renders one fit.
All guilt offerings are rams in their second year worth two shekels, except the nazirite's and the leper's.
More sacred offerings precede others in eating too: yesterday's peace offering precedes today's.
Rabbi Meir: yesterday's peace offering precedes today's sin offering; the Rabbis hold the sin offering precedes, as most sacred.
Priests may alter how offerings are cooked and season them with teruma spices, per Rabbi Shimon, while Rabbi Meir forbids teruma spices.
Raises a dilemma: a frequent offering or a more sacred one, which precedes?
Suggests resolving it from the first mishna of the chapter, where daily offerings precede additional ones for being frequent.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rejects the proof: Shabbat's sanctity raises the daily offerings too, so both are equal in sanctity.
Cites the mishna on Shabbat and New Moon additional offerings as a proof, then rejects it the same way.
Cites the mishna on New Moon and New Year additional offerings as a proof, which is rejected similarly.
Cites the Tosefta on the order of kiddush blessings as a proof, which is also rejected.
Cites Rabbi Yoḥanan on the afternoon and additional prayers as a proof, which is rejected as well.
Cites the mishna on yesterday's peace offering as a proof that frequency counts for peace offerings.
Rava replies: that concerns a common offering, and the dilemma is only about frequent versus higher-sanctity offerings.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda objects: a common obligation counts as frequent, as circumcision shows by comparison with Passover.
Rava replies that circumcision is frequent given its many commands, or relative to Passover.
Raises a dilemma: if a priest slaughtered the infrequent offering first, must he finish it or give it to another priest?
Rav Huna of Sura announces a proof from the mishna on yesterday's peace offering and today's sin offering.
Infers from the mishna that only yesterday's peace offering precedes, and the Gemara explains how the case must have arisen.
Returns to the kiddush baraita: frequency of the wine blessing outweighs the sanctity of the day blessing, as a parallel to slaughter order.
Cites Rabbi Yoḥanan's prayer ruling as a parallel, which is rejected since both obligations arise together.
Rav Aḥa son of Rav Ashi cites the Passover mishna: the daily offering is slaughtered first and the Paschal blood sprinkled after.
Rejects that proof: the daily offering was slaughtered first, and the mishna's wording shows the daily offering was already slaughtered.
Mishna: priests may alter how all eaten offerings are consumed.
The reason is the verse on gifts lemoshḥa, read as for greatness, so the flesh is eaten as kings eat.
Rabbi Shimon: oil seen in the Temple courtyard for priests is leftover wafer oil or a leper's log, not a gift.
Oil burned on the altar is leftover priestly or anointed-priest oil, and oil cannot be a gift offering; Rabbi Tarfon disagrees.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules that per Rabbi Tarfon oil may be a voluntary offering, its handful burned and remainder eaten
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's ruling
A verse about the meal offering is taken to teach that oil may be voluntarily contributed, with the same handling
Rabbi Zeira says we also learned this in a mishna
Rabbi Shimon's mishna about oil distributed in the Temple court is cited in support
Abaye tells Zeira to cite the last clause of the mishna, challenging his reading
The mishna's second clause about oil placed on the altar flames is brought as the contrasting source
Abaye infers from the mishna that the one who holds oil may be contributed is one who holds all goes to the altar fires
For Abaye the two clauses of the mishna contradict each other on Zeira's reading
Zeira's reply: the first clause refers to the leftover oil and the last to the handful, so no contradiction
For Abaye the difficulty remains: could a tanna teach the first clause because of the last
Would a tanna teach the first clause of a mishna because of the last clause
Reply: yes, Eretz Yisrael sages say a tanna did teach the first clause because of the last
A baraita on wine and oil contributions, following Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon, is brought as a proof
The Gemara asks whether the baraita should be read as a dispute between the two halves
Rejected reading: the baraita states each case as it stands, so no such dispute is needed
Rav Pappa says the disagreement is a dispute between tanna'im
A baraita is cited: oil should not be less than a log, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says three logs
The Gemara asks what the actual point of disagreement between them is
The Sages explain the dispute: whether the inference from the meal offering applies to oil, with the reasoning elaborated
An analogy from libations is brought: three logs for libations, so three logs for oil
Rav Pappa says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would not disagree if the source were the meal offering, so he derives it from libations
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan challenges Rav Pappa with a baraita where korban teaches oil, and asks who says three logs
Reply: if a baraita is taught, it is taught, so the source is accepted
Shmuel rules that one who contributes wine brings it and pours it on the altar fire
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's ruling
A verse on the wine libation as an offering made by fire is cited as the source
Extinguishing only part of a coal is not extinguishing, yet Rav Naḥman's statement says liability for extinguishing applies
Reply: the case is where only one coal remains, so the fire is fully extinguished; a mitzva extinguishing differs
A baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says one may not extinguish the coals before removing ashes
Distinction upholding the view: there it is possible to sit and guard the fire, so extinguishing is unnecessary
A second baraita on wine and oil contributions, with ‘or does it apply only to the altar’, challenges the view
No contradiction: the first baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda and the second follows Rabbi Shimon, and Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon
Shmuel's ruling on extinguishing a metal coal in the public domain is cited to show he follows Rabbi Shimon

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If one may not extinguish a wood coal, then on Shmuel's view following Rabbi Shimon even a wood coal should be permitted
Shmuel's statements do not conflict: for an unintended act he follows Rabbi Shimon, while for labor not needed for itself he follows Rabbi Yehuda
Rav Huna rules that impure wine libations get their own arrangement of wood and are burned there
A verse about burning in the holy place is cited, and a baraita extends the same rule to blood, oil, meal and libations
Shmuel tells Rav Hana of Baghdad to gather ten men so he can teach the rule on impure libations before them
Chapter-closing formula, then the mishna rules that blood of a sin offering sprinkled on a garment requires laundering
The mishna notes the verse speaks only of eaten offerings, citing the words in a holy place shall it be eaten
The mishna asserts that both eaten and inner sin offerings require laundering of the garment
The verse on the law of the sin offering is cited to show one law applies to all sin offerings
The mishna rules on disqualified sin offerings and when their blood needs laundering, with examples of each case
If one law covers all sin offerings, why would the bird offering be excluded? The Gemara asks this
A baraita is cited: the verse this is the law restricts the rule, so the bird offering's blood needs no laundering
Reish Lakish cites the verse shall the sin offering be slaughtered to show it speaks of slaughtered offerings
Perhaps the verse instead speaks of eaten offerings, as in the holy place it shall be eaten, so the rule is different
Explanation: the Merciful One restricts the rule with this is the law, which excludes the bird offering
What did you see that makes the verse include internal animal sin offerings and exclude birds, rather than the reverse?
It stands to reason: internal animal offerings need inclusion, since animals are slaughtered in the north and received in a vessel

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the list of places where the blood is placed: the horn, the finger, the edge, and the altar base
On the contrary, the bird sin offering should be included with the eaten animal offerings, since its blood is also placed on the altar
Rav Yosef cites a verse about the priest who offers it eating it, limiting the rule to eaten offerings, to show bird blood needs no laundering
If the verse already excludes bird offerings, why is the separate verse this is the law needed
Without the second verse one would read the phrase as the usual manner of the verse, so it teaches the exclusion
Rabba cites a verse about sprinkling to argue that internal sin offerings cannot be excluded from the laundering rule
A baraita says the verse speaks only of eaten offerings for rinsing, but for laundering it is written about sprinkling
If so, why would the tanna need to teach the internal and the eaten offerings in that order
If so, bird offering blood should need laundering too, since the Torah uses the term sprinkling for it
What did you see that makes you exclude bird offerings but include the external sin offering
It stands to reason: the animal offering should be included since its blood is received in a vessel and placed on the altar
On the contrary, the bird offering should be included in the laundering rule, since its sprinkling is like the others
Rabbi Avin asks whether the neck of a bird offering, where blood is inside, counts as a service vessel, or as an animal neck
A baraita on a convulsing offering that re-entered the Sanctuary is cited: if it entered it is disqualified, so it is proof
By your reasoning a faulty inference arises from the convulsing offering that moved to the south, so the proof fails
Rather, the halakha about the offering that left the area is taught for its own purpose, so it proves nothing
Rabbi Avin asks: if blood of a bird spills on the floor and is gathered, is it fit or disqualified, since no vessel was required
Rava cites a baraita: one might think bird blood needs laundering, so the verse this is the law excludes it
If bird blood were disqualified by entering a vessel's airspace, the Torah need not have excluded it, so the baraita is weak
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says the baraita is not decisive, referring to the case of a vessel attached to the neck
Levi asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whether a garment sprinkled from one garment onto another requires laundering of the first
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answers that the garment needs laundering either way, following Rabbi Akiva's view on the sprinkled blood

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rami bar Hama asks Rav Hisda whether a garment on which impure blood sprinkles becomes impure
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua infers from the question that blood of a disqualified offering that once was fit still needs laundering
Does this hold only when the blood is sprinkled one at a time, or also when all at once, or is there no difference
Rav Huna says it is a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis, as Abaye resolves it according to Rabba
A baraita of Rabbi Elazar is cited: impure sin offering blood purifies, since one sprinkles water of purification on a menstruant
Rabba says Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Akiva's view that moving a vessel over an impure place counts as placing it there
A mishna is cited about a man who reaches through a window to move a flask over an oven containing a creeping animal
Rabbi Akiva holds the moved item counts as placed, while the Rabbis disagree, and the dispute turns on that point
Abaye objects: Rabbi Akiva concedes in sprinkling from one vessel to another, which contradicts the reasoning just given
Abaye explains: all agree it is not as if placed, and the dispute is whether to enact a decree lest the item rest
Rabbi Akiva concedes for sprinkling because once the blood has departed, it has departed
The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis is really about
Abaye and Rava explain: the dispute is whether earlier impurity may be compared to later impurity, and whether sprinkling requires a measure
A baraita states the positions: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon each rule on blood of a disqualified offering needing laundering
What is the reason for Rabbi Shimon's position
Rabbi Shimon reads the verses to limit the rule to a time when the offering was fit, while Rabbi Akiva reads them to exclude terumah
The mishna rules that blood spraying from the neck or from the horn or base of the altar on a garment does not need laundering
The mishna adds that blood spilled on the floor and gathered does not need laundering, only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling
A baraita cites the verse that sprinkles, arguing that spray from the neck onto a garment must still be laundered, and the verse limits this to fit blood
Another baraita says spray from the horn and base would need laundering, and the verse excludes what was already sprinkled
Mishna case: blood spilled on the floor, and the same rule as before applies

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna need to say this, and what is the reason for the rule about blood spilled on the floor
Spilled blood needs no laundering because only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling counts
What is the mishna excluding, given that a sprinkling-amount received in one vessel or another is not an issue
A baraita of Rabbi Chalafta ben Shaul is cited: less than a sprinkling-amount in one vessel does not consecrate
A dilemma: is the rule about blood derived as a halakha, or is it like water, since both verses say immerse
A baraita is cited, with Rabbi Elazar's view that even blood does not consecrate the one who is immersed
Rava explains why the verse says in the blood, to exclude remnants on the finger, which supports Rabbi Elazar
Rabin tells Rav Ada that his student quoted Rav Amram, introducing a teaching to be examined
A mishna is cited: if the sprinkler spills before he finishes sprinkling, the garment needs laundering; after sprinkling it does not
Does the mishna not mean the reverse, that before he finishes sprinkling it needs laundering and after he finishes it does not
No, the mishna means before the sprinkling leaves his hand it needs laundering, and after it leaves it does not
Abaye objects with a case of a man who finishes sprinkling and wipes his hand on the cow's body, and asks how he wipes his finger
Abaye answers: he wipes his finger on the rim of the basin, as the verse says of golden basins
The mishna rules on blood sprayed on skin before and after flaying, and lists garments, sacks and skins that require laundering
Where do the words of the baraita come from
The verse on the garment on which the blood was sprinkled, shall be laundered, is cited to include the hide after flaying
The baraita derives from the word garment that only the garment's kind is covered, and Rabbi Elazar then includes the sack

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse about garments where it is laundered is read to include only items that receive impurity, as a garment does
What is the difference between the two readings of the verse
Abaye: the difference is a cloth less than three handbreadths, which can be intended for use and counts as a garment
Rava: the difference is a garment whose purpose was set for a use, so it is still a garment that receives impurity
Rava: the difference is a piece of cloth intended for cutting, which is not yet an item able to receive impurity until cut
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says a piece of cloth intended for cutting is pure until it is cut, which conflicts with Rava
From where do we know the baraita's rule
A baraita reasons from the verse that only the spot where blood fell is laundered, not the whole garment
The anonymous mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda: an item able to receive impurity and fit for laundering includes sack and skin
If skin is laundered, a contradictory baraita says a hide is to be rubbed with cloth and water poured on it until it finishes
Abaye: there is no contradiction, since one baraita is by the Sages and the other by others
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi's practice of washing his sandals in water is brought as evidence that he follows the Sages
Rava objects: how can anyone hold that skin is not laundered, since the verse explicitly says garment or hide to be laundered
Rava: the verse and mishna are disputing about reeds, not skin
But Rav Ḥiyya said he saw him wash his sandals in water about reeds and held with the Sages
Rava offers a distinction about a leprous mark that spreads from the body itself and softens the material, resolving the apparent conflict
Rava says: if this is difficult for me, then that is also difficult for me

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Are rugs and cushions to be classed as garments that need laundering
A mishna is cited: a hide over which water is poured until it finishes, showing how such items are cleaned
Rava: any laundering that lacks rubbing does not count as laundering
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi's practice of washing sandals by soaking is an objection, since soaking a garment would then count as laundering
Rava's view, applied to cloth and linen: throwing a cloth into water renders one liable because it does the work of laundering
Why is sowing flax forbidden, and what is the reason for the rule
If the reason is softening, wheat and barley also have slime, and the objection does not hold

ranges.en: Mishna principle: if the altar did not acquire the flesh of a burnt offering, the priests do not acquire its hide.
