A baraita on Leviticus 17:3: in the camp and outside the camp exclude slaughter of an offering in the south of the courtyard.
The baraita continues: the three concentric camps are used to exclude slaughter outside all three, and to include slaughter inside.
Without outside the camp, one might think slaughter in the south of the courtyard is liable, so the verse excludes it.
Outside the camp excludes areas unfit for any offering, so in the camp must mean the same, excluding the south of the courtyard.
Ulla: one who slaughters on the roof of the Sanctuary is liable, since the roof is unfit for slaughtering any offering.
Rava objects: then the verse need not write to the Tent of Meeting, which excludes the roof; the Gemara challenges that reasoning in turn.
Rav Mari defends Rava: in the camp includes slaughter when the body is inside and the neck outside.
The Gemara modifies Rav Mari: the Merciful One is particular about the slaughter, so the in the camp must mean the body outside and the neck inside.
Amoraic dispute: one who offers up outside the courtyard today is liable per Rabbi Yohanan and exempt per Reish Lakish.
Rabbi Yohanan: the Temple's initial sanctity was forever, so it can still be used; Reish Lakish: it was only for its time.
Shall we say they disagree like Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the same matter?
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says curtains were used in building the Temple and its courts, with walls built inside or outside them.
Rabbi Yehoshua: offerings are still sacrificed without a Temple, since initial sanctity was for its time and forever.
Can one not infer that Rabbi Eliezer holds the sanctity was not forever?
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: perhaps all agree on eternal sanctity, and the curtains are only for modesty.
Amoraic dispute: one who offers up a limb lacking an olive-bulk of flesh, with bone completing it, is liable per Rabbi Yohanan and exempt per Reish Lakish.
Rabbi Yohanan: attached parts count as offered; Reish Lakish: attached parts are not treated as offered.
Rava raises a dilemma about one who offers up outside the courtyard.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a pigeon's head lacks an olive-bulk of flesh but salt completes the measure, is one liable for offering it up outside?
Rava of Parzakya asks Rav Ashi whether this is the same dispute as Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish over an attached bone.
Rav Ashi: no; the dilemma can be raised on either view, since salt and bone differ in kind and in whether they must be offered up.
The dilemma is left unresolved.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that slaughter inside followed by offering outside is liable, while slaughter outside is exempt for offering up.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi defends Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: the inside-slaughtered offering had a period of fitness, unlike one slaughtered outside.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon defends him: an offering disqualified inside is accepted on the altar, unlike one disqualified outside.
What is the practical difference between these two responses?
Ze'eiri: slaughter at night inside. Rabba: collection of the blood in a non-sacred vessel inside. Each case splits the two responses.
Mishna: an impure person who eats sacrificial food, pure or impure, is liable for karet if intentional.
The Rabbis rightly respond to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili; why does he disagree?
Rava: if the person became impure first, all agree he is liable; if the meat became impure first, the disputants differ on whether the more inclusive prohibition takes effect.
Even by Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the more stringent impurity-of-the-body prohibition should take effect over the meat's impurity.
Rav Ashi: the meat's impurity may be the more stringent, since impure meat cannot be purified in a ritual bath while a person can.
Mishna: slaughter outside is more stringent in one respect and offering up outside in another, with examples on liability, partners, and altar requirements.
The Gemara analyzes why one who offers up for an ordinary purpose is exempt, given the verse says to sacrifice to the Lord.
The ish ish in slaughter teaches liability even for an ordinary purpose; in offering up it teaches liability for two people together.
If so, the ish ish phrase should teach two people slaughtering together are liable, contrary to the mishna; why do the phrases differ?
If so, offering up also has that man in the verse, so why is it not expounded to exclude two acting together?
That term is necessary for another purpose.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The term that man excludes one who acted unwittingly, under compulsion, or by mistake.
Challenge: if so, the term here must also exclude those cases, so how can it teach that only one acting alone is liable?
There are two instances of that man for slaughter outside, one for intent and one for acting alone.
Why does the verse also need the phrase to the Lord?
To exclude from liability one who slaughters the Yom Kippur scapegoat outside the courtyard.
Mishna: the greater stringency for offering up outside is that two who slaughter together are exempt, while two who offer up a limb together are liable.
A baraita: the doubled ish ish teaches that two people who offer up a limb together are liable, per Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yosei: that man is singular and teaches only one acting alone is liable; ish ish is the language of people.
What does Rabbi Shimon derive from the term that man?
How does Rabbi Yosei derive liability for slaughtering outside for an ordinary purpose if he holds the doubled phrasing is not expounded?
From Leviticus 17:4, blood shall be imputed to that man, which includes even one slaughtering for an ordinary purpose.
Mishna: one who unwittingly offers up parts in separate lapses is liable per part per Rabbi Shimon, and once per Rabbi Yosei.
Reish Lakish: the dispute concerns four or five limbs offered in separate lapses, and the derivations of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon from to sacrifice it.
Rabbi Yohanan: everyone agrees one is liable for a single limb; the dispute concerns a single limb of an offering taken outside.
Ulla: all agree on fit offerings offered up outside; the dispute concerns unfit offerings burned outside.
A second version of Ulla agrees with Rabbi Yohanan: the dispute concerns fit offerings offered outside.
Shmuel's father disagrees with the first version of Ulla: Rabbi Yosei holds incomplete limbs are never restored to the altar.
Mishna: one is liable for offering up outside only when offering it on top of an altar erected there, per Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Huna: Genesis 8:20 shows Noah used an altar rather than a rock, so offering up requires placing on an altar.
Rabbi Yohanan: Judges 13:19 shows Manoah offered on a rock, so placing on a rock is offering up, per Rabbi Shimon.
Each verse is explained: Noah's verse refers to an elevated place, and Manoah's rock was a provisional edict in exigent circumstances.
Rabbi Shimon's reason is a baraita on Leviticus 17:6: only the Sanctuary requires a specifically erected altar.
The Gemara questions the baraita's formulation, which concludes liability rather than fulfilling the obligation.
During periods when private altars are permitted, no erected altar is required; so during prohibition, offering on a rock is liable.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina asks whether the corner, ramp, base, and square are indispensable for a private altar.
Rabbi Yirmeya: a baraita says these are indispensable for a great public altar but not for a small private one.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: fit offerings, and unfit ones disqualified in sanctity, are liable if sacrificed outside the courtyard.
Mishna: one who offers up outside an olive-bulk combining burnt-offering flesh and its sacrificial portions is liable.
A baraita on Leviticus 17:8: burnt offering, then sacrificial portions of other offerings are included by the word sacrifice.
The word sacrifice includes the handful, frankincense, incense, priests' and anointed priest's meal offerings, and libation wine and water.
Leviticus 17:9, he will not bring it to the entrance, limits liability to offerings fit to be brought there.
From where is liability derived also for unfit offerings?
Examples of unfit offerings: leftover, taken outside, impure, disqualified intentions, misplaced blood, and Paschal or sin offerings sacrificed not for their sake.
From where is liability for these derived?
Leviticus 17:9 says anything acceptable on the altar at the entrance is liable when offered outside, even if unfit ab initio.
The mishna restated: liability for an olive-bulk of burnt-offering flesh and its sacrificial portions offered up outside.
The Gemara infers that a peace offering's flesh and portions do not combine for liability outside.
A baraita: burnt offering flesh and portions combine for offering outside, piggul, notar, and impurity, but peace offering parts do not.
Granted the combination in offering up outside is logical, why does the baraita differ for piggul, notar, and impurity?
The mishna says piggul combines with piggul and notar with notar, so the baraita's rulings conflict with it.
The mishna concerns liability for eating piggul, while the baraita concerns intention to make an offering piggul, which requires an olive-bulk of the parts.
The mishna concerns liability for eating notar, while the baraita concerns notar when only a combined olive-bulk remains before the blood is sprinkled.
Whose opinion is the baraita? It is Rabbi Yehoshua's, as taught in a baraita.
Rabbi Yehoshua: for all Torah offerings, if an olive-bulk of meat remains after the rest is destroyed or impure, it may be sprinkled.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continues: for offerings whose meat is eaten, half an olive of meat and half of fat do not combine; a burnt offering's parts do combine.
Asks what the meal offering mentioned at the end of the baraita actually refers to.
Rav Pappa explains it is a meal offering of libations brought together with an animal sacrifice.
Mishna: burning an olive-bulk of any of these meal-type items outside the Temple makes one liable.
Rabbi Eliezer exempts unless the whole item is sacrificed outside the Temple.
Remainder of an olive-bulk burned outside is liable, while lacking items are exempt.
Sacrificing the burnt portions outside is liable, but sacrificing the meat is not.
Baraita: incense of a half-peras is required; burning an olive-bulk outside is liable, a half-peras inside exempts.
Asks what the word exempt means in the baraita.
Proposes that exemption applies to a non-priest who burns incense inside the Temple.
Objects: why exempt, since burning is itself sacrificial burning even for less than a peras?
Rabbi Zeira transmits Rav's teaching on the incense of the priest's daily offering.
Asks again what the word exempt refers to.
Explains that exempt means the community fulfils its obligation.
Rabbi Zeira objects that Rabbi Eliezer would not accept fulfilment by less than a peras.
Rabba replies that all agree the peras is only a rabbinic requirement, not a Torah measure.
The mishna's dispute concerns incense burned in the inner sanctum, according to one Sage.
Cites Leviticus 16:12 as the basis for the requirement of a handful.
One Sage reads the word handful as a strict measure; the other does not.
Abaye objects that the term statute makes the handful requirement binding for inner incense.
Abaye offers an alternative: all agree the inner sanctum needs a handful and the outer needs an olive-bulk.
The dispute concerns outer burning of inner-sanctum incense, derived from the outer sanctum by one Sage.
Rava rejects Abaye's reading: the Rabbis would not derive the inner measure from outer incense.
Asks which rite Rava is referring to.
A baraita teaches that liability arises only for sacrificing a complete offering outside the courtyard.
Explains Rava's inference: a libation of less than three log still has olive-bulks, yet the Rabbis do not derive it.
Rava resolves Rabbi Zeira's difficulty: the case is two half-peras portions of incense designated separately.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Two Sages disagree on whether designating incense by placing it in a vessel has any legal effect.
Rava draws the consequence for the wine libation of a bull, if the designation is binding and four log are removed.
The same consequence for a ram libation: three log removed and offered outside incurs liability.
Less than three log is never a valid libation, so offering a lacking amount outside is exempt.
Rav Ashi defends Abaye: the Rabbis do not derive outer rites from each other, but do derive outer incense from inner incense.
The mishna lists the items that are wholly burned, and rules that lacking ones offered outside are exempt.
Raises the dilemma whether a lack arising outside the courtyard counts as a lack, or whether the offering must stay complete.
Abaye cites the mishna, where Rabbi Eliezer requires the whole offering, to suggest the offering must remain complete.
Rabba bar Rav Hanan objects: Abaye cannot settle the dilemma from Rabbi Eliezer, since the Rabbis disagree with him.
Abaye replies that he heard from Rav that the Rabbis only dispute Rabbi Eliezer for complete offerings, not lacking ones.
Challenges whether Rav was not speaking of a lack that occurred outside the courtyard.
Rejects the challenge: Rav was speaking of a lack that occurred inside the courtyard.
Attempts to resolve the dilemma from the continuation of the mishna about lacking offerings sacrificed outside.
Rejects this proof too: the mishna addresses a lack occurring inside the courtyard.
Mishna: one who offers eaten meat and burnt portions outside is liable for the portions, not for the meat.
Asks why he is liable, since the meat placed under the portions would interpose between the altar and them.
Shmuel: the mishna refers to a case where the meat was turned over so the portions lie directly on the fire.
Rabbi Yohanan offers another reading: even without turning, it follows Rabbi Shimon, who requires no exact parallel to the Temple method.
Rav offers a third reading: meat and portions of the same animal do not interpose on each other, even in the Temple.
Mishna: a meal offering whose handful was not removed is exempt if offered outside; once removed, the offering is liable.
Asks why the remainder does not nullify the handful, so that the mixed offering would be unfit and not liable.
Rabbi Zeira derives by verbal analogy that a remainder does not nullify a handful, as two handfuls do not nullify each other.
Mishna: burning the handful and frankincense permits the remainder; Rabbi Eliezer exempts one who burns only one of them.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha asks whether burning only the handful permits half the remainder or merely weakens its prohibition.
Asks whose opinion the dilemma follows, considering first Rabbi Meir's view on piggul intention.
Shows the dilemma cannot follow the Rabbis either, since their view means one act alone has no effect.
Shows the dilemma cannot follow Rabbi Eliezer's view either, since he also holds with the Rabbis.
Concludes the dilemma must follow the Rabbis taught in this mishna, who hold that each act alone has effect.
The Gemara concludes that the dilemma remains unresolved.
Mishna opens a new case: one who sprinkles only part of an offering's blood outside the courtyard.

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: pouring the festival water libation outside is liable according to Rabbi Eliezer; Rabbi Nehemya holds remnant blood offered outside is liable.
Rava says Rabbi Elazar concedes that even part of an offering's blood sprinkled outside creates liability.
Cites a Yoma mishna where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon let sprinkling continue, showing each sprinkling is a complete act.
Quotes Rabbi Elazar's ruling that pouring the festival water libation outside is liable.
Rabbi Yohanan reports that Rabbi Elazar follows his teacher Rabbi Akiva, who holds the water libation is a Torah mitzva.
Rabbi Akiva derives from the plural libations in the verse that there are two distinct libations, one of water.
Reish Lakish objects that the derivation would imply a three-log minimum and year-round liability, which Rabbi Elazar does not state.
Resolves the objection: Rabbi Asi's tradition says the water libation is a halakha given to Moses at Sinai, derived separately.
Baraita: pouring three log of water outside on Sukkot is liable; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon adds consecration in a service vessel.
Asks what distinguishes the two tannaitic opinions.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says they disagree whether a precise measure of water can be consecrated for the libation.
Rav Pappa's view is introduced here; the statement continues on the next daf.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening framing: the tannaim disagree about wilderness libations and whether wine libations need prior consecration.
Baraita: pouring three log of wine outside the courtyard creates liability.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon adds that this applies only if the wine was first consecrated in a service vessel.
Asks what the difference between the two tannaim is.
Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzhak: they differ on whether the overflow above a vessel's rim is also consecrated.
Rava bar Rabba: they differ on whether libations offered on private altars show a non-consecrated libation can create liability.
Baraita on private altars: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says no libations, the Rabbis say libations are required, which fits this dispute.
The two disputes are parallel, since the same tannaim divide on both questions.
Verse Numbers 15:2 about entering the land is read as requiring libations with offerings on a great public altar.
Asks whether the verse refers to a great altar or even to a small private one.
Rabbi Yishmael reads the plural lakhem in a second verse as pointing to one public altar used by all.
Rabbi Akiva reads the phrase when you come as requiring libations even on small private altars.
Asks whether the verse speaks of a small private altar or only a great public one.
Reads the phrase into all your dwellings as referring to private altars, since there was only one public altar.
Explains the difference: Rabbi Yishmael means no libations in the wilderness, Rabbi Akiva means there were.
Mishna: Rabbi Nehemya holds one is liable for sacrificing the remainder of an offering's blood outside the courtyard.
Rabbi Yohanan explains that Rabbi Nehemya follows the view that the remainder of the blood disqualifies the offering if missing.
Raises a baraita objection: Rabbi Nehemya holds liability for blood remainder outside the courtyard.
Rabbi Akiva objects that pouring the blood remainder is a non-essential mitzva, so liability should not follow.
Rabbi Nehemya replies that limbs and fats are also non-essential yet liable when offered outside.
Rabbi Akiva rebuts: burning limbs starts the rite, but pouring the blood remainder does not start the rite.
Explains the challenge: if the blood remainder disqualifies, Rabbi Nehemya could answer that it is a rite in itself.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the dispute concerns inner-altar remainders only, so the outer-altar ruling is agreed upon.
Explains that Rabbi Akiva misunderstood Rabbi Nehemya's point, applying it to the outer altar remainder.
Mishna: liability and exemption rules for pinching or slaughtering a bird offering inside and outside the courtyard.

111b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: slaughtering a bird offering outside and then offering it outside creates liability.
Summarizes the mishna's pattern: preparation inside causes exemption outside, and preparation outside causes exemption inside.
Rabbi Shimon's rule: parallel killing outside creates liability for an inside-killed offering, except slaughtering a bird inside.
Objects that the word preparation fits poorly, since slaughter disqualifies a bird; the mishna should say liability.
Introduces Rabbi Shimon's ruling as cited in the mishna.
Asks to which clause of the mishna Rabbi Shimon's ruling refers.
Quotes the first clause of the mishna about pinching the nape of a bird offering inside and outside.
Tests the hypotheses about Rabbi Shimon's disagreement with the first clause and rejects each as inconsistent with his wording.
Turns to the latter clause: slaughter inside and offering outside exempts, while slaughter outside and offering outside liable.
Rejects the hypotheses on the latter clause, since Rabbi Shimon's wording and the mishna's final ruling do not fit them.
Ze'eira suggests the dispute concerns slaughter of an offering at night inside the courtyard.
Quotes the mishna's night-slaughter ruling: inside at night exempts, outside at night liable.
Quotes Rabbi Shimon's parallel rule on night slaughter and the bird exception.
Rava suggests the dispute concerns collecting blood in a non-sacred vessel, and quotes the matching mishna ruling.
Quotes Rabbi Shimon's parallel rule on collecting blood and the bird exception.
Offers another explanation based on a baraita taught by Shmuel's father, son of Rav Yitzhak.
Baraita: pinching a bird inside and offering outside is liable; pinching outside and offering outside exempt, with Rabbi Shimon disagreeing.
Explains that Rabbi Shimon speaks of the first clause, so the mishna should be emended to a parallel formulation.
Mishna on a sin offering whose blood was placed partly inside and partly outside the courtyard.
Mishna continues: blood in two cups, with liability or exemption depending on placement inside or outside.
Mishna's analogy: a sin offering animal set aside, lost, replaced, then found, governs which slaughter creates liability.
Mishna applies the analogy to slaughtering both animals inside or outside, or one of each.
Mishna concludes that blood or slaughter of one animal exempts the meat of the other from misuse.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why one is liable when blood placed inside is followed by remaining blood offered outside, since that remainder should not count.
Explains the mishna follows Rabbi Nehemya, who holds liability for the remainder of blood offered outside.
Asks how the two-cup clause can be attributed to Rabbi Nehemya, who holds liability for remaining blood offered outside.
Attributes the clause to the first tanna, who holds the blood of the other cup is disqualified, not a mere remainder.
Mishna offers an analogy: a sin offering separated, lost, replaced by another, then the first is found.
Asks what the analogy adds and whose opinion it follows, namely Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on disqualification by loss.
Explains the analogy: a lost-then-replaced sin offering is disqualified, while a doubly separated one becomes a burnt offering, so its blood is liable.
Cites Rav's ruling, transmitted by Rav Huna, that a guilt offering left to graze and slaughtered is still fit as a burnt offering.
Asks whether the cases are comparable, since a sin offering is female and cannot be a burnt offering.
Rav Hiyya of Yostiniyya: the mishna concerns the male goat of the Nasi, which can be a burnt offering.
Closes the chapter and opens the next mishna.
Mishna: burning the red heifer outside its pit, or sacrificing the scapegoat outside, is exempt from the outside-slaughter penalty.
Derives from Leviticus 17:3-4 that unfit animals, such as the red heifer and scapegoat, incur no liability for outside slaughter.
Mishna lists disqualified animals, such as a tereifa or one born by caesarean section, which if sacrificed outside are exempt.
Derives from Leviticus 17:4 that any animal unfit for the altar is not liable when offered outside the courtyard.
Begins the ruling on blemished animals, whether permanent or temporary blemishes, which continues past the daf's end.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one sacrificing outside a temporarily blemished animal is exempt from liability.
Rabbi Shimon: permanently blemished animals are exempt, while temporarily blemished ones violate a prohibition without karet.
Rabbi Shimon on doves and pigeons whose time has passed, versus those not yet fit: different liability.
Mishna: an animal whose time has not arrived, or an offspring slaughtered with its mother, is exempt when sacrificed outside.
Rabbi Shimon: sacrificing a not-yet-fit animal outside violates a prohibition but carries no karet.
The Rabbis: where there is no karet, there is no violation of a prohibition.
Defines premature animals, whether premature intrinsically or for the owner, such as a zav or a woman after childbirth.
Mishna lists sacrificial meat, such as sin and guilt offering meat and the lesser holy offerings, whose outside handling is exempt.
Continues the list: omer surplus, shewbread, meal offering handfuls, and collecting blood outside the courtyard, all exempt.
Adds that these actions create no liability for non-priestly service, impurity, missing vestments, or unwashed hands.
Historical sequence of permitted and prohibited private altars from the Tabernacle to Gilgal, Shiloh and Nov or Gibeon.
Jerusalem era: private altars were prohibited, and offerings consecrated under prohibition and sacrificed outside are liable.
Lists cases of consecration and sacrifice under prohibition or permission of private altars, and the resulting karet or exemption.
Lists offerings that must be sacrificed only in the Tabernacle, and offerings of individuals that may go on private altars.
Asks what distinguishes a private altar from the public altar at the Tabernacle site; the answer continues on the next daf.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda: meal offerings, priestly vestments and purity rules do not apply on private altars, though piggul and notar rules do.
Asks what the phrase outside its pit means in the red heifer rule.
Reish Lakish: it means outside the place inspected to rule out a gravesite.
Rabbi Yohanan objects: all of Eretz Yisrael is inspected, so such an inspection would be unnecessary.
Rabbi Yohanan explains: the heifer was slaughtered inside the walls of Jerusalem rather than outside them.
Challenges that the phrase may instead mean slaughter outside the wall but not opposite the Temple entrance, which is disqualified.
Cites the juxtaposition of slaughter and sprinkling in Numbers 19 to derive that slaughter must face the entrance.
Tests whether Rabbi Yohanan's juxtaposition reasoning holds, given his disqualification and Reish Lakish's contrary reading.
Records the amoraic dispute on burning the heifer not opposite the entrance: Rabbi Yohanan disqualifies, Rabbi Oshaya allows.
Rabbi Oshaya reads the word dung as meaning the place where the soul departs, so location of burning is not fixed.
Explains Rabbi Yohanan's reading as a case where the heifer was slaughtered closer to the Temple but still disqualified.
Returns to the earlier dispute between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish over whether the land must be inspected.
Asks on what point the two Sages disagree.
The flood question: Reish Lakish holds it covered the land so inspection is needed, Rabbi Yohanan holds it did not.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says both Sages derived their positions from the same verse in Ezekiel.
Quotes Ezekiel 22:24, read as a rhetorical question by Rabbi Yohanan and as a statement by Reish Lakish.
Explains how each reading of the Ezekiel verse supports the respective position about the land and the flood.
Reish Lakish raises an objection to Rabbi Yohanan from a mishna.
Mishna in Para: courtyards over hollow spaces in Jerusalem, and mothers raising children there to be pure for the rite.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: the Sages set a higher purity standard for the red heifer alone.
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from a baraita about bones found in the woodshed chamber.
Baraita: bones were found, and the Sages wanted to decree impurity on Jerusalem.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks: where are the dead of the flood and of Nebuchadnezzar?
Rabbi Yohanan infers from Rabbi Yehoshua's words that there were no lost graves from the flood in Jerusalem.
Reish Lakish replies: by that logic, there were no victims of Nebuchadnezzar either, yet they existed and were removed.
Asks why there would still be concern about impurity if the bodies had been removed.

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita concerns only Jerusalem, where bones were removed; elsewhere in the land a site must still be inspected.
Introduces the alternative view that the earlier objection should be reversed, with Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yohanan.
Reish Lakish argues from Yehoshua's question that the flood dead must have been in the land, as Nebuchadnezzar's dead were.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that they died from the heat that spread from the floodwaters into the land.
Rav Hisda: the flood generation was punished with boiling heat, supported by parallel verses using the word for abating.
Introduces the parallel version in which Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from the verse about dry land.
Rabbi Yohanan asks what dry land could mean during the flood if the flood covered Eretz Yisrael, and Reish Lakish answers.
Rav Hisda explains that dry land excludes fish, so no decree was issued on fish in the sea during the flood.
Asks how the reima creature survived the flood if the flood reached Eretz Yisrael, since it was too large for the ark.
Rabbi Yannai: they brought reima cubs into the ark, so they survived.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports a reima cub so large it dammed the Jordan, which challenges the claim that it fit into the ark.
Rabbi Yohanan says only the cub's head entered the ark while the body stayed outside.
Objects that the head alone would still be too large by Rabba bar bar Hana's measure.
Rather, only the tip of the cub's nose entered the ark so that it could breathe.
Asks why Rabbi Yohanan needed this answer if he holds the flood did not reach Eretz Yisrael.
Challenges how the reima's horns could be tied to a moving ark, and how it survived boiling water.
Replies that the ark was pitched, Og survived too, so a miracle cooled the water beside the ark.
Even if the flood reached the land, Reish Lakish's Babylonia etymologies imply the dead all sank there, leaving none in the land.
Rabbi Abbahu explains Shinar as a place that shakes its wealthy, so wealth does not last.
Objects that wealthy people in Babylonia do keep their wealth.
Replies that their wealth does not extend beyond three generations.
Rabbi Ami and a baraita: eating Babylonian dust is like eating one's ancestors' flesh, or repugnant creeping things.
Mishna: the Yom Kippur scapegoat sacrificed outside the Temple is exempt, since it is not fit for the entrance of the Tent.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita, asking whether consecrated items for Temple maintenance are also covered by the rule.
Cites Numbers 31:50, where spoils given as an offering to the Lord show that the term offering applies to non-sacrificial items.
The verse adds the words entrance of the Tent, teaching that only items fit for sacrifice are covered.
The baraita derives from the word to the Lord that the scapegoat is excluded, as it is not dedicated to God.
Resolves the apparent conflict by dating the two baraitot to before the lottery or before the confession, when the goat was still fit.
Mishna: an animal that copulated with a person, or was used in bestiality, is exempt when sacrificed outside.
Asks whether this exemption could also be derived from the phrase entrance of the Tent, without the other verse.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Granted, a consecrated animal that was then used for bestiality is disqualified by another verse, since it was once fit to enter the Temple courtyard.
Objects that an animal set aside for idol worship could not become disqualified, since a person cannot forbid what is not his.
Responds: lesser-sanctity offerings belong to their owner, following Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, so they can be disqualified.
Cites Leviticus 5:21, where the phrase against the Lord includes lesser offerings as owned property, per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Summarizes that each mishna case was once fit and then disqualified, including the view that offspring are holy only after birth.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree on temporarily blemished animals, doves not yet fit, and an animal with its offspring.
Explains why the mishna must teach each case separately, since each case alone could be read as implying a different ruling.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon's reason is for holding a prohibition is violated.
Rabbi Ile'a for Reish Lakish: Deuteronomy 12:8-9 forbids obligatory offerings before reaching the rest at Shiloh, showing the prohibition.
Infers that since obligatory offerings in Gilgal were not yet due, offering them there violates the prohibition of you shall not do.
Rabbi Yirmeya challenges Rabbi Zeira: then anyone sacrificing an unfit offering inside the courtyard would also violate it.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether one who sacrifices an unfit offering should also receive lashes for violating the general prohibition.
Rabbi Zeira: the verse turned that negative precept into a positive command, so no lashes are given for it.
Replies that this applies only per the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Shimon on whether the you shall not do prohibition applies.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: even Rabbi Shimon gives no lashes inside, because the Gilgal prohibition is only outside the courtyard.
Rabba: Rabbi Shimon's reason comes from another verse about sacrificing the Paschal offering on a private altar, not from Reish Lakish's verse.
Derives from the word be-ehad, within one gate, that the prohibition applies only when all Israel enters through one gate.
Asks when this Paschal offering was slaughtered, since slaughter after midday would also carry karet.
Suggests the Paschal offering could be slaughtered after midday on a private altar at a time when private altars were permitted.
Asks why the baraita speaks of a time when private altars are prohibited, if that time allowed them for other offerings.
Mishna: offerings whose time has not come because of the owner, such as a zav or zava, are exempt when sacrificed outside.
Asks whether these owners are obligated to bring guilt offerings.
Ze'eira: the mishna should list a leper, who brings a guilt offering, alongside the zav and zava.
The mishna also says that burnt and peace offerings sacrificed outside by such owners are liable.
Asks whether these owners are obligated to bring peace offerings.
Rav Sheshet: add a nazirite, who brings a peace offering; the Gemara notes the leper addition was fixed in the mishna but this one was not.
Rabbi Hilkiya: a guilt offering slaughtered outside for its own sake is exempt, but slaughtered for another purpose is liable.
States the reasoning that a guilt offering slaughtered outside not for its own sake remains fit for the courtyard.
Asks why the one who slaughters for its own sake should not also be liable, since it could be fit inside.
Replies that a guilt offering slaughtered outside must first have its status uprooted to be fit inside.
Rav Huna objects: is there anything unfit when done for its own sake but fit when done not for its sake?

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Paschal offering sacrificed during the rest of the year is treated as a peace offering, so it is not a Paschal offering slaughtered not for its sake.
Suggests a baraita supporting Rabbi Hilkiya, but the verse listing ox, lamb and goat shows a sin offering was omitted from liability.
Asks what case the baraita addresses if the guilt offering was slaughtered at its proper time or not at its time.
Concludes the baraita concerns a guilt offering slaughtered at its proper time but not for its sake, following Rabbi Eliezer.
Explains Rabbi Eliezer's juxtaposition of guilt and sin offerings, so the derivation about the secondary offering is needed.
Brings a baraita on liability for burnt and sin offerings sacrificed before their time, and derives exclusion from the entrance verse.
Asks what case the omitted guilt offering in that baraita concerns, and why liability would follow for it.
Resolves that the baraita concerns a sin offering not for its sake, and Rabbi Eliezer's juxtaposition makes the guilt offering exempt too.
Rav Dimi cites a baraita of the school of Rabbi Livai that imposes liability on guilt offerings sacrificed before their time.
Ravina derives the liability from the ox, lamb and goat verse, which supports Rabbi Hilkiya against Rav Huna.
Rav Nahman says a baraita of Levi contradicts Rabbi Livai's school, since the disqualified offering does not satisfy the owner's obligation.
Rav Dimi resolves the contradiction: one baraita concerns a sacrifice for its sake and the other not for its sake.
Rav Ashi raises a contradiction between the mishna and a baraita, and asks if this refutes Rav Huna.
Rav Huna's reply: the case is two guilt offerings set aside as a guarantee, one of which is a burnt offering from the outset.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna quoting Rav: a guilt offering left to graze, slaughtered without specifying its purpose, is fit as a burnt offering.
Mishna and baraita: offering outside the courtyard a portion of sin, guilt, or lesser offering meat is exempt, since those are eaten by priests.
Derives from the word burnt offering in Leviticus 17:8 that anything fit for the altar is included in the liability rule.
Derives that the meal-offering rites such as pouring, salting and waving, done outside, are exempt.
Derives from the verse about sacrificing a burnt offering or sacrifice that only rites that conclude the service create liability.
Mishna on private altars before the Tabernacle, with Rav Huna reading Exodus 24:5 to Rav Hisda, who reports Rabbi Asi's view.
Rav Huna plans to raise a contradiction from the mishna against Rav Hisda's statement about the burnt offering needing no flaying.
Cites a baraita: before the Tabernacle private altars were allowed, and the firstborn served, and burnt offerings were flayed.
Rav Hisda: this is a tannaitic dispute over Exodus 19:22, whether it refers to the firstborn or to Nadav and Avihu.
Asks how the Nadav and Avihu reading fits with the verse about being sanctified through those near to God.
Explains that the verse is read as by My honored ones, so God is sanctified through those honored by His presence.
God told Moses this, and Aaron was silent after his sons died, receiving reward for his silence.
Cites Psalms 37:7, Ecclesiastes 3:7, and Rabbi Yohanan's reading of Psalms 68:36 about God being feared through His holy ones.
Resolves the tension with the baraita about flaying as a dispute between two tannaim.
Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva disagree on when the details of the mitzvot were given, affecting flaying before the Tabernacle.
Rav Huna derives from Genesis 8:20 that all animals and birds, including undomesticated ones, were fit for sacrifice before the Tabernacle.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's principle: male, female, unblemished and blemished are fit for animals and birds; the phrase excludes animals missing a limb.
Rabbi Elazar derives from Genesis 6:19 that an animal lacking a limb is unfit for sacrifice, even for Noah's descendants.
Challenges whether the phrase of every living being instead excludes a tereifa, and whether to keep seed alive or with you does the work.
Asks whether Noah himself was a tereifa, given the verse calling him complete.
Counters that Noah's completeness refers to his deeds, and argues Noah could not have been a tereifa.
Asks why the verse needs to say to keep seed alive if with you already excludes tereifot.
Without that phrase one might think Noah brought old or castrated animals as companions, so the phrase limits to breeding animals.
The baraita notes that only pure animals were offered before the Tabernacle, based on Noah's sacrifice.
Asks whether pure and impure categories existed in Noah's time, before the Torah's distinctions.
Rabbi Yonatan: the pure animals Noah took were those not used in any sin.
Asks how Noah and his sons knew which animals had been used in sin.
Rav Hisda: animals passed before the ark, which drew in the pure; Rabbi Abbahu: the pure came in on their own.
Quotes the Master's statement that all offerings before the Tabernacle were burnt offerings, so peace offerings were not sacrificed.
Challenges with Exodus 24:5, where peace offerings were sacrificed at Sinai before the Tabernacle, and another baraita denying it.
Resolves the baraita as following the view that Noah's descendants did not sacrifice peace offerings.
States the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina on whether Noah's descendants sacrificed peace offerings.
Reasons that Abel's offering of the fat shows peace offerings were sacrificed, since fat of an offering is burned on the altar.
Infers that the offering whose fat is burned but not wholly burned must be the peace offering.
Cites Song of Songs 4:16 to argue that the nations sacrifice only burnt offerings, and Israel also offers peace offerings.
Asks whether Abel's fats verse shows the other view that peace offerings were sacrificed.
Replies that the fat verse means the choicest animals, and the north verse refers to the ingathering of exiles.
Asks whether Moses's request for zevahim before Sinai and Yitro's sacrifice prove peace offerings existed before the Torah.
Records the dispute between Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on whether Yitro came before or after the Torah's giving.
Explains that if Yitro came before the Torah, peace offerings were sacrificed by Noah's descendants, and Yitro converted after hearing.
Rabbi Yehoshua derives from the Amalek battle verse that Yitro heard of the war, supporting his earlier arrival.
Rabbi Eliezer HaModai says Yitro heard of the giving of the Torah, when its voice carried across the world and idolaters trembled.
Cites Psalm 29:9 to show that the heavenly host said song and glory in the Temple.
Narrative: the nations gathered around Balaam, were told God swore no water flood, and God's treasure was given to Israel by Psalm 29.
Rabbi Eliezer derives that Yitro heard of the Red Sea from Joshua 5:1 and Rahab's report in Joshua 2:10.
Asks why the verse says no spirit remained in them in one case and no spirit remained in a man in the other.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains Rahab's phrase as euphemism for fear, and says her knowledge comes from reports that the princes all visited her.
Traditions about Rahab's conversion, then the ruling that gentiles today may sacrifice outside the Temple.
Asks from where the rule that gentiles may sacrifice outside the Temple is derived.
Cites Leviticus 17:2, which addresses only the Israelites, so gentiles are not commanded about outside slaughter.
Each gentile may build his own altar; Jews may not assist, though teaching them is allowed, as in Ifera Hurmiz's case with Rava.
Asks whose opinion requires new wood, perhaps that of Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua.
Quotes Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua: the wood, like the altar, must not be used by ordinary people.
Objects: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua concedes that wood for a private altar need not be new.
Cites the two verses about David's purchase of the threshing floor, which seem to give different prices.
Resolves the prices: each tribe paid fifty shekels, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and Rava explain the purchase of tools and wood.
Asks what morigim are, and explains from Isaiah 41:15 that a morag is a threshing board.
Rava teaches his son the verses and notices their apparent contradiction.
Raises the contradiction between the verses on David's purchase, one with gold shekels and one with silver.
Asks how the verses can be reconciled, since one says silver and one says gold.
Proposes that the silver shekels equalled fifty gold shekels by weight, so the total was six hundred gold.
Mishna: lesser offerings are eaten throughout the camp; Rav Huna says that means wherever Israelites were, not a fixed camp.
Rav Nahman objects with a baraita describing the camps of the wilderness and Jerusalem, which implies a fixed camp existed.
Explains that the mishna means the Israelite camp wherever it is, so meat is not disqualified if it leaves the enclosure.
Asks whether the meat might be disqualified because it leaves the camp while traveling.
Numbers 2:17 shows the Tent of Meeting and the camp keep their status while traveling.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's baraita: the women's courtyard rampart was a camp in Jerusalem, and Shiloh had only two camps.
Asks which of the three wilderness camps was absent in Shiloh.
Rabba: the Levite camp was present while the Israelite camp was not, since that camp would otherwise be missing.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that without a Levite camp, zavim and corpse-impure people would both be sent out of one camp.
Cites Numbers 5:3 and its plural camps to show each impure group needs its own specific camp.
Rava counters: if the Israelite camp was absent, zavim and lepers would share one place, but the verse says a leper dwells alone.
Concludes that all three camps were present in Shiloh, and the two-camp remark concerns refuge for unintentional killers.
A baraita says the wilderness Levite camp gave refuge to unintentional killers, drawn from Exodus 21:13.
From this the Sages say a Levite who killed unintentionally is exiled between Levite cities, and within a city he is admitted.
Asks what verse supports exiling a killer within a city where he was already admitted.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika cites Numbers 35:28, calling it his city, so the refuge applies to the same city.
Baraita: at Gilgal, vow and voluntary offerings, including meal offerings and nazirite offerings, were sacrificed on private altars, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda: any offering sacrificed in the wilderness Tent could be sacrificed at Gilgal, with private altars limited to burnt and peace offerings.
The Rabbis: only burnt and peace offerings were sacrificed on private altars, and both Tents were limited to burnt and peace offerings for individuals.
Rabbi Shimon: even the public did not sacrifice every offering at Gilgal, only Paschal offerings.

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: compulsory offerings with a set time were sacrificed on the public altar at Gilgal, untimed ones were not
What is the reason for Rabbi Meir's position
Rabbi Meir cites a verse in Deuteronomy as his source
The verse: you shall not do all that we do here today
Moses's instruction: only voluntary offerings may be brought in Eretz Yisrael, and meal and nazirite offerings count as voluntary
The Rabbis: meal offerings are never brought on private altars and nazirite offerings are obligatory
Shmuel: the dispute covers only sin and guilt offerings, while burnt and peace offerings are voluntary by consensus
Rabba raises an objection from a baraita against Shmuel
The baraita: breast, thigh and loaf teruma apply only to the great altar and not to private altars
Rabba notes the baraita omits the cooked foreleg of the nazirite's ram
If Shmuel's view is granted, the baraita that omits the nazirite's ram must follow the Rabbis, which is problematic
Rather, the view should be restated the way Shmuel actually said it
Shmuel restated: the dispute covers only burnt and peace offerings, while sin and guilt offerings are obligatory even for Rabbi Meir
Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree on what individuals and the public may offer at Gilgal
What is the reason for the Rabbis' position
The Rabbis cite a verse: a man does what is right in his own eyes
The verse refers to an individual, who may offer only voluntary offerings, while the public may offer obligatory ones too

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda reads fitting in his own eyes as a private altar, so even obligatory offerings may be brought on the great altar
But man is written, so doesn't it mean an individual may bring only voluntary offerings
Man is written to qualify a non-priest to perform the service on a private altar
The non-priest's qualification is derived from the verse saying the priest dashes the blood, implying only priests serve at the great altar
Lest one think firstborns must still perform the service, the verse teaches that each individual may sacrifice his own offerings
The Rabbis' view seems identical to the first tanna's, so what is the difference between them
Rav Pappa: the difference is whether libations were offered in the wilderness and in Gilgal
Rabbi Shimon's baraita: even the public sacrificed only Paschal and fixed-time compulsory offerings in Gilgal
What is the reason for Rabbi Shimon's opinion
A verse says the children of Israel kept the Passover in Gilgal
Isn't it obvious that the Paschal offering was brought, so the verse must teach something more
The verse teaches that only offerings similar to the Paschal offering, with a set time, were sacrificed in Gilgal
The Rabbis' reading of the verse is needed for Rabbi Yohanan's halakha
Rabbi Yohanan's halakha: an uncircumcised man who became impure from a corpse receives the sprinkling
A tanna taught the baraita in the presence of Rav Adda bar Ahava
The baraita: only Paschal and fixed-time compulsory offerings are sacrificed on a great altar and not on a private one
The baraita adds compulsory offerings with a set time
Rav Adda objects: from where would an individual get compulsory offerings with a set time, since none exist
Rav Adda suggests reading the mishna as referring to a compulsory burnt offering of an individual
Are there compulsory sin offerings with a set time at all
Let him explain it as the compulsory meal offering with a set time, the griddle-cake offering of the High Priest
Rav Adda holds that no meal offering is sacrificed on any altar outside the Temple
The mishna: when they came to Shiloh, private altars were prohibited
From where are these matters derived
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yohanan as the source of the following teaching
One verse calls the Shiloh Tabernacle a house, while another calls it a tent that God forsook
A further verse says God abhorred the tent of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim
Reconciliation: Shiloh had stone below and curtains above, so it was called both a house and a tent, a period of rest
The mishna: offerings of the most sacred order were eaten within the curtains in Shiloh
From where are these matters derived
Rabbi Oshaya cites a verse: take heed not to offer your burnt offerings in every place you see
The verse prohibits offering burnt offerings in every place that one sees
The inference: one may not offer in every place, but may eat offerings in every place one sees
Say instead that slaughtering is permitted anywhere, so it would be allowed anywhere overlooking Shiloh
Rabbi Yannai: the next verse says offer in the chosen place, so only eating is permitted elsewhere
Rabbi Avdimi bar Hasa cites a verse about the boundaries of the portions of the children of Joseph

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shiloh's fig tree teaching: whoever sees it grieves over eating his offerings
Rabbi Abbahu cites Genesis 49:22 about a fruitful son, the eye that did not want to enjoy what is not its own
Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Hanina cites Deuteronomy 33:16 with the same eye image
Baraita on the hated ones: one who sees it, not one who has a barrier between himself and it
Rabbi Shimon b. Elyakim explains the case to Rabbi Elazar: a synagogue in Me'on
Rav Pappa's teaching: seeing means seeing the whole of it, not just part of it
Rav Pappa and Rabbi Yirmeya ask about a standing viewer versus a seated one, and the matter is left unresolved
Rav Dimi: the Shekhinah rested on Israel in three places, Shiloh, Nob, Givon and Beit Olamim, but only in Benjamin's portion
Deuteronomy 33:12 says God dwells between his shoulders, so the Shekhinah rests only within Benjamin's portion
Abaye's remark in Rav Yosef's presence, a story of a child who was not made fit
Isn't it written that God forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, and abhorred the tent of Joseph
Rav Adda: the difficulty is whether the Shekhinah was in Benjamin's and the Sanhedrin in Judah's portion
Abaye: the portions were adjacent, and a strip ran from Judah's portion into Benjamin's, where the altar stood
The strip ran from Joseph's portion into Benjamin's portion, and the altar was built there
This is what is written in Joshua 16:6 about the fig tree of Shiloh
A tannaitic dispute: between the shoulders means the first Temple and second Temple, and the days of the Messiah
Rabbi Omer: the verse refers to this world and the world to come
Baraita enumerating the years the Tabernacle stood at Shiloh, Gilgal, Nob, Givon and in the wilderness
From where do we know what the Master said about the first and second years
Moses built the Tabernacle in year one and erected it in year two, with the spies sent from Gilgal, and the seven conquered and seven divided years
Caleb says he was forty years old when Moses sent him to spy the land, from Joshua 14:7
Caleb says he is now eighty-five years old, from Joshua 14:10
From where do we know the seven conquered years and the seven divided years
Answer: from the seven conquered years also being seven divided, or from Ezekiel 40:1 about the fourteenth year after the city was struck
From where do we know that the Tabernacle at Nob and Givon lasted fifty-seven years
First Samuel 4:18 says when he mentioned the ark of God
Baraita: when Eli the priest died Shiloh was destroyed and they went to Nob, and when Samuel died Nob was destroyed and they went to Givon
First Samuel 7:2 says the ark dwelt in Kiriath-Jearim twenty years, and all Israel followed God
Chronology: ten years Samuel reigned alone, then Samuel and Saul together, then two years of Saul, and seven years of David

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: First Kings 2:11: David reigned over Israel forty years, seven of them in Hebron
Second Chronicles 3:2: Solomon began building in the fourth year, leaving Shiloh 370 years less one
The Tabernacle came to Nob and Givon
From where do we know this teaching of the Sages
Deuteronomy 12:9: rest refers to Shiloh and inheritance refers to Jerusalem
Why were they divided, namely to permit eating between the two places
Resh Lakish objects to Rabbi Yohanan: second tithe should also have been taught here
Rabbi Yohanan: second tithe is derived from the ark, and since there was no ark, there was no second tithe
If so, then peace offerings and other offerings should be derived from the ark too, and they were not offered there
Rabbi Yohanan: this is the view of Rabbi Shimon, who holds the public offered only Passover and fixed-time compulsory offerings
Compulsory offerings without a fixed time were not brought in either place
Animal tithe is compulsory without a fixed time and is linked to grain tithe by a verse
Does this imply that Rabbi Yehuda holds such offerings may be brought
Rav Adda bar Matna said second tithe and animal tithe are eaten in Nob and Givon, according to Rabbi Yehuda
Rav Yosef taught three high places, Shiloh, Nob and Givon, and Beit Olamim, and explained the eating of second tithe
The Tabernacle came to Jerusalem
A baraita: for you have not come to the rest and the inheritance, rest is Shiloh and inheritance is Jerusalem
Jeremiah 12:8 says my inheritance is like a lion in the forest
Jeremiah 12:9 says my inheritance is a spotted hyena with birds around it
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree on which of rest and inheritance refers to Jerusalem and which to Shiloh
Psalms 132:13-14: this is my rest forever, for God chose Zion as his dwelling
If rest is Shiloh, the verse order fits; but if rest is Jerusalem, why does the verse say inheritance first
The order shows that you did not reach rest, and even did not reach inheritance either
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: both rest and inheritance refer to Shiloh
Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai: both rest and inheritance refer to Jerusalem
Granted, for the one who says rest is Shiloh, but what of the one who says rest is Jerusalem

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shiloh is the inheritance and Jerusalem the rest, or the reverse, and this is what is written
Deuteronomy 12:9: you have not yet come to the rest and to the inheritance
For the one who says both are Shiloh or both Jerusalem, why does the verse need both words
Granted for the one who says both are Shiloh: rest refers to the conquest and inheritance refers to the division there
Joshua 18:10: Joshua divided the land and cast lots for them in Shiloh before the Lord
But for the one who says both are Jerusalem, inheritance is eternal, so what is rest
Rest refers to the rest of the ark, as written: when the ark rested
Granted for the one who says both are Jerusalem, but Shiloh had high places, so the ark's rest is in Jerusalem
Judges 13:19: Manoah took the kid and the meal offering and offered upon the rock to the Lord
For the one who says both are Shiloh, why were high places forbidden there, given Manoah offered on one
Manoah's offering was a temporary ruling, a horaat shaah, made for that occasion only
A baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai: both are Jerusalem, and a mnemonic is given
All sacrifices, as the Gemara begins its discussion
Rav Kahana: the rule applies only to slaughter, but for offering up on the altar one is also liable for karet
What is the reason for Rav Kahana's view
Leviticus 17:8: the verse says to them you shall say, and to those who adjoin them
Rabbah objects: the text says upon them, so the verse is read differently
The text is read ve-aleihem, and furthermore a baraita is taught on this point
Rabbi Shimon's baraita of four categories: sanctified and slaughtered in the time of prohibition of high places, with or without karet
The remaining categories of the baraita: sanctified in permitted high places and offered outside, with no liability at all
This baraita is a refutation of Rav Kahana
And these are the sacrifices, the Gemara begins a new list
Semikha is from Leviticus 1:3, and northern slaughter from Leviticus 1:11, before the Lord
Sprinkling around the altar, from Leviticus 1:5
Waving, from Leviticus 14:12
Bringing near to the altar, from Leviticus 2:8
Rabbi Yehuda says there is no meal offering on a high place
Rav Sheshet: whoever holds there is a meal offering on a high place also holds there are birds, and vice versa
Leviticus 17:5: the sacrifices and not meal offerings, the sacrifices and not birds
Leviticus 17:6 says the priest sprinkles, with the garments of service and vessels of service from Exodus 28:43 and Numbers 4:12
Leviticus 1:9: an offering of pleasing aroma to the Lord
Exodus 27:5: the grate shall reach halfway up the altar, a barrier for the blood
Exodus 40:32: when they approach the altar they wash, the washing of hands
Rami bar Hama: the rule was taught only for small-altar sacrifices offered on the small altar, and there is a requirement of hitzui
Rabbah objects: chazeh, shoulder and teruma of loaves are practiced for great-altar sacrifices only, perhaps on the high places
Some say that Rami bar Hama taught the opposite distinction
Rami bar Hama's view restated: only great-altar sacrifices offered on the great altar, but small-altar sacrifices, even offered on the great altar, need hitzui
Let this support Rami bar Hama: say instead that chazeh and shoulder are practiced for great-altar sacrifices but not small ones, on the high places
Rabbi Elazar rules: a burnt offering of an individual on a high place that he brought inside, the partitions catch it for everything
Rabbi Zeira asks about a burnt offering of an individual on a high place

120a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If an offering was brought inside and taken out, does the partition still catch it, given it returned, and is this the dispute of Rava and Rav Yosef
Mishnah: sacrifices slaughtered in the south are invalid, and if they went up they did not come down
If they came down, may they go up again
Rava says they may not go up, while Rav Yosef says they may go up
Asked of Rava and of Rav Yosef, is it the same question for each
Rava's view applies only to an altar that is fit for the offering, and a partition catches a sacrifice that is not fit
Perhaps even for Rav Yosef the partition catches it, so Rav Yosef's view is unclear
Rav Yosef: there the altar is a single place, but here the two places are distinct
Or perhaps there is no difference between the cases, and the matter is left unresolved
The point clear to Rava on one side and Rav Yosef on the other must be asked of Rabbi Yannai
Rabbi Yannai asks about an individual burnt offering that went up and came down, where the fire had or did not have a hold, and it is left unresolved
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether night slaughter of an individual high place offering is valid or invalid
They dispute based on a ruling of Rabbi Elazar
Two verses of Rabbi Elazar's contradict each other
First Samuel 14:33: you have dealt treacherously, roll a great stone to me today
First Samuel 14:34: bring to me each man his ox and slaughter it here, and do not sin by eating with the blood
One resolves the contradiction by distinguishing non-sacred from sacred, and the other by distinguishing great and small high places
Burnt offering of an individual on a high place: Rav says it needs no flaying and dissection, Rabbi Yohanan says it does
A baraita: Rabbi Yose the Galilean says burnt offerings in the wilderness need no flaying and dissection until the Tent of Meeting
One view makes no distinction between great and small altars; the other requires a great altar; the baraita follows Rabbi Yohanan
Baraita: matters that differ between great and small altars, such as horn, ramp, base, laver and chazeh and shoulder
Baraita: matters that make the small altar equal to the great, such as slaughter, flaying, dissection, blood, blemish and time
From where do we learn that time in a small high place is like time in a great high place
The verse says piggul shall be burned, and piggul is invalid on a high place, so the same holds for the small one
The Torah says the leftover shall be burned, and leftover is kosher on a high place, so likewise for small high places
Isn't this a kal vachomer from birds

120b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A kal vachomer: as a blemish invalidates a small high place offering, and time invalidates it too, so time should invalidate birds
Birds differ: a non-priest is never fit to offer them
Objection: in a small high place a non-priest is fit, so time should not invalidate there
Leviticus 7:11 teaches that the time of a peace offering in a small high place equals that in a great high place
Closing formula: the end of the chapter Parah Hatatat, and the tractate Zevachim is complete
